teile.einleitung: The degree Fahrenheit is a unit of temperature used mainly in the USA. The freezing point of water is at 32 °F, the boiling point at 212 °F. The scale was invented by the physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1724.
wichtigste: The Fahrenheit scale was proposed by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1724.
0 °C equals 32 °F, and 100 °C equals 212 °F.
You convert Celsius into Fahrenheit by multiplying by 1.8 and adding 32.
20 °C is 68 °F, and 50 °F is 10 °C.
At minus 40 degrees the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same value.
The normal body temperature of 37 °C equals 98.6 °F.
Fahrenheit fixed the zero point with a freezing mixture of ice, water and sal ammoniac.

abschnitte.text: The **degree Fahrenheit**, abbreviated °F, is a unit of temperature like the degree Celsius. Between the freezing point of water at 32 °F and the boiling point at 212 °F there are 180 Fahrenheit degrees. In Celsius there are only 100 degrees, which is why a Fahrenheit degree is smaller. One degree Celsius equals 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit.

**Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit** was born in Danzig in 1686 and died in The Hague in 1736. He built very accurate thermometers and was one of the first to use mercury in them. In 1724 he proposed his temperature scale. He fixed the zero point with a **freezing mixture** of ice, water and sal ammoniac, the coldest temperature he could produce in the laboratory at that time.

To convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit: multiply by 1.8 and add 32. So 20 °C is exactly 68 °F and 37 °C exactly 98.6 °F. The other way round, you first subtract 32 and then divide by 1.8, so 50 °F becomes exactly 10 °C. At **minus 40 degrees** both scales are the same; this is the only such point.

Today it is mainly the **USA** that uses degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life, for example in the weather forecast or when baking. Some smaller countries in the Caribbean and the Pacific also use it. Most countries in the world, including Switzerland, measure temperature in degrees Celsius. In science people calculate with **kelvin**, where 0 kelvin is absolute zero at minus 273.15 °C.

Anyone travelling to the USA should know the rule of thumb: values around 70 °F feel pleasantly warm. At 32 °F it freezes, and above 90 °F it is very hot. A fever of 104 °F equals 40 °C. Many oven recipes from America give temperatures such as 350 °F, which is about 175 °C.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed system of numbers used to measure how warm or cold something is.
The temperature at which water turns into ice: 0 °C or 32 °F.
The temperature at which water boils: 100 °C or 212 °F at sea level.
A mixture, for example of ice and salt, that gets colder than pure ice.
The unit of temperature in science, which starts at absolute zero.

gewusst: At minus 40 degrees it makes no difference whether you say Celsius or Fahrenheit; both show the same number.
Fahrenheit was originally a merchant and taught himself how to make measuring instruments.
The Celsius scale was proposed only about 20 years after the Fahrenheit scale.

teile.einleitung: The gram is a unit of mass used to weigh light things. One gram is a thousandth of a kilogram, which is very little: a paper clip weighs about that much. The symbol for gram is a small g.
wichtigste: The gram is a unit of mass, abbreviated g.
1000 grams make 1 kilogram.
A paper clip weighs about one gram.
A standard bar of chocolate weighs 100 grams.
A five-franc coin weighs about 13 grams.
One millilitre of water weighs about one gram.
Very small masses are measured in milligrams, a thousandth of a gram.

abschnitte.text: The **gram** is a unit of mass, that is of how heavy something is. It is a thousandth of a **kilogram**, which is the base unit in the International System of Units. So 1000 grams are 1 kilogram, which is why 1 kilogram is more than 900 grams. The word comes from the Greek gramma, which originally meant a small weight.

The gram was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century, when the metric system was invented. At that time it was decided that one gram is the mass of one cubic centimetre of **water** at the temperature of melting ice. That is why a millilitre of water still weighs about one gram today. A litre of water accordingly weighs about one kilogram.

A paper clip weighs about 1 gram, a sheet of A4 printer paper about 5 grams. A Fünfliber, the five-franc coin, weighs about 13 grams. A standard **bar of chocolate** has 100 grams, a hen's egg about 60 grams. Two packets of butter of 250 grams each make 500 grams together, which in Switzerland is a pound.

Many small animals are weighed in grams, for example a **mouse**, which often weighs only 20 to 30 grams. The smallest hummingbirds weigh only about 2 grams. An ant weighs much less than a gram, often only a few **milligrams**. That is why it would take hundreds of ants to make a single gram.

On food it says how many grams are in the packet, for example 500 g of pasta. The nutrition table usually shows how much sugar, fat and protein there is in **100 grams**. This makes it easy to compare different products. When baking, too, you weigh out flour and sugar in grams with kitchen scales.

A **milligram** is a thousandth of a gram, a microgram a millionth of a gram. The active ingredient in medicines, for example, is given in these units. For gemstones the carat is used; one carat equals 0.2 grams. Gold and silver are often traded in grams, because even small amounts cost a lot of money.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that shows how much matter a body has and how heavy it is.
1000 grams, the base unit of mass.
A thousandth of a gram.
A device used to determine mass.

gewusst: A five-franc coin weighs about as much as thirteen paper clips together.
In everyday life in Switzerland, a pound means 500 grams.
A single grain of rice weighs only about a fiftieth of a gram.

teile.einleitung: Isotopes are different kinds of atoms of the same chemical element. They have the same number of protons in the nucleus but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different weights. Some isotopes are stable; others decay and give off radiation as they do so.
wichtigste: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes whose nuclei do not decay are called stable isotopes.
Carbon-12 is by far the most common isotope of carbon.
Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons and is radioactive.
Archaeologists use carbon-14 to work out the age of finds.
Deuterium is hydrogen with one proton and one neutron; tritium has two neutrons.
With ten stable isotopes, tin has the most of all the elements.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a nucleus made of **protons** and **neutrons**. The number of protons decides which element it is: carbon always has 6 protons. But the number of neutrons can vary, and this creates different **isotopes**. They are named after the total number of particles in the nucleus, for example carbon-12 or carbon-14.

The word isotope comes from Greek and means same place. This refers to the fact that all isotopes of an element are in the same place in the periodic table. The term was coined by the British chemist **Frederick Soddy** in 1913. With a mass spectrometer, isotopes can be separated by their mass and measured precisely.

Isotopes whose nuclei do not decay are called **stable isotopes**. Other isotopes are unstable and decay over time; they are radioactive. Carbon-12 makes up almost 99 per cent of natural carbon and is stable. Carbon-14, with 6 protons and 8 neutrons, on the other hand, is radioactive and occurs only in tiny amounts. With ten naturally occurring stable isotopes, tin holds the record among the elements.

Ordinary hydrogen has just one proton and no neutron. The isotope with one proton and one neutron is called **deuterium**, and it is twice as heavy. Water made from deuterium is called heavy water. The isotope with two neutrons is called tritium; it is radioactive and is used, for example, in self-luminous watch hands.

Living things take in carbon throughout their lives, including a little carbon-14. After death this isotope slowly decays, and its amount halves in about 5730 years. By measuring how much is left, you can work out the age of bones, wood or remains of cloth. This **radiocarbon method** was developed by the American Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.

In nuclear power stations such as Gösgen, the isotope **uranium-235** is split; it makes up only about 0.7 per cent of natural uranium. In medicine, radioactive isotopes help make organs visible or treat diseases, for example iodine-131 for the thyroid. Researchers study isotopes in ice cores to find out about the climate of past times. The age of the Earth was also worked out with isotopes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
Particle with no charge in the atomic nucleus.
Substance made of atoms with the same number of protons, for example gold or oxygen.
Table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.

gewusst: Heavy water looks like normal water, but an ice cube made from it sinks to the bottom in ordinary water.
Using isotopes in tooth enamel, researchers can find out in which area a person grew up thousands of years ago.
Of the 118 known elements, only about 80 have any stable isotopes at all.

teile.einleitung: Church bells are large metal bells that hang in church towers and can be heard far across a village or town. They call people to worship, show the time and ring at celebrations. In terms of physics they are fascinating sources of sound that keep ringing for a long time after being struck.
wichtigste: Church bells are usually made of bronze, a mixture of copper and tin.
Bells are cast, which means liquid metal is poured into a mould.
Many church bells strike every full hour and so show the time.
On Sundays the bells often ring for a long time before the service.
The largest bell in Switzerland weighs about 10 tonnes.
Zurich's Sechseläuten gets its name from the ringing of bells at six o'clock.
The larger and heavier a bell is, the lower it sounds.

abschnitte.text: A bell has the shape of an upside-down cup. At the top is the **crown**, by which it hangs in the bell frame. Inside hangs the **clapper**, a heavy metal striker. When the bell swings back and forth, the clapper hits the thick rim, the **sound bow**. Many bells carry inscriptions, decorations and the year they were cast.

Church bells are usually made of **bronze**, mixed from about four parts copper and one part tin. First the bell founder builds a mould out of clay that has exactly the shape of the bell. Then the metal is melted at over 1000 degrees and **cast** into the mould. A large bell then has to cool slowly for days. Only then is the mould broken, the bell cleaned and its sound tested.

When the bell is struck, all the metal starts to **vibrate**. Many notes are produced at the same time, and together they make the typical sound of a bell. Large, heavy bells vibrate more slowly and sound lower, while small bells sound higher. Several bells in one tower are usually tuned so that they sound well together; this is called a **ring of bells**. The note of a large bell can still be heard after a minute.

Church bells invite people to **worship**, and on Sundays they often ring for a long time beforehand. Many bells strike every full hour and so show the time, often every quarter of an hour as well. They ring at weddings, baptisms and funerals and on major holidays. In the past bells also warned of fire, storms or danger. In Switzerland the bells ring in many places on the evening of 1 August for the national holiday.

The largest bell in Switzerland hangs in **Bern Minster** and weighs about 10 tonnes. Zurich's **Sechseläuten** in spring recalls the old ringing of bells at six o'clock in the evening, which used to announce the end of the working day in the summer half of the year. At this festival the Böögg, a large artificial snowman, is burnt. Switzerland still has bell foundries that make new bells and repair old ones. Cowbells and the large cowbells called Treicheln are also part of Swiss tradition, but they are made differently.

begriffe.erklaerung: A metal mixture of copper and tin that is hard and sounds beautiful.
The heavy striker inside the bell that hits its rim.
All the bells of a church tower together, tuned to each other.
The structure in the tower from which the bells hang.

gewusst: The largest bell in the world, the Tsar Bell in Moscow, has never really rung, because a piece broke off.
In the past bells were often cast right next to the church, because transporting them was too difficult.
The sound of a bell depends so much on its shape that even small differences in the thickness of the wall change the note.

teile.einleitung: In physics a lever is a rigid body that can turn about a fixed axis and transmits forces. With the law of the lever you can calculate exactly how much force is needed to lift a load. The lever is one of the simple machines, like the pulley, the wedge and the inclined plane.
wichtigste: A lever is a rigid body that can turn around a pivot.
The law of the lever says: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.
With a long effort arm you need less force, but you have to move further.
A distinction is made between one-sided and two-sided levers.
If a much heavier child sits on a seesaw, its side sinks down.
A lever saves force, but not work.
Archimedes formulated the law of the lever in the 3rd century BC.

abschnitte.text: A lever is in **balance** when effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. The **effort arm** is the distance from the pivot to the place where the force acts, and the load arm is the distance to the load. An example: a load of 600 N hangs 0.5 m from the pivot. If you push 3 m from the pivot, 100 N is enough to hold it in balance.

In a **two-sided lever** the pivot lies between the effort and the load, as with the seesaw, the scissors or the crowbar. In a **one-sided lever** the effort and the load are on the same side of the pivot. Examples are the wheelbarrow, the nutcracker and the bottle opener. The forearm is also a one-sided lever, with the muscle attached close to the elbow.

A lever is not a magic trick; it only saves force. Whatever you save in force, you have to make up in extra distance. If you lift a load with half the force, the end of the lever has to be moved twice as far. This rule is called the **golden rule of mechanics** and applies to all simple machines.

In physics the product of force and lever arm is called **torque**, measured in newton metres. A lever is in balance when the torques on both sides are equal. That is why screws are easier to undo with a long spanner. On a bike, too, the length of the pedals and the gear wheels decide what torque acts.

The classic **beam balance** is a two-sided lever with arms of equal length. If both sides are equally heavy, the beam is level. With a steelyard, a small weight is moved along a long arm to weigh heavy loads. Scales like these used to be used often on farms and at markets in Switzerland.

The Greek mathematician **Archimedes** of Syracuse described the law of the lever mathematically in the 3rd century BC. But levers were used much earlier, for example in building large stone structures and in sweep wells. In the Middle Ages levers powered catapults and presses. Today levers are found in diggers, cranes and brake pedals.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts.
The distance from the pivot to the load.
Force times lever arm; it tells you how strongly something is turned.
A basic device that changes forces, such as a lever, pulley or wedge.

gewusst: A construction crane uses a heavy counterweight on the short arm so that it can carry large loads on the long arm.
Many bones in the body act as levers that gain distance rather than force, so that we can throw and run fast.
A rubber doorstop works better if you push it under the door far away from the hinges.

teile.einleitung: The calorie is an old unit of energy, especially of heat. Today we come across it almost only on food packaging, where it shows how much energy a food gives the body. The official unit of energy, however, is the joule.
wichtigste: Originally a calorie was the energy that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius.
When people talk about “calories” in everyday life, they usually mean kilocalories.
One kilocalorie is 1000 calories and equals about 4.2 kilojoules.
The calorie is not an SI unit; the SI unit of energy is the joule.
One gram of fat provides about 9 kilocalories.
One gram of protein or carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories.
Swiss food usually shows both figures, kilojoules and kilocalories.

abschnitte.text: The word **calorie** comes from the Latin “calor”, which means heat. Originally a calorie was the amount of heat needed to warm 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. This amount is very small, so people usually work with the **kilocalorie**, abbreviated kcal. One kilocalorie warms a whole litre of water by 1 degree. When a packet or a conversation mentions “calories”, it almost always means kilocalories.

In the international system of units, the **SI**, energy is measured in **joules**, named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. One kilocalorie equals 4.184 kilojoules, or about 4.2 kJ. A yoghurt with 100 kcal therefore provides about 420 kJ. Because the joule applies to all forms of energy, such as electricity, movement and heat, everything can easily be compared with it. That is why the calorie is hardly used in science and technology any more.

The body gets energy from three **nutrients**: fat, protein and carbohydrates. One gram of fat provides about 9 kcal, and one gram of protein or carbohydrate about 4 kcal each. A snack with 20 grams of fat therefore provides about 180 kcal from the fat alone. The 7 grams of protein in a glass of milk provide about 28 kcal. You can read such figures in the **nutrition table** on a packet.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs energy for
abschnitte.text: The body needs energy all the time, even when asleep, for example for the heartbeat, breathing and keeping a steady body temperature. This basic need is called the **basal metabolic rate**. Anyone who moves, does sport or is growing needs extra energy. Children and teenagers need a lot of energy because their bodies are still growing. What matters is not just the amount but also a balanced diet with vegetables, fruit and wholegrain products.

The energy content of a food can be measured with a **calorimeter**. A small sample is burnt in a closed container surrounded by water. From how much the water warms up, you calculate how much energy was in the sample. Today the figures on packets are usually calculated from the amount of fat, protein and carbohydrates. The figures are often given per 100 grams and sometimes also per portion.

begriffe.erklaerung: 1000 calories, abbreviated kcal, the usual figure on food.
The official unit of energy in the international system of units.
The energy the body needs at complete rest for its life processes.
A measuring device used to find out how much heat is released in a process.

gewusst: The energy in a bar of chocolate would be enough to bring several litres of cold water to the boil.
Water also has a place in the nutrition table, but it provides zero kilocalories.
One gram of fat provides more than twice as much energy as one gram of sugar.

teile.einleitung: A cooker is a kitchen appliance on which you cook, fry and heat food. It turns electricity or gas into heat, which is passed on to pots and pans through hotplates or flames. Today there are different kinds of cooker that work in quite different ways.
wichtigste: On a cooker the hotplate gets hot and passes the heat on to the pan.
A hotplate stays hot for a long time after cooking.
On many ceramic hobs a glowing “H” shows that the plate is still hot.
An induction hob needs pans with iron in the base.
You can use a magnet to check whether a pan is suitable for induction.
On a gas cooker a blue flame burns.
There is often an oven built in under the hob.

abschnitte.text: A cooker usually consists of a **hob** with two to five cooking zones and often an **oven** underneath. In Switzerland most households cook with electricity. In the past people cooked with wood or coal on a brick stove, which also heated the kitchen. Electric cookers spread from the first half of the 20th century.

Older cookers have round **cast-iron hotplates** with a heating wire inside. When current flows through it, the wire gets hot, much as in a toaster. On a **ceramic hob** the heating elements lie under a smooth glass plate and make the cooking zones glow red. A glowing “H” warns that the surface is still hot, even when it is no longer glowing.

An **induction hob** uses a coil under the glass plate to create a rapidly changing magnetic field. This field makes electric currents flow in the iron-containing base of the pan, which heat the pan directly. The glass plate itself only gets warm from the hot pan. That is why you need pans with iron in the base, which you can easily test with a **magnet**: if it sticks, the pan is suitable.

On a **gas cooker** natural gas or bottled gas flows out of a burner and is lit. With a good air supply the flame burns blue, because the gas burns completely. Gas cookers can be adjusted very quickly, which is why they are popular in many restaurant kitchens. In Swiss homes, however, they are rather rare.

The hotplate should be about the same size as the base of the pan, otherwise a lot of heat is lost. A **lid** on the pan saves a lot of energy, because less heat escapes with the steam. Pan handles are turned inwards so that nobody catches on them. Burning fat must never be put out with water; instead you cover the pan with a lid.

begriffe.erklaerung: Top part of the cooker with the cooking zones.
Production of electric current by a changing magnetic field.
Heat-resistant, smooth material under which the heating elements lie.
Glowing sign that warns that a plate is still hot.

gewusst: An induction hob stays cold if you just put a sheet of paper on the cooking zone, because paper contains no iron.
Putting out burning oil with water can cause a dangerous burst of flame.
Cooking with a lid needs much less energy than without; you often save more than a third.

teile.einleitung: An igloo is a dome-shaped house made of snow blocks. Traditionally the Inuit in the Arctic built igloos as shelter for the winter or for hunting trips. Although it is made of snow, it is much warmer inside than outside in the icy wind.
wichtigste: An igloo is a snow hut shaped like a dome.
Traditionally the Inuit in Canada and Greenland built igloos.
The blocks are best cut from firm, compacted snow.
Snow contains a lot of air and therefore insulates very well.
The inside is warmed mainly by the body heat of the people.
The entrance is small and low so that little heat escapes.
Inside it is only a little warmer than zero degrees, so the igloo does not melt away.

abschnitte.text: The word **igloo** comes from the language of the Inuit and simply means house. In English, though, it means the round hut made of snow. The **Inuit** live in the cold regions of northern Canada, Alaska and Greenland. In the past, hunters on the move built an igloo in a few hours to spend the night in it. Today the Inuit live in permanent houses but still know how to build igloos.

With a long knife or a saw you cut blocks from firm **snow** that has been compacted by the wind. Loose powder snow is no good because it crumbles. The blocks are stacked in a spiral that gets narrower towards the top. This creates a **dome** that supports itself without any props. Gaps are filled with snow, and a small air hole is often left at the top.

Snow consists largely of trapped air, and air conducts heat poorly. That is why the snow wall acts like thick **insulation**, rather like a down jacket. The body heat of the people and sometimes a small blubber lamp heat the room. Outside it can be minus 30 degrees, while inside it often stays around zero degrees. Because it hardly gets above zero inside, the wall melts slightly at the surface at most and then freezes into a smooth, solid layer of ice.

The entrance is a low tunnel that lies lower than the living space. Warm air rises and cold air sinks. The cold air therefore stays trapped in the low entrance as if in a **cold trap**. The sleeping places are on a raised snow bench, where the warmest air is. Furs on the bench give extra protection from the cold below.

In the Swiss Alps, too, mountaineers, scouts and families build igloos, whether for fun or as emergency shelter. Some ski areas have igloo villages in winter where guests can even spend the night. To build your own igloo you need enough firm snow, patience and ideally experienced helpers. An **air hole** is always important so that enough fresh air gets in.

begriffe.erklaerung: A people who live in the cold regions of Canada, Alaska and Greenland.
A round, curved roof that looks like half a ball.
A layer that stops heat or cold from getting through.
A low spot where heavy, cold air collects.

gewusst: A skilled Inuit hunter could build a small igloo in about an hour.
An igloo dome is so stable that an adult can often stand on it.
In the language of the Inuit, the word igloo simply means house.

teile.einleitung: The kelvin is the unit of temperature that researchers all over the world calculate with. Unlike degrees Celsius, the kelvin scale starts right at the bottom at absolute zero, the coldest temperature there can possibly be. That is why there are no negative values in kelvin.
wichtigste: The kelvin (symbol K) is a base unit of the International System of Units (SI).
It is named after William Thomson, who became known as Lord Kelvin.
0 kelvin is absolute zero, which is at minus 273.15 °C.
0 °C equals 273.15 K, and 100 °C equals 373.15 K.
A temperature difference of 1 kelvin is exactly the same size as 1 degree Celsius.
Kelvin is written without a degree sign, for example 300 K.
A temperature in kelvin is called an absolute temperature.

abschnitte.text: The **kelvin** is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, **SI** for short. It is used to measure absolute temperature. The kelvin scale starts at the lowest possible point and so has no negative values. Temperatures in kelvin are written without the ° sign, so 300 K and not 300 °K.

**Absolute zero** is at 0 K, which is minus 273.15 °C. The colder a substance is, the more slowly its tiniest particles move. At absolute zero they would have the least possible movement; it cannot get any colder. This point can never quite be reached, but researchers in laboratories get to within tiny fractions of a kelvin.

To convert from degrees Celsius to kelvin, you add 273.15. So 0 °C is 273.15 K, and 373.15 K is 100 °C, the boiling point of water. If you simplify and use 273, then minus 73 °C is exactly 200 K. For temperature differences you do not need to convert anything: if the temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C, it has risen by 10 K.

The unit is named after **William Thomson**, who lived from 1824 to 1907. He was an important physicist in Scotland and taught in Glasgow. Because he was so famous, he was made a lord in 1892 with the title Lord Kelvin, named after a small river near his university. He realised that there must be a lowest temperature and proposed an absolute temperature scale.

abschnitte.titel: Kelvin in science and everyday life
abschnitte.text: In physics and chemistry people almost always calculate with kelvin, for example in the gas laws. You will also find kelvin on light bulb packaging as the **colour temperature**: about 2700 K means cosy warm white light, higher values mean bluish cold light. The surface of the Sun is about 5800 K hot. Space has a background temperature of only about 2.7 K.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest possible temperature, 0 K or minus 273.15 °C.
Basic unit from which other units are derived, for example the metre, the second or the kelvin.
Temperature measured in kelvin from absolute zero.
Figure in kelvin that describes whether light looks warm or cold.

gewusst: With kelvin you do not say “degrees kelvin”, just “kelvin”.
The superconducting magnets in the LHC particle accelerator near Geneva are cooled to about 1.9 K, which makes them colder than space.
Lord Kelvin also helped to lay the first telegraph cable across the Atlantic.

teile.einleitung: The joule is the unit used to measure energy, work and heat. Whether you lift a bar of chocolate, make a lamp shine or heat water, the energy can always be given in joules. The unit is named after the English scientist James Prescott Joule.
wichtigste: The joule (symbol J) is the unit of energy, work and heat in the International System of Units.
One joule is the work done by a force of 1 newton over a distance of 1 metre.
One joule is exactly the same as one watt second.
To lift a 100 g bar of chocolate one metre you need about 1 joule.
Power is not measured in joules but in watts.
James Prescott Joule showed that mechanical work can be turned into heat.
1000 joules are one kilojoule, a million joules are one megajoule.

abschnitte.text: The **joule** is the unit of energy. Energy is found in movement, in heat, in light, in electric current and in food. Because energy can be turned from one form into another, all these forms are measured with the same unit. The symbol for the joule is a capital J.

In physics you do **work** when a force moves something over a distance. You calculate force times distance: 1 newton times 1 metre gives 1 joule. If you push a box with 50 newtons for 4 metres, you do 50 times 4, or 200 joules of work. A 100 g bar of chocolate weighs about 1 newton, so you need about 1 joule to lift it one metre.

**Power** tells you how much energy is converted per second and is measured in watts. One watt means 1 joule per second, so 1 joule is the same as one **watt second**. A 10 watt LED lamp therefore uses 10 times 60, or 600 joules, in one minute. The electricity bill shows kilowatt hours; one kilowatt hour equals 3.6 million joules or 3.6 megajoules.

On food packaging you find the energy content in **kilojoules** (kJ) and also in kilocalories. One kilocalorie equals about 4.2 kilojoules. A bar of chocolate contains more than 2000 kilojoules, in other words more than two million joules. This shows that a single joule is quite a small amount of energy.

**James Prescott Joule** lived from 1818 to 1889 in England and came from a brewing family. In famous experiments he let a falling weight turn a paddle wheel in a container of water. He measured that the water warmed up a tiny bit. In this way he showed that mechanical work can be turned into heat and that energy is not lost.

For large amounts of energy, prefixes are used. One kilojoule is 1000 joules, so 2.5 kilojoules are exactly 2500 joules. One **megajoule** is a million joules or 1000 kilojoules, so 3.6 megajoules equal 3600 kilojoules. For very large amounts there are also gigajoules and terajoules.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to move something, heat it or make it shine.
Force times distance, the energy you use when moving something.
Energy that a 1 watt device uses in one second, exactly 1 joule.
1000 joules, often given on food packaging.

gewusst: If you climb one storey of about 3 metres and weigh 40 kilograms, you already do about 1200 joules of work.
The old energy unit, the calorie, is no longer used in physics today, but it is still given on food.
Joule is even said to have tried to measure the temperature difference between the top and bottom of a waterfall on his honeymoon.

teile.einleitung: A gyroscope is a fast-spinning top that stubbornly keeps the direction of its axis of rotation. This property makes it a brilliant measuring device for position and rotation. Gyroscopes are found in aeroplanes, satellites and even in every smartphone.
wichtigste: A gyroscope is a fast-spinning top that keeps the direction of its axis.
The French physicist Léon Foucault gave the device its name in 1852.
In a gimbal mounting the spinning wheel can point freely in any direction.
The artificial horizon in an aeroplane uses a gyroscope to show the position relative to the horizon.
Tiny micromechanical gyroscopes in smartphones measure rotations with the help of the Coriolis force.
Ring laser gyroscopes are based on the Sagnac effect and have no moving parts at all.
The Gravity Probe B satellite mission tested the general theory of relativity with extremely precise gyroscopes.

abschnitte.text: A gyroscope consists of a heavy, fast-spinning wheel or top. As long as it is spinning, it resists tilting its **axis of rotation**. Physicists speak of **angular momentum**, which is conserved. If you try to tilt the axis anyway, the gyroscope moves out of the way to the side. This strange sideways movement is called **precession**.

In 1852 the French physicist **Léon Foucault** studied such a spinning top. He wanted to use it to show that the Earth turns. He called the device a gyroscope, from the Greek words for “circle” and “to look at”. Foucault also became famous for his pendulum, which likewise makes the Earth's rotation visible. So that the wheel can turn freely, it is hung in a **gimbal mounting** made of rings that can turn inside each other.

In the cockpit the **artificial horizon** shows the pilots how the aeroplane is tilted relative to the ground. It works with a gyroscope that keeps its position even when the aeroplane turns. This is especially important in clouds or at night, when you cannot see the real horizon. Ships use the gyrocompass, which points north independently of magnetic fields. Rockets and submarines are also steered with gyroscopes.

Smartphones, games consoles and drones contain tiny **micromechanical gyroscopes** that are smaller than a grain of rice. They contain no spinning wheels, but vibrating structures made of silicon. When you turn the device, the Coriolis force deflects the vibration slightly. A chip measures this deflection and works out the rotation from it. In this way the phone knows how you are holding it, and games react to your movements.

A **ring laser gyroscope** sends laser light in two directions around a closed path. If the device turns, one beam of light takes a little longer than the other; this is the Sagnac effect. Satellites often change their position with **reaction wheels**: if you change the speed of a wheel, the satellite turns in the opposite direction, without any fuel. The Gravity Probe B mission was launched in 2004 with four almost perfectly round quartz spheres as gyroscopes. It confirmed two predictions of Einstein's general theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of the momentum of a turning movement.
The sideways movement of the axis when you try to tilt a spinning top.
Rings that can turn inside each other, in which an object can freely point in any direction.
An apparent force that deflects moving things sideways in a turning system.

gewusst: One of the reasons a moving bike tips over less easily is that the wheels behave like gyroscopes.
The quartz spheres of Gravity Probe B were among the roundest objects ever made.
The Hubble Space Telescope points very precisely at distant stars with the help of gyroscopes.

teile.einleitung: An insulator is a material that does not conduct electric current, or hardly at all. Insulators protect us from electric shocks; one example is the plastic sheath around a cable. In electrical engineering, the porcelain or glass parts from which power lines hang are also called insulators.
wichtigste: Insulators are materials that do not conduct electric current.
Examples are plastic, rubber, glass, porcelain, dry wood and dry air.
The plastic sheath of a cable stops current flowing into your hand.
In insulators there are almost no freely moving charge carriers.
At very high voltage even an insulator can break down.
On pylons the lines hang from insulators made of porcelain, glass or plastic.
Water with dissolved substances conducts electricity, which is why wet hands are dangerous.

abschnitte.text: An **insulator** is the opposite of a conductor. In metals such as copper, electrons can move freely and so carry current. In insulators the electrons are tightly bound to their atoms. That is why hardly any current can flow there.

Every cable consists of a copper wire in the middle and plastic **insulation** on the outside. Plugs, sockets and light switches also have plastic casings. Tools for electricians have insulated handles. Many devices carry a symbol of two squares, one inside the other, which stands for **double insulation**.

High-voltage lines carry voltages of several hundred thousand volts. To stop the current flowing down the pylon into the ground, the wires hang from long chains of porcelain, glass or plastic. These parts are also called insulators. Their ribbed shape makes the path along the surface longer, so that no current can creep along it when it rains.

Every insulator only holds up to a certain voltage. If this is exceeded, the current suddenly jumps through the material; this is called **breakdown**. Lightning is a breakdown through the air, which normally insulates well. Moisture and dirt can also weaken insulators.

Completely pure water conducts electricity very poorly. But tap water, sweat and sea water contain dissolved salts and therefore conduct well. That is why you must never use electrical devices with wet hands or in the bath. In Swiss bathrooms, **residual current devices** therefore provide protection by switching off the current in a flash when there is danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material that conducts current well, for example copper.
Protective covering made of non-conducting material.
Sudden flow of current through an insulator when the voltage is too high.
Tiny, negatively charged particle that carries current in conductors.

gewusst: Diamond is a very good electrical insulator but conducts heat better than copper.
Birds can sit on a power line because they touch only one wire and no current flows through them to the earth.
The first insulators for telegraph lines in the 19th century were often made of glass.

teile.einleitung: The kilowatt hour is the unit used to measure electrical energy in the home. Every electricity bill shows how many kilowatt hours have been used. A kilowatt hour is the energy that a device with a power of 1000 watts uses in one hour.
wichtigste: The kilowatt hour, abbreviated kWh, is a unit of energy.
Electrical energy in the home is usually measured in kilowatt hours.
1 kWh is the energy that a 1000 watt device uses in one hour.
One kilowatt hour equals 3.6 million joules.
The electricity meter in the house counts the kilowatt hours used.
In Switzerland a kilowatt hour of electricity cost about 30 centimes on average in 2025.
Watts give the power; kilowatt hours give the energy used.

abschnitte.text: The **kilowatt hour** is a measure of energy. “Kilo” means thousand, so a kilowatt is 1000 watts. If a 1000 watt device runs for one hour, it has used 1 kWh. Otherwise in physics energy is measured in **joules**, and 1 kWh equals 3.6 million joules.

You have to tell two things apart: the **power** in watts tells you how much energy a device needs per second. The energy in kilowatt hours tells you how much has been used altogether. The calculation is power times time. A 2000 watt hairdryer therefore uses 1 kWh in half an hour, whereas a 10 watt LED lamp only does so after 100 hours.

Every house and every flat has an **electricity meter** that counts the kilowatt hours used. Many new meters in Switzerland are so-called smart meters, which send the data to the electricity company automatically. A household of four people in Switzerland uses a few thousand kilowatt hours a year. The biggest users of electricity are often the cooker, oven, tumble dryer, fridge and hot water.

abschnitte.titel: What does a kilowatt hour cost?
abschnitte.text: The price of electricity is given in centimes per kilowatt hour. In Switzerland a kilowatt hour cost about 30 centimes on average in 2025, more or less depending on the municipality and the electricity company. The prices are set anew each year and published by the Federal Electricity Commission, **ElCom**. So anyone who saves electricity also saves money.

With 1 kWh you can do roughly one load of washing, bring about 10 litres of cold water to the boil in a kettle or charge a smartphone around 50 times. An electric car travels about 5 to 7 kilometres on 1 kWh, depending on the model. Devices on **standby** use a little electricity all the time, so it is worth switching them off completely. The energy label on devices also helps you find economical models.

begriffe.erklaerung: 1000 watts, a unit of power.
Basic unit of energy in physics.
Device that measures the electrical energy used.
Ready mode in which a device seems to be off but still uses electricity.

gewusst: A cyclist pedalling for an hour can produce only about 0.1 kilowatt hours of energy.
Large power stations measure their output in gigawatt hours, millions of kilowatt hours.
Switzerland uses about 55 to 60 billion kilowatt hours of electricity a year.

teile.einleitung: Inductance describes how strongly an electrical component, above all a coil, resists changes in current. When current flows through a coil, it builds up a magnetic field and stores energy in it. Inductance is measured in henries and is found in transformers, radios and induction hobs.
wichtigste: Inductance is given in the unit henry.
The unit is named after the American physicist Joseph Henry.
1 henry equals 1 volt times second per ampere.
If you double the number of turns of a coil, its inductance becomes four times as large.
An iron core greatly increases the inductance of a coil.
Coils connected in series without coupling add up their inductances.
A coil and a capacitor together form an oscillating circuit.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, a magnetic field is created. If you wind the wire into a **coil**, this field becomes much stronger. If the current changes, the magnetic field changes too, and this produces a voltage in the coil itself that works against the change. This behaviour is called **self-induction**, and its strength is given by the inductance L.

For a long coil with air inside: L equals the magnetic constant times the number of turns squared times the cross-sectional area divided by the length. An air coil with 500 turns, a cross section of 4 cm² and a length of 20 cm therefore has about 0.63 millihenries. Because the **number of turns** is squared, L becomes four times as large when the number of turns is doubled. An **iron core** concentrates the magnetic field and often increases the inductance by a hundred to a thousand times.

The unit of inductance is the **henry**, abbreviated H. A coil has 1 henry if a change in current of 1 ampere per second produces a voltage of 1 volt. Therefore 1 H = 1 V · s/A. The unit honours the American Joseph Henry, who studied self-induction around 1830, at about the same time as Michael Faraday in England.

With alternating current a coil acts like a resistance, which is called **inductive reactance**. It is calculated as 2 times pi times frequency times inductance. A coil of 0.1 henries has about 31 ohms at the 50 hertz of our mains supply. The higher the frequency, the more strongly the coil holds back the current.

If you connect a coil to a **capacitor**, you get an oscillating circuit. In it the energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor. With L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF it oscillates at about 1.6 kilohertz. Oscillating circuits like this select a particular station in radios.

Inductances are found in many devices. In **transformers** two coils are coupled by an iron core and so change the voltage, for example in chargers. An induction hob uses a coil to create a rapidly changing magnetic field that heats the bottom of the pan directly. If you suddenly switch off a large coil, self-induction can produce a spark.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wound-up wire that can produce a strong magnetic field.
A coil produces a voltage itself when its current changes.
The unit of inductance, named after Joseph Henry.
A circuit of a coil and a capacitor in which energy swings back and forth.
A device made of two coils that makes an alternating voltage larger or smaller.

gewusst: The ignition coil of a petrol engine uses induction to turn 12 volts into many thousands of volts for the spark plug.
Wireless chargers for mobile phones work with two coils that transfer energy through a magnetic field.
Even a straight piece of wire has a tiny inductance.

teile.einleitung: Kirchhoff's laws are two basic rules for electrical circuits. They say how current divides at junctions and how voltages behave in a closed loop. With them, even complicated circuits can be calculated.
wichtigste: The laws come from the German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff.
He formulated them in 1845 as a student.
The junction rule: whatever flows into a junction also flows out again.
The loop rule: in every closed loop the sum of all the voltages is zero.
Put simply, current and voltage are conserved at every junction and in every loop.
The junction rule is based on the fact that no electric charge is lost.
The loop rule is based on the fact that energy is conserved.

abschnitte.text: A **junction** is a point in a circuit where wires branch. The junction rule says that the sum of the currents flowing in equals the sum of the currents flowing out. For example, if 3 amperes flow into a junction and divide between two wires, it could be 1 and 2 amperes, but together always 3 amperes. You can picture it like water in a pipe that branches.

A **loop** is a closed path through a circuit. The loop rule says that the sum of all the voltages around this path is zero. So the voltage a battery supplies is used up completely by the lamps and resistors in this loop. If a battery has 9 volts and three identical bulbs are connected one after another, 3 volts are dropped across each.

The junction rule follows from the fact that electric **charge** cannot simply disappear or appear. The loop rule follows from the conservation of energy. An electron that travels once all the way round a loop arrives with the same energy it started with. So both laws are applications of great laws of nature.

**Gustav Robert Kirchhoff** lived from 1824 to 1887 and came from Königsberg. As early as 1845, while still a student, he set out the two laws. Later, together with the chemist Robert Bunsen in Heidelberg, he developed spectral analysis. This made it possible to find out what substances the Sun and the stars are made of.

Engineers and electronics technicians use Kirchhoff's laws to calculate circuits in mobile phones, cars and household appliances. Together with **Ohm's law**, all the currents and voltages in a network can be worked out. Computer programs for simulating circuits also use these rules. At school they are usually learnt with series and **parallel circuits**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Branching point in a circuit.
Closed path around an electrical circuit.
What drives the current, measured in volts.
Amount of charge flowing per second, measured in amperes.
Circuit in which the current divides between several paths.

gewusst: Kirchhoff was only about 21 years old when he set out his famous laws.
Using spectral analysis, Kirchhoff and Bunsen discovered the new elements caesium and rubidium.
In a string of Christmas lights connected in series, all the bulbs share the mains voltage.

teile.einleitung: When climbing, a climbing rope connects the climber with the person belaying them. It is built to catch a fall safely and slow it down gently. There is a lot of physics behind this lifesaver.
wichtigste: Climbing ropes for falls are designed to stretch, so that the fall is slowed down more gently.
A rope that stretches a lot in a fall is called a dynamic rope.
A typical climbing rope consists of a core and a protective sheath.
The fall factor is the height of the fall divided by the length of rope paid out.
The force acting on the climber through the rope when a fall is caught is called the impact force.
A short fall close to the belay can be especially hard, because there is little rope to absorb it.
A belay device on the belayer's harness brakes the rope by friction.

abschnitte.titel: How a climbing rope is built
abschnitte.text: Modern climbing ropes are **kernmantle ropes**. Inside is the core of many synthetic fibres, usually nylon, which carries most of the load. On the outside a braided **sheath** protects the core from rubbing, dirt and sharp edges. Climbing ropes for climbing walls and rock are usually about 9 to 11 millimetres thick and often 50 to 80 metres long.

A **dynamic rope** stretches noticeably in a fall. This way the energy of the fall is absorbed over a longer distance and time, and the body is slowed down more gently. A static rope, on the other hand, hardly stretches. It is used, for example, in caves, in mountain rescue or for work at height, but not for catching lead falls.

How hard a fall is does not depend only on the height of the fall. What matters is the **fall factor**: the height of the fall divided by the length of rope paid out. If someone falls 4 metres and 8 metres of rope are out, the fall factor is 4 divided by 8, or 0.5. A short fall right above the belay can have a high fall factor, because only a little rope can absorb the energy.

When a fall is caught, a force acts on the body through the rope, the **impact force**. The more the rope stretches, the longer the braking takes and the smaller the force. This is the same principle as with an airbag. After a very hard fall, a rope should be checked carefully or replaced, because it may have lost some of its stretch.

The belayer has a **belay device** on their climbing harness through which the rope runs. The device brakes the rope by friction, so that even a lighter person can hold a heavier climber. In addition, while climbing, the rope is clipped into running belays with karabiners. Before every climb both partners check each other's knot, harness and belay device; this is called the partner check.

With its Alps and the Jura, Switzerland is a popular climbing country with crags, climbing walls and long alpine routes. A well-known maker of climbing ropes is the Swiss company **Mammut**, which started as a rope works in the canton of Aargau. Climbing ropes must meet strict standards and are tested with standardised drop tests. Sport climbing has also been an Olympic sport since 2021.

begriffe.erklaerung: Climbing rope that stretches in a fall and so brakes gently.
Rope with a load-bearing core and a protective braided sheath.
Height of the fall divided by the length of rope paid out; shows how hard a fall is.
Force acting through the rope when a fall is caught.

gewusst: In a hard fall a dynamic climbing rope can stretch by up to about a third of its length.
People used to climb with hemp ropes, which could snap in hard falls; only synthetic fibres made ropes truly safe.
A fall with a high fall factor is more dangerous than a long fall with a lot of rope out, even though you fall less far.

teile.einleitung: Hail is precipitation made of balls of ice that fall from the sky during violent thunderstorms. The hailstones can be as small as peas or as big as tennis balls. In Switzerland hail often causes great damage to cars, roofs and harvests in summer.
wichtigste: Hail consists of balls of ice that form in thunderclouds.
Strong updraughts carry the stones upwards again and again, and so they grow.
A hailstone falls when it becomes too heavy for the updraughts.
Very large hailstones can become as big as a tennis ball.
Hailstones that are cut open often show layers like an onion.
Fruit farmers protect their trees with hail nets.
When it hails, you go indoors at once.

abschnitte.text: Hail forms in tall thunderclouds, the **cumulonimbus** clouds. Inside them there are very strong **updraughts**, which sweep air and water droplets far upwards. At the very top it is very cold, but many tiny droplets stay liquid despite temperatures below zero; they are called **supercooled droplets**. When they hit a small grain of ice, they freeze onto it.

The core of a hailstone is often a grain of soft hail or a frozen droplet. The updraughts carry the stone upwards again and again, and each time new water freezes onto it. That is why you can often see **layers** like those of an onion in a hailstone that has been cut open, alternately clear and milky. Only when the stone is too heavy for the updraughts does it fall to the ground.

Balls of ice from about 5 millimetres across are called hail. Small, soft pellets of ice that look like polystyrene are called **soft hail** or graupel. Soft hail often falls in spring or in cool weather. Hail, on the other hand, comes mainly on hot summer days, because that is when thunderstorms are at their most violent. Because it falls fast and is large, it does not melt completely on the way down.

Large hailstones can dent car roofs, smash windows and break roof tiles. In Switzerland hailstorms often cause great damage to cars, roofs and **harvests**. A short band of hail can destroy a whole wine-growing area or fields of grain in a few minutes. In Switzerland it hails especially often in the Central Plateau, in the Jura, in the Napf area and in Ticino.

When it hails, you look for shelter in a house or car at once. Fruit farmers stretch **hail nets** over their trees so that the fruit is not damaged. Many farmers take out insurance against hail damage. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss warn of violent thunderstorms so that people can put their cars under cover in time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tall, mighty thundercloud, often shaped like an anvil.
Air that flows powerfully upwards.
Small, soft pellets of ice that look like polystyrene, also called graupel.
Water droplets that are still liquid despite temperatures below zero.

gewusst: The largest hailstone ever measured in the world fell in the USA in 2010 and was about 20 centimetres across.
After a hailstorm in summer the ground can look white for a short time, as if it had snowed.
In thunderclouds updraughts can be stronger than a storm on the ground.

teile.einleitung: A saucepan is a pot in which you heat water, soups, pasta or vegetables on the cooker. When cooking, you can observe a lot of physics: heat travels, water flows and turns into steam. If you look closely, you will discover several laws of nature in the pan.
wichtigste: Many saucepans are made of metal, because metal conducts heat well.
Plastic handles do not get as hot as metal.
By the sea water boils at about 100 degrees.
In the mountains water boils at less than 100 degrees, because the air pressure is lower.
When cooking, bubbles of steam rise up.
Warm water rises, which is why the water at the top of the pan also gets warm.
Above the pan you see a white cloud of tiny water droplets.

abschnitte.text: Saucepans are usually made of **stainless steel**, aluminium, cast iron or copper. Metal conducts the heat from the hotplate well into the pan. The handles are often made of **plastic** or wood, because these materials conduct heat poorly and therefore do not get so hot. Many pans have a thick base so that the heat is spread evenly.

At first the hotplate warms only the base of the pan and the water just above it. Warm water is lighter than cold water and so rises, while cold water sinks. This flow is called **convection**. In this way all the water in the pan gradually gets warm.

By the sea water boils at about **100 degrees Celsius**. Then bubbles of **steam** form at the bottom, rise and burst at the surface. Above the pan you see a white cloud. It is not made of invisible steam but of tiny water droplets that have condensed again in the cooler air.

The higher you go, the lower the **air pressure**. At lower pressure water boils at a lower temperature. On the Jungfraujoch at about 3450 metres, water already boils at about 89 degrees. That is why it takes longer in the mountains for pasta or eggs to be cooked.

abschnitte.titel: Boiling over and the pressure cooker
abschnitte.text: If you fill a pan too full, it boils over and the water runs onto the cooker. With milk or pasta, foam also forms and rises quickly. A **pressure cooker** is tightly sealed, so the pressure inside rises. As a result the water only boils at about 120 degrees and the food is cooked much faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: Temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour.
Transfer of heat by flow; warm water rises.
Material that passes on heat well, for example metal.
Weight of the air pressing on us and everything else.

gewusst: Real steam is invisible; the white cloud above the pan is already made of water droplets again.
At the top of Mount Everest water boils at only about 70 degrees.
Salt in the cooking water raises the boiling point only very slightly; the usual amount hardly changes it noticeably.

teile.einleitung: Nuclear fusion is the joining of light atomic nuclei into a heavier nucleus, which releases huge amounts of energy. This is how the energy of the Sun and all stars is produced. For decades researchers have been trying to make nuclear fusion usable on Earth as a clean source of energy.
wichtigste: In nuclear fusion light atomic nuclei join together; in nuclear fission a heavy nucleus breaks apart.
The Sun produces its energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
Fusion needs extremely high temperatures and pressures.
On Earth the fuel mixture has to be heated to more than 100 million degrees.
The hot gas, a plasma, is held by magnetic fields in facilities such as tokamaks.
The large research reactor ITER is being built in France.
So far no fusion power station supplies electricity to the grid.

abschnitte.text: In **nuclear fusion** light atomic nuclei, for example of hydrogen, are pressed together so strongly that they merge. The new nucleus is slightly lighter than the two starting nuclei together. The missing mass is released as energy according to Einstein's formula E = mc². In contrast, in **nuclear fission** a heavy nucleus such as uranium is split.

abschnitte.titel: The power station of the stars
abschnitte.text: The **Sun** is a huge fusion reactor. In its core there is a temperature of about 15 million degrees Celsius and a tremendous pressure. There, hundreds of millions of tonnes of hydrogen fuse into helium every second. The energy released reaches us as light and warmth and makes life on Earth possible.

Atomic nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. To make them merge anyway, they have to be extremely fast, in other words extremely hot. On Earth you need more than 100 million degrees, because the enormous pressure of the Sun is missing. At these temperatures the fuel turns into a **plasma**, an electrically charged gas that must not touch any wall.

In a **tokamak** the plasma is held suspended in a ring-shaped chamber by strong magnetic fields. The largest tokamak in the world, **ITER**, is being built jointly by many countries at Cadarache in southern France. In Germany the stellarator Wendelstein 7-X is exploring a twisted shape of magnetic field. The Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL in Lausanne also has a tokamak for research.

The fuel is usually the hydrogen types **deuterium** and tritium. Deuterium can be obtained from sea water and is available in almost unlimited amounts. Fusion produces no CO₂ and much less long-lived radioactive waste than nuclear fission. A chain reaction getting out of control is not possible, because the plasma cools down immediately if anything goes wrong.

In 2022 the National Ignition Facility in the USA succeeded for the first time in using lasers to produce more fusion energy than the lasers had put into the fuel. But a great deal of research is still needed before a power station delivers electricity continuously. Experts expect it to take several decades. Private companies are now also working on smaller fusion facilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Joining of light atomic nuclei into a heavier nucleus.
Extremely hot, electrically charged gas.
Ring-shaped facility that holds plasma with magnetic fields.
Heavy hydrogen, a possible fuel for fusion.

gewusst: The plasma in a fusion reactor is hotter than the inside of the Sun.
The word tokamak comes from Russian, because the facility was invented in the Soviet Union.
In theory, the deuterium in a bathtub full of water could provide as much energy as many tonnes of coal.

teile.einleitung: The Gösgen nuclear power station is in Däniken in the canton of Solothurn, on the River Aare. It is one of the largest power stations in Switzerland and produces electricity by splitting uranium. It is best known for its cooling tower, about 150 metres high, from which white clouds of steam rise.
wichtigste: The Gösgen nuclear power station is in Däniken in the canton of Solothurn.
It began commercial operation in 1979.
It works with a pressurised water reactor.
Uranium is split as fuel.
The electrical output is about 1000 megawatts.
The cooling tower is about 150 metres high.
ENSI supervises the safety of the plant.

abschnitte.text: The **Gösgen nuclear power station** is in the municipality of Däniken in the canton of Solothurn, between Olten and Aarau. It stands on the **Aare**, whose water is used for cooling. The area around the plant is called Niederamt. The cooling tower is about 150 metres high and can be seen from far away in the region.

The power station was built in the 1970s and began commercial operation in 1979. At the time there were big protests against the building of nuclear power stations, especially at Kaiseraugst, where another planned plant was never built. Gösgen is run by a company in which several energy firms have shares. In 2017 Swiss voters decided with the **Energy Strategy 2050** that no new nuclear power stations may be built.

In the **reactor** uranium nuclei are split, releasing a great deal of heat. Gösgen is a **pressurised water reactor**: the water in the reactor is under such high pressure that it does not boil despite the great heat. In a steam generator it passes its heat to a second water circuit, where steam is produced. The steam drives a turbine, and a generator turns this into electricity.

After the turbine the steam has to be cooled again. This is done by the large **cooling tower**, in which warm water trickles down and is cooled by rising air. The white cloud above the tower is not smoke but water vapour that condenses into fine droplets. The cooling tower protects the Aare, because less warm water gets into the river.

With an electrical output of about 1000 megawatts, Gösgen supplies a significant part of Switzerland's electricity. Only the **Leibstadt** nuclear power station has an even higher output in Switzerland. The other nuclear power stations are Beznau I and II; Mühleberg was shut down at the end of 2019. Nuclear power stations emit hardly any CO2 while running, but they leave radioactive waste.

The safety of all Swiss nuclear power stations is monitored by **ENSI**, the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate. It regularly inspects the plants, procedures and staff. Every year the plant is shut down for a few weeks for an overhaul, during which part of the fuel elements is replaced. Spent fuel elements go to an interim store and are later to go into a deep geological repository.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting of heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium, which releases a lot of energy.
Reactor in which water under high pressure carries away the heat without boiling.
One million watts, a unit for large amounts of power.
Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate, the supervisory authority.

gewusst: In clear weather the cloud of steam above the Gösgen cooling tower can be seen from many kilometres away.
A single small uranium fuel pellet can provide about as much energy as several hundred kilograms of coal.
In one hour Gösgen produces about as much electricity as a Swiss household uses in many decades.

teile.einleitung: Huygens' principle is an idea that explains how waves spread out. It says that every point on a wave itself becomes the starting point of a new small wave. With it you can understand the refraction, reflection and diffraction of water, sound and light.
wichtigste: Every point on a wavefront is the starting point of a small spherical or circular wave, the wavelet.
The new wavefront is the envelope of all the wavelets.
The principle comes from the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens.
He published his wave theory in the work “Traité de la lumière”.
Augustin Jean Fresnel extended the principle to include the interference of the wavelets.
The law of refraction can be derived from the principle.
Behind a very narrow slit, a straight wave turns into a circular wave.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a stone into water, circular waves spread out. Huygens imagined that every point on a wave crest acts like a new small stone and sends out its own little wave, the **wavelet**. All these small waves overlap. The line that touches them at the front, the **envelope**, is the new wavefront.

Christiaan Huygens lived from 1629 to 1695 and came from the Netherlands. He was a physicist, mathematician and astronomer, and among other things he invented the pendulum clock. He also discovered Saturn's moon Titan and recognised that Saturn is surrounded by a ring. He published his wave theory of light in 1690 in the book **Traité de la lumière**, in English Treatise on Light.

If a wave hits an area at an angle where it travels more slowly, for example water over shallow ground, the wavelets become smaller there. As a result the wavefront bends, and the wave is **refracted**. From this reasoning follows the law of refraction: the ratio of the sines of the angles equals the ratio of the speeds. If a water wave travelling at 0.4 m/s arrives at 30 degrees at a zone with 0.2 m/s, the angle of refraction is about 14.5 degrees.

If a straight wave hits a wall with a very narrow slit, only a single wavelet is left. That is why a **circular wave** spreads out behind the slit. In this way the wave also reaches the area behind the wall, which you would actually expect to be in shadow. This **diffraction** explains, for example, why you can hear voices round the corner of a house.

In the early 19th century the French physicist Augustin Jean Fresnel added to Huygens' idea. He took into account that the wavelets can strengthen or cancel each other out, that is interfere. This extended **Huygens Fresnel principle** also explains the coloured stripes and rings that appear with light behind fine slits. It helped to establish that light is a wave.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line or surface on which all points of a wave are in the same state of vibration, for example a wave crest.
A small circular or spherical wave that starts from one point.
A line that just touches many circles from the outside.
The spreading of a wave into the shadow area behind an obstacle.

gewusst: In his day Huygens was a rival of Isaac Newton, who saw light rather as a stream of tiny particles.
The European landing probe that landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005 is named Huygens.
In a ripple tank in the physics room you can watch Huygens' principle directly with water waves.

teile.einleitung: A compass is a device used to find the points of the compass, above all north. Its magnetic needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field. For centuries it has helped sailors, hikers and scouts to find the right way.
wichtigste: With a compass you can find out where north is.
The needle is a small magnet that lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
The magnetic North Pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole.
The compass was invented in China.
In Europe it was used for sailing from the 12th century.
Iron and magnets nearby can disturb the compass.
Smartphones also have a built-in electronic compass.

abschnitte.text: A **compass** consists of a magnetic needle that turns easily inside a case with a scale. The needle points north with its tip, which is usually red. On the scale, the **compass rose**, are the directions north, east, south and west. Many compasses also have a scale in degrees from 0 to 360.

The Earth is like a giant magnet and is surrounded by a **magnetic field**. It is created by currents of liquid iron in the Earth's outer core. The compass needle lines up with this field. Because the magnetic pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole and moves slowly, the needle points slightly to one side; this is called **magnetic declination**.

More than 2000 years ago the Chinese already knew magnetic spoons that pointed south and used them for fortune-telling. By the 11th century at the latest they were using magnetic needles for navigation. In Europe the compass was used for sailing from the 12th century. Only with it could ships sail far out onto the open sea even when the sky was cloudy.

For hiking and **orienteering** a baseplate compass is used. You put it on the map, turn the map so that its north matches the needle, and can then read off the direction to your destination. In Switzerland orienteering is a popular sport, also among children and in the scouts. Well-known compasses have been made for over a hundred years by the company Recta in Biel.

Today smartphones have an electronic compass, a sensor called a **magnetometer**. It measures the Earth's magnetic field and shows in map apps which direction you are facing. Aircraft and ships also use gyrocompasses and satellite navigation. Even so, many mountaineers take an ordinary compass with them, because it works without a battery.

A compass can be fooled. Iron objects, magnets, power lines or a mobile phone right next to it deflect the needle. Near the magnetic poles the compass becomes very inaccurate. You should therefore hold it level and keep a little distance from metal.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small magnetic needle that lines up towards the north.
Magnetic field that surrounds the whole Earth.
Disc showing the points of the compass on a compass.
Difference between magnetic north and geographic north.

gewusst: Migratory birds and sea turtles can also sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.
The magnetic North Pole is currently moving by several dozen kilometres every year.
A magnetised sewing needle floating on a leaf in water becomes a simple compass.

teile.einleitung: A glove is a piece of clothing that covers and protects the hand, usually with its own pocket for each finger. Gloves keep you warm in winter and protect you from heat, dirt and injuries. There is a lot of physics behind them, above all to do with heat.
wichtigste: Gloves keep your hands warm because they hold in the body's warmth.
A glove produces no heat itself; on its own on the table it does not get warm.
The air between the fibres of a woollen glove protects well against the cold.
Mittens usually keep the fingers warmer than gloves with fingers.
Wet gloves make your hands cold, because water carries heat away well.
Oven gloves protect you when holding hot baking trays.
Rubber gloves protect your hands when washing up with hot water.

abschnitte.text: A glove wraps around the hand and still lets it move. In a **glove with fingers**, each finger has its own pocket. In a **mitten**, four fingers sit together and only the thumb has its own pocket. Gloves are made of wool, leather, rubber, plastic and many other materials. In Switzerland people often say “Händsche” in dialect.

A glove produces no warmth of its own; it holds in the **body's warmth**. Countless small pockets of air are trapped between the fibres of wool or fleece. Still air conducts heat very badly and therefore acts as **insulation**. In this way the warmth of the hand stays in the glove for longer. Mittens are warmer because the fingers warm each other and there is less surface giving off heat.

When playing with snowballs, gloves often get wet. Water conducts heat much better than air, and the pockets of air fill with water. That is why hands get cold quickly in wet gloves. **Ski gloves** therefore often have a waterproof outer layer so that no snow gets in. Inside, a soft lining provides the warmth.

An **oven glove** is thickly padded so that the heat of a baking tray reaches the hand only slowly. This lets you briefly hold hot trays and tins without burning yourself. When washing up with hot water, **rubber gloves** protect the skin from heat and washing-up liquid. Firefighters wear especially heat-resistant gloves. Welders also need thick leather gloves against sparks.

In hospitals, doctors and nurses wear thin **disposable gloves** so that no germs are passed on. Gardeners, builders and craftspeople protect their hands with tough work gloves. In sport there are goalkeeper gloves, boxing gloves and cycling gloves. Gloves have existed for a very long time: gloves were found in the tomb of the Egyptian king Tutankhamun. In the past, fine gloves were also a sign of wealth.

begriffe.erklaerung: A layer that lets heat through badly and so keeps things warm or cold.
The passing on of heat from a warm place to a cold one.
A glove in which only the thumb has its own pocket.
A soft, fluffy fabric made of artificial fibres that traps a lot of air.

gewusst: A glove lying on its own outside in the snow is just as cold as its surroundings.
Water conducts heat about 25 times better than air, which is why wet hands get cold so quickly.
There are heated gloves with small batteries that really do produce warmth themselves.

teile.einleitung: Hans Christian Ørsted was a Danish physicist and chemist who discovered in 1820 that electric current deflects a compass needle. With this he was the first to show that electricity and magnetism are connected. This discovery laid the foundation for electric motors, generators and much more.
wichtigste: Hans Christian Ørsted lived from 1777 to 1851 and came from Denmark.
In 1820 he discovered that a wire carrying a current deflects a compass needle.
The needle turns crosswise to the wire, and if the current is reversed, it swings the other way.
With this discovery he founded electromagnetism.
In 1825 he was one of the first to produce a small amount of aluminium.
Today's Technical University of Denmark goes back to the school he founded in 1829.
A Danish satellite and an old unit of magnetic field strength bear his name.

abschnitte.text: **Hans Christian Ørsted** was born in 1777 in Rudkøbing on the Danish island of Langeland. As a boy he helped in his father's pharmacy and learned a lot about chemistry there. Later he studied in Copenhagen and became a professor of physics. He died in Copenhagen in 1851.

In 1820 Ørsted showed in an experiment that an electric current moves a **compass needle**. If you place a needle under a straight wire and let a strong current flow, it turns crosswise to the wire. If you reverse the direction of the current, the needle swings in the opposite direction. This made it clear that a current produces a **magnetic field** around itself.

Ørsted's observation spread quickly throughout Europe. Researchers such as André-Marie Ampère in France and Michael Faraday in England built on it. In this way the new field of **electromagnetism** came into being. Without this discovery there would be no electric motors, loudspeakers or electromagnets today.

Ørsted was not only a physicist but also a gifted chemist. In 1825 he was one of the first to succeed in producing a small amount of the metal **aluminium**. At that time aluminium was as rare and expensive as gold. Today it is one of the most important metals and is found in bikes, aeroplanes and drinks cans.

In 1829 Ørsted founded a polytechnic school in Copenhagen, which became today's **Technical University of Denmark**. The old unit of magnetic field strength in the CGS system is called the oersted. The Danish satellite **Ørsted**, which measured the Earth's magnetic field, was launched into space in 1999. A large Danish energy company that builds wind farms also bears his name today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The field of physics that shows how electricity and magnetism are connected.
The area around a magnet or current in which magnetic forces act.
A device with a magnetic needle that points north.
An older unit of measurement for magnetic field strength.

gewusst: Besides his research, Ørsted also wrote poems.
His younger brother Anders Sandøe Ørsted became a famous lawyer and even head of the Danish government.
In Ørsted's time aluminium was considered so precious that jewellery was made from it.

teile.einleitung: A harmonic oscillation is the simplest and most even form of a back-and-forth movement. Its course can be described with a sine curve, as with a weight on a spring. Many oscillations in nature and technology, from the pendulum to the clock, are roughly harmonic.
wichtigste: A harmonic oscillation arises when the restoring force is proportional to the displacement and points the opposite way.
The displacement over time is described by a sine function.
The velocity is 90° out of phase with the displacement.
At the turning points the acceleration is greatest, at the rest position the velocity.
The total energy grows with the square of the amplitude.
A harmonic oscillation is the projection of a steady circular movement.
The corresponding differential equation is ẍ = −ω²·x.

abschnitte.text: In an oscillation a body moves back and forth again and again around a **rest position**. The greatest distance from the rest position is called the **amplitude**. The time for one whole back and forth is the **period** T, and the number of oscillations per second is the frequency in hertz. In a harmonic oscillation a force pulls the body back more strongly the further it is displaced. The force always points towards the rest position.

If you plot the displacement against time, you get an even **sine curve**. You can picture it like this: a point runs steadily round a circle, and you look only at its shadow on the wall. This shadow moves up and down in an exactly harmonic way. That is why we also speak of the angular frequency ω. The formula is x(t) = A·sin(ω·t).

At the rest position the body is fastest; at the **turning points** it stands still for a moment. On the other hand, the acceleration is greatest at the turning points and zero at the rest position. The velocity is shifted by a quarter of a period, that is 90°, compared with the displacement. The greatest acceleration is A·ω². For x(t) = 0.05 m · sin(10 s⁻¹ · t), that is 0.05 · 100 = 5 m/s².

During the oscillation the energy keeps switching between **kinetic energy** and energy stored in the spring. Without friction the total energy always stays the same. It is proportional to the square of the amplitude. So if you triple the amplitude, the energy becomes 9 times as great. In reality friction slowly brakes the oscillation; it is damped.

A weight on a spring, a tuning fork and a pendulum with a small swing all oscillate roughly harmonically. It is especially important that the period does not depend on the amplitude. Christiaan Huygens used this property in the 17th century for the first accurate **pendulum clock**.
