In mechanical Swiss wristwatches a small **balance wheel** with a hairspring swings back and forth. In quartz watches a tiny quartz crystal vibrates 32,768 times a second.

begriffe.erklaerung: The greatest displacement of an oscillation from the rest position.
The time for one complete back-and-forth movement.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
A force that pulls a displaced body back to the rest position.
The time offset between two oscillations.

gewusst: Galileo Galilei is said to have noticed that a swinging chandelier in Pisa Cathedral always took the same time for one swing.
The concert pitch A of a tuning fork vibrates 440 times a second.
Atoms in a crystal also vibrate around their rest position, rather like tiny springs.

teile.einleitung: A cat's eye is a reflector that sends light back exactly where it came from. You find them on bikes, cars, school bags and marker posts at the side of the road. It does not shine by itself but needs light from outside, for example from a headlight.
wichtigste: A reflector does not shine in complete darkness; it needs light from outside.
It sends the light back mainly towards the headlight, so the driver sees it brightly while a pedestrian beside it sees it as dark.
In a cat's eye, three small mirror surfaces always stand at right angles to each other.
Road markings often contain tiny glass beads so that they look bright at night.
The Apollo 11 crew set up a reflector on the Moon in 1969.
Reflectors at the back of cars and bikes are red; on bike pedals they are often yellow.
Pedestrians wearing reflective clothing are seen much sooner by drivers at night.

abschnitte.text: Cats' eyes light up in the dark when you shine a torch at them. This is because of a mirror-like layer behind the retina that throws the light back. Because reflectors light up in a very similar way, they are called **cat's eyes**. The technical term is **retroreflector**, meaning a mirror that sends light back.

A cat's eye consists of many small plastic prisms shaped like the corner of a cube. At each corner three surfaces stand at right angles to each other; this is called a **corner reflector**. A beam of light is reflected by all three surfaces and then travels back exactly parallel. That is why the light arrives back at the headlight, and so at the driver, while a pedestrian beside it sees almost none of it.

In 1934 the Englishman **Percy Shaw** patented cat's eyes that were set into the middle of the road. In Switzerland you see reflectors mainly on white **marker posts** at the side of the road and on traffic signs. Tiny **glass beads** are mixed into the paint of road markings and send the light back in a similar way. This makes the lines easy to see in headlights at night.

Bikes have a red **reflector** at the back and a white one at the front. The pedals often also have yellow reflectors, which move up and down as you pedal and so stand out especially. School bags, jackets and high-visibility vests also have reflective strips. Pedestrians in dark clothing are seen very late at night, but with reflectors they are seen from a long way off.

During the **Apollo 11** mission in 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set up a panel with many corner reflectors on the Moon. Later Apollo missions and Soviet moon rovers took similar reflectors there. From Earth, laser beams are sent there and the time until the light comes back is measured. This way the distance to the Moon is known to within a few centimetres, and we know that it moves about 4 centimetres further from the Earth each year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Arrangement of mirrors that sends light back exactly in the direction it came from.
Three mirror surfaces standing at right angles to each other like the corner of a cube.
Transparent object with flat surfaces that directs light.
White post at the side of the road with reflectors that shows the course of the road at night.

gewusst: Percy Shaw is said to have had the idea when he saw the shining eyes of a cat at the roadside at night.
Laser measurements to the Moon are still carried out today using the mirrors from Apollo 11.
Many life jackets and firefighters' jackets have reflective strips so that people can be found quickly in a searchlight.

teile.einleitung: A rubber band is a small ring of elastic rubber that can be stretched and then springs back into its old shape. It is used to hold things together, for playing and for experiments. It is a wonderful way of showing what elasticity means.
wichtigste: A rubber band gets longer when you pull at both ends.
If you let go of a stretched rubber band, it contracts again.
The further you stretch it, the harder it pulls back.
If a rubber band is stretched far too much, it snaps.
Substances that return to their old shape after being stretched are called elastic.
Natural rubber is obtained from the milky sap of the rubber tree.
French skipping is a popular jumping game with a long, stretched elastic band.

abschnitte.text: A rubber band is a closed ring of **rubber**. They come in many sizes, thicknesses and colours. In everyday life they are used to hold pencils, letters or open bags together. Hair bands, waistbands and preserving jars also contain rubber that can stretch. The inventor of the rubber band is considered to be the Englishman Stephen Perry, who had it patented in 1845.

Rubber is **elastic**: after being stretched it returns to its old shape. This is because of its long, tangled chains of molecules, which lie jumbled up like cooked spaghetti. When you pull on the band, the chains are stretched out and put in order. When you let go, they tangle up again by themselves. The further you stretch it, the stronger the **restoring force**, until the band finally snaps.

Natural rubber comes from the milky sap of the **rubber tree**, which originally comes from South America. The bark is cut, and the white sap, the latex, is caught in cups. Today most rubber trees grow on plantations in Southeast Asia, for example in Thailand and Indonesia. Raw rubber becomes sticky when warm and hard when cold. Only by heating it with sulphur, **vulcanisation**, which Charles Goodyear discovered in 1839, does it become permanently elastic.

If you hold a rubber band against your lips and stretch it quickly, you can feel that it gets warm. If you let it snap back, it cools down. This surprising behaviour has to do with the order of the chains of molecules. If you heat a stretched rubber band with a hairdryer, it even contracts instead of expanding. Most other substances, on the other hand, expand when heated.

In **French skipping**, two children stretch a long elastic band around their legs, and a third jumps in and out in certain patterns. With each round the band is raised higher, from the ankles up to the hips. Rubber bands can also be used to power toy cars or small propeller aeroplanes. Energy is stored in the stretched band and turned into movement when it is let go. Careful: you should never fire a stretched rubber band at people or animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that returns to its old shape after being stretched or squeezed.
The raw material for rubber, from the sap of the rubber tree.
The white milky sap of the rubber tree.
Heating raw rubber with sulphur so that it becomes permanently elastic.

gewusst: A stretched rubber band gets warm; you can try this out yourself with your lips.
Many rubber bands today are made from artificially produced rubber.
With a wound-up rubber band, small model aeroplanes can fly several metres.

teile.einleitung: The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest space telescope ever built. It mainly observes infrared light and can therefore see the first galaxies after the Big Bang. It was built jointly by the space agencies NASA, ESA and CSA.
wichtigste: The telescope was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket.
The main mirror is made up of 18 hexagonal segments.
It observes mainly in the infrared range.
The mirrors are coated with a thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared light well.
A sunshield made of five layers of foil protects the telescope from heat.
NASA, ESA and CSA built it together.
It can see the strongly redshifted light of the first galaxies.

abschnitte.text: The **James Webb Space Telescope**, JWST for short, is a huge telescope in space. It is regarded as the successor to the famous Hubble telescope. It was built by the American NASA, the European ESA and the Canadian CSA. It is named after James Webb, who led NASA in the 1960s.

The telescope was launched on **25 December 2021** on a European Ariane 5 rocket from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana. Because it was too big for the rocket, it was folded up and only unfolded in space. It now orbits around the **Lagrange point L2**, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. The first colour images were published in July 2022.

The main mirror has a diameter of about 6.5 metres and is made up of 18 hexagonal **segments** of beryllium. They are coated with a very thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared light particularly well. Hubble's mirror, by contrast, was only 2.4 metres across. The larger a mirror is, the more light it collects and the fainter the objects you can see.

A huge **sunshield**, about the size of a tennis court, protects the telescope from the light and heat of the Sun, Earth and Moon. It consists of five very thin layers of foil. As a result the shaded side gets colder than minus 220 degrees Celsius. This cold is necessary because warm parts give off infrared radiation themselves and would disturb the measurements.

The universe is expanding, so the light of very distant galaxies is stretched on its long journey. Visible light turns into **infrared light**; this is called **redshift**. That is why only an infrared telescope can see the first galaxies after the Big Bang. Infrared also passes through clouds of dust in which new stars and planets are forming.

The telescope has already found very early galaxies whose light has been travelling for more than 13 billion years. It also studies the atmospheres of **exoplanets**, planets around other stars, and has found carbon dioxide there, for example. Researchers from Switzerland also worked on the MIRI instrument for the mid-infrared. Its pictures of nebulae and galaxies are among the most beautiful images of space.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light with a longer wavelength than red, invisible to us but felt as warmth.
Stretching of the light of distant galaxies by the expansion of the universe.
Place in space where a satellite travels round the Sun together with the Earth.
Planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.

gewusst: The gold layer on all the mirrors together weighs only about as much as a golf ball.
The telescope is so far away that, unlike Hubble, it cannot be repaired by astronauts.
Because the launch on the Ariane 5 was so precise, a lot of fuel was left over, which extends the possible lifetime of the telescope.

teile.einleitung: Ionising radiation is very high-energy radiation that can knock electrons out of atoms. It includes X-rays, gamma rays and particle radiation from radioactive substances. It is useful in medicine and technology but can damage cells, so good radiation protection is needed.
wichtigste: Ionising radiation has enough energy to ionise atoms and molecules, in other words to give them an electric charge.
Neutrons have no charge and ionise only indirectly through particles they knock into or create.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts, often in millisieverts or microsieverts.
The effective dose takes into account that organs differ in how sensitive they are.
Deterministic damage only occurs above a threshold dose; stochastic damage such as cancer has no safe threshold.
A short whole-body dose of around 4 to 5 sieverts is fatal without treatment for about half of those affected.
The ALARA principle requires keeping the dose as low as reasonably achievable.

abschnitte.text: To ionise means to knock an electron out of an atom so that a charged **ion** is left behind. This takes a great deal of energy, more than visible light or radio waves have. **Alpha radiation**, beta radiation, gamma radiation and X-rays can do this directly. Neutron radiation has no charge and acts only indirectly, because it knocks other particles or triggers nuclear reactions.

Part of the radiation is completely natural and has always been there. It comes from space as **cosmic radiation**, from rocks in the ground and from the radioactive gas **radon**, which can collect in cellars. In Switzerland radon makes up the largest part of the radiation a person receives in a year. On top of that come artificial sources such as X-rays and CT scans at the doctor's.

The energy absorbed per kilogram of body tissue is called the **absorbed dose** and is measured in grays. Because alpha rays are more harmful than gamma rays, this is converted into the equivalent dose in **sieverts**. The effective dose also takes into account that bone marrow, for example, is more sensitive than skin. In Switzerland a person receives on average a few millisieverts a year, a large part of which comes from radon.

Radiation can damage the genetic material in cells. At very high doses **deterministic damage** occurs, for example acute radiation sickness, which only starts above a threshold and gets worse with the dose. At small doses the concern is **stochastic damage** such as cancer, whose likelihood rises with the dose. For this, radiation protection assumes a linear model without a threshold, to be on the safe side.

In radiation protection three simple rules apply: keep your **distance**, keep the time spent short and use shielding. Distance has a particularly strong effect, because with a point source the dose rate falls with the square of the distance. If you measure 90 microsieverts per hour at 2 metres, it is only 10 at 6 metres. Lead and thick concrete are good for shielding gamma rays, while even a sheet of paper stops alpha rays.

Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays named after him (X-rays) in 1895, and Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896. Today X-rays are used to take pictures of bones and teeth. In **radiotherapy** cancer cells are destroyed in a targeted way. Food, syringes and dressings are also sterilised with radiation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Atom or molecule that is electrically charged because it has lost electrons or has too many.
Unit for the effect of radiation on humans.
Natural radioactive gas from the ground that can collect in houses.
Abbreviation for “as low as reasonably achievable”, a principle of radiation protection.

gewusst: On a long-haul flight you receive more cosmic radiation than on the ground, because the protective layer of air is thinner.
Bananas contain a tiny amount of radioactive potassium, but the dose is completely harmless.
Röntgen never patented his discovery, so that everyone could benefit from it.

teile.einleitung: Hydraulics is the technology of transmitting and amplifying forces with liquids. It is found in diggers, car brakes, vehicle lifts and aeroplanes. The secret: liquids can hardly be squeezed together.
wichtigste: Hydraulics transmits forces with liquids.
This is possible because liquids can hardly be squeezed together.
Oil is usually used in hydraulic machines.
The braking system of a car usually works hydraulically.
The arms of large diggers are moved with hydraulic cylinders.
In garages, hydraulic lifts raise whole cars.
Air in a brake line is dangerous because it can be squeezed together.
The word comes from the Greek hydor, water.

abschnitte.text: The word **hydraulics** comes from the Greek hydor for water and aulos for pipe. It means the transmission of force by a liquid in pipes and hoses. Today a special **hydraulic oil** is almost always used for this, because it lubricates, does not rust and hardly freezes. Hydraulics is an important part of mechanical engineering.

If you press on an enclosed liquid, the pressure spreads out evenly everywhere, as Blaise Pascal described in the 17th century. Because liquids are almost **incompressible**, movement at one end is passed on to the other end at once. A pump produces the pressure, valves control the route, and a **hydraulic cylinder** turns the pressure into movement. With a large piston, a small force can be greatly amplified in this way.

The arms of a digger are moved by shiny cylinders in which oil pushes out a piston. In this way a digger can lift tonnes of earth and stones. Cranes, refuse lorries, tipper lorries and piste bashers in the Swiss ski resorts also work with hydraulics. The advantage is that very large forces can be controlled finely and evenly.

When someone steps on the brake pedal, a small piston pushes **brake fluid** through thin pipes to all four wheels. There, larger pistons press the brake pads against the brake discs. If air gets into the line, it can be squeezed together, the pedal feels soft and the brakes work less well. That is why a garage has to bleed the brakes carefully after repairs.

In the garage a hydraulic **vehicle lift** raises a whole car into the air. Aeroplanes move their control surfaces and landing gear hydraulically. Office chairs with gas springs, door closers and canal locks also use similar principles. The counterpart is **pneumatics**, which uses compressed air instead of liquid.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tube with a moving piston that turns liquid pressure into movement.
A moving disc in a cylinder that is pushed by the liquid.
Cannot be squeezed together, or hardly at all.
Technology that works with compressed air instead of liquid.

gewusst: Even in ancient times people used water power for pumps and organs; the water organ is considered one of the earliest hydraulic machines.
Thanks to hydraulics, a pilot can move the heavy control surfaces of a large aeroplane with little force.
Because brake fluid takes in water from the air over time, it has to be changed regularly in a car.

teile.einleitung: The piano is a keyboard instrument in which small hammers inside strike tightly stretched strings. It can play very quietly and very loudly, which is why it was originally called the pianoforte, meaning “soft-loud”. Hardly any instrument has such a wide range of notes.
wichtigste: In a piano, small hammers inside strike the strings.
A modern piano usually has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black.
The low notes are on the left, the high notes on the right.
The black keys are arranged in groups of two and three.
A large piano with horizontal strings and a lid that opens is called a grand piano.
The pedals are used to change the sound.
Someone who plays the piano is called a pianist.

abschnitte.text: The **keyboard** of a modern piano usually has 88 keys. The white keys play the notes C, D, E, F, G, A and B (called H in German), and the black ones lie in between. The black keys are always arranged alternately in **groups of two and three**, which makes it easy to find your way around. To the left of each group of two is the key C. The further right you play, the higher the notes sound.

When you press a key, a clever **mechanism** starts to move. A felt-covered **hammer** strikes the strings from below or from the front and bounces straight back. This lets the strings vibrate freely. When you let go of the key, a damper presses on the strings and stops the note. The harder you strike, the faster the hammer hits and the louder it sounds.

A piano has more than 200 steel strings, because most notes have two or three strings. Low strings are long and wound with copper wire; high strings are short and thin. A large wooden board, the **soundboard**, picks up the vibrations and makes the sound loud. Because the strings are stretched with enormous force, the piano needs a heavy cast-iron frame. A piano tuner regularly brings the strings back to the right pitch.

abschnitte.titel: Pedals, grand piano and upright piano
abschnitte.text: Most pianos have two or three **pedals**. The right pedal lifts all the dampers so that the notes ring on for a long time. The left pedal makes the sound quieter and softer. In a **grand piano** the strings lie horizontally under a large lid that can be opened. In an upright piano, which is often found in homes and schools, the strings stand vertically.

The piano was invented around 1700 in Florence by **Bartolomeo Cristofori**. He called it the pianoforte because it could play soft and loud, which was hardly possible on the older harpsichord. Famous composers such as Mozart, Beethoven and Chopin wrote many works for piano. A **pianist** can play whole melodies with accompaniment alone. Today there are also digital pianos that produce the sound electronically.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole row of keys on a keyboard instrument.
A large piano with horizontal strings and a lid that opens.
A thin wooden board that vibrates along and makes the sound louder.
A piece of felt that rests on the string and ends the note.

gewusst: Together, the strings of a concert grand piano pull on the frame with a force of about 20 tonnes.
The German word for piano, Klavier, comes from the Latin “clavis”, which means key.
In terms of physics, the piano is a percussion instrument and a string instrument at the same time.

teile.einleitung: A semiconductor is a material that conducts electric current or not, depending on the conditions. It therefore lies between good conductors such as copper and insulators such as glass. Without semiconductors there would be no computers, smartphones, LED lamps or solar cells.
wichtigste: Semiconductors conduct electricity less well than metals but better than insulators.
The most important semiconductor is silicon, which is obtained from quartz sand.
With heat or light, semiconductors conduct better.
By doping, that is deliberately adding foreign atoms, you control how well they conduct.
Semiconductors are used to build diodes, transistors, LEDs and solar cells.
A computer chip contains billions of tiny transistors.
The transistor was invented in the USA in 1947.

abschnitte.text: Substances can be sorted by how well they conduct electricity. Metals such as copper are good **conductors**; plastic and glass are insulators. **Semiconductors** lie in between: at very low temperatures they conduct almost nothing, but with heat, light or an applied voltage they do. This ability to be controlled makes them so valuable.

The best-known semiconductor material is **silicon**. After oxygen it is the second most common element in the Earth's crust and is found, for example, in quartz sand. For chips it is made extremely pure and cut into thin slices called wafers. Other semiconductors are germanium or gallium arsenide, which is found in some LEDs and lasers.

Pure silicon conducts only a little. If you mix in tiny amounts of other atoms such as phosphorus or boron, this changes a great deal. This process is called **doping**. It produces n-type semiconductors with extra free electrons and p-type semiconductors with so-called holes, and where the two meet, useful components are created.

In 1947 John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley invented the **transistor** at Bell Labs in the USA. A transistor is a tiny electronic switch with no moving parts. Modern computer chips contain billions of them on an area smaller than a fingernail. They calculate, store and control everything, from the mobile phone to the washing machine.

Semiconductors can turn light and electricity into each other. In a **light-emitting diode** electricity produces light; in a **solar cell** light produces electricity. On many Swiss roofs, solar cells made of silicon now supply electricity. The camera in a smartphone also uses semiconductors to turn light into pixels.

Semiconductor chips are found in cars, games consoles, traffic lights and hospitals. They are made in huge, dust-free factories, above all in Taiwan, South Korea, the USA and China. A shortage of chips can slow down whole industries, as was seen during the coronavirus pandemic. Swiss universities such as ETH Zurich and EPFL also research new semiconductor technologies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that lets electricity flow well, for example copper.
A common chemical element and the most important semiconductor.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to change how well a material conducts.
A tiny electronic switch and amplifier made of semiconductor material.
A thin, round slice of silicon on which chips are made.

gewusst: A modern smartphone chip contains more transistors than there are people on Earth.
“Silicon Valley” in California is named after the semiconductor silicon.
The clean rooms of chip factories are a thousand times cleaner than an operating theatre.

teile.einleitung: Isaac Newton was an English physicist and mathematician who lived more than 300 years ago. He was the first to explain that the same force makes an apple fall to the ground and keeps the Moon in its orbit. Pupils still learn his laws of motion today.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton lived from 1643 to 1727 in England.
He was professor of mathematics at the University of Cambridge.
He explained gravity as a force with which all bodies attract each other.
He set out three basic laws of motion.
With a prism he showed that white light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.
He improved the telescope by using a mirror instead of a lens.
Later he ran the Royal Mint in London.

abschnitte.text: Isaac Newton was born at the beginning of 1643 in **Woolsthorpe** in England and died in London in 1727. He studied at the University of **Cambridge** and became professor of mathematics there in 1669. He was a physicist, mathematician and astronomer all at once. He is regarded as one of the most important natural scientists in history.

According to the story, Newton saw an apple fall from a tree and wondered why it falls straight down. He realised that the same **gravity** acts on the apple and on the Moon. The Moon stays in its orbit because the Earth attracts it. Newton described this force in the **law of gravitation**, which he published in 1687 in his book “Principia”. The famous apple tree still stands in Woolsthorpe today.

The first law is called the **law of inertia**: a ball at rest stays where it is if nothing pushes it. The second law says that a larger force accelerates an object more strongly. The third law states **action equals reaction**: every force has an equal opposite force. That is why a balloon shoots forwards when air rushes out of the back.

Newton let sunlight pass through a triangular piece of glass, a **prism**. In this way he showed that white light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow. He also built a **reflecting telescope**, which works with a curved mirror instead of lenses. Telescopes like this are still used in astronomy today.

From 1696 Newton worked for the Royal **Mint** in London and later ran it. There he fought counterfeiters and made sure the coins were better. From 1703 he was President of the Royal Society, a famous society of scholars. He was buried in **Westminster Abbey** in London.

The unit of force is called the **newton** in his honour. His laws can be used to calculate how rockets fly and how bridges stay up. Newton also developed a new method of calculation, **calculus**, at almost the same time as the German Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Only Albert Einstein extended Newton's picture of gravity more than 200 years later.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force with which all bodies attract each other.
An object tends to stay as it is: at rest or in steady motion.
Triangular piece of glass that splits light into its colours.
Unit of force, abbreviated N.

gewusst: When the plague broke out in England, the university closed, and at home Newton had time for many of his most important ideas.
Newton was knighted and was therefore allowed to call himself “Sir Isaac Newton”.
Cuttings from Newton's apple tree now grow in gardens and universities all over the world.

teile.einleitung: Holography is a method with which you can record and reproduce three-dimensional images of objects. Such an image is called a hologram. Unlike an ordinary photo, it stores not only the brightness but also the phase of the light waves.
wichtigste: Dennis Gabor invented the principle of holography in 1947 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1971.
As well as the brightness, a hologram also stores the phase of the light wave.
When recording, an object wave and a reference wave overlap to form an interference pattern.
Classic holograms need coherent laser light.
If you break a piece off a transmission hologram, you can still see the whole image in it.
The Greek word part “holos” means “whole”.
In everyday life holograms are used above all as protection against forgery on identity cards, bank cards and banknotes.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary photo only shows how bright or dark an object is at each point. A **hologram** also stores the **phase** of the light waves, that is when their crests and troughs arrive. As a result it contains the complete information about the light wave. If you look at a hologram from different directions, you see the object from different sides. That is why the image looks three-dimensional, as if the object were really floating there.

A **laser beam** is split into two parts. One part lights up the object and is reflected by it; this is the object wave. The other part falls directly onto the photographic plate; this is the reference wave. On the plate the two waves overlap to form a fine pattern of stripes, the **interference**. If you later light up the developed plate with laser light again, the three-dimensional image is created anew.

For a clean interference pattern to form, the light waves must vibrate exactly in step. Such light is called **coherent**. Ordinary lamps give a jumble of waves, whereas lasers give very even light. Gabor had the idea as early as 1947, but the first laser was only built in 1960. After that the first really good holograms were made in the USA and in the Soviet Union.

In a classic **transmission hologram**, the information about the whole image is spread over the whole plate. If you break off a piece and light it up with laser light, you still see the whole image. But it is less sharp, and you can only look at it from a narrower angle. This fits the name, because “holos” means “whole” in Greek. In 1962 the Soviet physicist **Yuri Denisyuk** developed reflection holograms, which can also be viewed with ordinary white light.

We most often come across holograms as **protection against forgery**. They shine in rainbow colours on credit cards, identity cards, banknotes and branded products. Such security features are very difficult to copy. The Swiss firm OVD Kinegram from Zug specialises in such shimmering security images. By the way, when people talk about “holograms” at concerts, these are usually just clever projections onto glass or film.

begriffe.erklaerung: The overlapping of waves, which strengthen or cancel each other out.
Light whose waves vibrate exactly in step, as with a laser.
Tells you at which point in its vibration a wave is at the moment.
A light source that produces a very narrow and even beam of light.

gewusst: Dennis Gabor actually wanted to use his idea to improve electron microscopes.
In a real hologram you can look behind an object by moving your head.
Swiss banknotes also have shiny security features that change their appearance depending on the viewing angle.

teile.einleitung: Nuclear energy is the energy contained in the nuclei of atoms. In nuclear power stations it is released by splitting heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium and turned into electricity. In Switzerland nuclear energy provides a large share of the electricity, but it is also politically disputed.
wichtigste: Nuclear energy comes from the splitting or fusing of atomic nuclei.
Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered the fission of uranium at the end of 1938.
In light water reactors it is mainly uranium-235 that is split.
The moderator slows down the fast neutrons so that they can split more nuclei.
According to Einstein's formula E = mc², 1 gram of mass equals about 9 · 10^13 joules.
Beznau became Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station in 1969.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good in 2019.
Radioactive waste has to be stored safely for a very long time.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a tiny nucleus made of protons and neutrons. These particles are held together by enormous forces. If a heavy nucleus is split, part of this binding energy is released. According to Albert Einstein's formula **E = mc²**, just 1 gram of mass equals about 9 · 10^13 joules, as much energy as burning several thousand tonnes of coal.

At the end of 1938 the German chemists **Otto Hahn** and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin discovered that uranium nuclei burst when bombarded with neutrons. The physicist Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained the process shortly afterwards. In 1942 Enrico Fermi built the first nuclear reactor in Chicago. Sadly, nuclear fission was also used for atomic bombs, which fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

abschnitte.titel: How a nuclear power station works
abschnitte.text: The reactor contains fuel rods with uranium, in which mainly **uranium-235** is split by slow neutrons. This produces new neutrons that split more nuclei: a **chain reaction**. The **moderator**, ordinary water in light water reactors, slows down the fast neutrons so that they split uranium-235 better. The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine with a generator, and control rods regulate the power.

Beznau in the canton of Aargau became Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station in 1969. Mühleberg, Gösgen and Leibstadt followed later. **Mühleberg** in the canton of Bern was shut down for good in December 2019. The remaining plants together supply about a third of Swiss electricity, a little more or less depending on the year.

Nuclear power stations emit hardly any CO₂ while running, but they carry risks. Serious accidents such as Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011 have contaminated large areas with radioactivity. In Switzerland, too, there was a serious accident in 1969 at the experimental reactor in Lucens. Spent fuel rods stay **radioactive** for a very long time, which is why Nagra is planning a deep geological repository in the Nördlich Lägern area.

In 2017 Swiss voters approved the Energy Strategy 2050, under which no new nuclear power stations will be authorised. The existing plants may keep running as long as they are safe. For some years there has been political debate again about whether new nuclear power stations should be allowed. Opinions on this differ among the population.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny centre of an atom made of protons and neutrons.
Process in which each splitting triggers new splittings.
Substance in the reactor that slows down neutrons, for example water.
Decay of atomic nuclei that produces dangerous radiation.
Store deep in the rock for radioactive waste.

gewusst: A single uranium fuel pellet, hardly bigger than a thimble, provides about as much energy as around a tonne of coal.
The Beznau nuclear power station is one of the oldest nuclear power stations still running in the world.
The cooling towers of Gösgen and Leibstadt give off only water vapour, not smoke.

teile.einleitung: Wood is the hard material that the trunks, branches and roots of trees and shrubs are made of. In physics wood is exciting because it usually floats on water, even though a tree trunk can weigh tonnes. Here you can find out why, and why some wood sinks anyway.
wichtigste: Wood consists mainly of cellulose and lignin and contains many tiny spaces filled with air.
Most kinds of wood have a lower density than water and therefore float.
A floating wooden board lies only partly under water; the rest sticks out.
If you push a block of wood under water and let go, buoyancy makes it shoot upwards.
Balsa wood is especially light and is used for model aeroplanes.
There are very heavy woods, for example lignum vitae, that sink in water.
Wood that soaks up water for years can also sink.
In the past the fact that wood floats was used to transport tree trunks on rivers.

abschnitte.text: Trees form new wood every year, and this creates the **annual rings**. Wood consists of long cells whose walls are made mainly of **cellulose** and **lignin**. Cellulose makes the wood strong when pulled, and lignin makes it hard and strong when pressed. Inside the cells there are many spaces filled with air or water.

Whether an object floats depends on its **density**, that is on how much mass there is in a certain volume. Water has a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimetre. Spruce wood has roughly half the density of water, oak about three quarters of it. That is why a wooden stick floats while an iron nail of the same size sinks at once, because iron is almost eight times as dense as water.

Every body in water feels an upward force, **buoyancy**. It is as great as the weight of the water pushed aside, as the Greek Archimedes already recognised. A wooden board sinks only until the water pushed aside weighs as much as the whole board. If you push wood completely under water, the buoyancy is greater than its weight, and it shoots upwards.

**Balsa wood** from Central and South America is one of the lightest woods in the world and often has less than a fifth of the density of water. That is why model aeroplanes are built from it, and in the past even rafts. Quite different is **lignum vitae** from the Caribbean, which is so dense that it sinks in water. Wood that lies in water for a long time can also sink, because water fills the air spaces in the cells.

About a third of Switzerland is covered with forest, and the most common tree species is the spruce. In the past, tree trunks were tied together into **rafts** and floated down rivers such as the Aare, the Reuss or the Rhine. This timber rafting was cheaper than transport by horse and cart. Today Swiss wood is used for houses, furniture, paper and as fuel for heating.

A little wooden boat floats in the bath because it is lighter than the water it pushes aside. Wood conducts heat badly, which is why a wooden spoon in hot tea does not feel as hot as a metal spoon. Wood is also a good electrical **insulator**, as long as it is dry. Because wood grows back, it is considered an environmentally friendly building material.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tells you how heavy a substance is in relation to its size.
The force with which water pushes an object upwards.
A substance in wood that makes the cell walls hard and strong.
Transporting tree trunks tied together on rivers.

gewusst: Balsa wood can be lighter than cork.
There are woods such as lignum vitae that are so heavy that they sink like a stone.
A freshly felled tree contains so much water that it can make up about half its weight.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais and, at 285 metres, the tallest structure in Switzerland. It holds back the Lac des Dix, whose water is used to produce electricity. It is the tallest gravity dam in the world.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence dam is 285 metres high.
It is the tallest structure in Switzerland and the tallest gravity dam in the world.
It was completed at the beginning of the 1960s, more than 60 years ago.
Behind the dam lies the Lac des Dix reservoir.
The water is used to produce electricity.
Through pumping stations and about 100 km of tunnels, water from other valleys as far as the Zermatt area reaches the lake.
French is spoken in the valley.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence stands in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in French-speaking Lower Valais. The top of the dam lies at about 2365 metres above sea level, right in the high mountains. From Sion you can reach it in summer by PostBus. All around are the peaks and glaciers of the Valais Alps. In winter the road to the dam is closed.

The dam was built from the early 1950s and was finished in 1961. At **285 metres** it is almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower without its aerial. The dam is about 700 metres long, 15 metres thick at the top and about 200 metres thick at the bottom. About 6 million cubic metres of **concrete** were needed to build it. With that you could build a wall 6000 kilometres long that is one metre high and one metre wide.

The Grande Dixence is a **gravity dam**. It withstands the water pressure by its enormous weight alone, rather like a giant wedge. At the bottom of the reservoir, at a water depth of 280 m, there is a **hydrostatic pressure** of about 27 bar. That is why the dam is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. Engineers constantly monitor whether the dam moves.

The **Lac des Dix** can store up to 400 million cubic metres of water. Most of the water comes from glaciers; there are 35 glaciers in its catchment area. Because its own streams are not enough, extra water is brought in from other valleys as far as the Zermatt area. For this there are pumping stations and about 100 km of **tunnels** through the mountains. In summer the lake fills with meltwater, and in winter it is emptied to produce electricity.

The water flows through tunnels and penstocks down into the Rhône valley to the power stations. There it drives **Pelton turbines**, which turn generators. When it went into operation at the end of the 1990s, the associated **Bieudron** power station held the world record for the greatest head of a hydroelectric power station, almost 1900 metres. One cubic metre of water falling 1000 m supplies about 2.7 kWh of energy. The plants produce valuable electricity for the whole of Switzerland, especially in winter.

The Grande Dixence is a popular place for an outing. In summer you can take a guided tour through the inside of the dam. A cable car takes you up to the top of the dam, from which you have an impressive view of the lake and down the valley. A hiking path runs along the shore of the lake to its far end.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that blocks off a valley and holds back water to form a lake.
A dam that holds back the water by its great weight alone.
An artificial lake behind a dam.
A passage through the mountain through which water flows.
The difference in height that the water falls down to the turbine.

gewusst: The dam weighs more than the Great Pyramid of Cheops in Egypt.
Before today's dam there was a smaller dam, the Dixence, which now lies sunk in the Lac des Dix.
The Lac des Dix is the largest reservoir in Switzerland by volume of water.

teile.einleitung: Kilometres per hour is the unit we use in everyday life to give speeds. It appears on road signs, on the speedometer in the car and on the bike computer. The number tells you how many kilometres you would travel in one hour if you kept going at the same speed.
wichtigste: Kilometres per hour is abbreviated km/h.
60 km/h means: in one hour you travel 60 kilometres.
In Switzerland cars may normally drive at no more than 50 km/h in built-up areas, 80 km/h outside them and 120 km/h on motorways.
A person walks at about 5 km/h.
On slow e-bikes in Switzerland the motor helps up to 25 km/h.
If you drive at 100 km/h for 2 hours, you travel 200 kilometres.
In physics speed is often measured in metres per second; 1 m/s is 3.6 km/h.

abschnitte.text: **Speed** tells you how fast something is moving. With km/h you divide the distance travelled in kilometres by the time in hours. If a car drives at 60 km/h, it covers 60 kilometres in one hour and 30 kilometres in half an hour. But this calculation is only right if the speed stays the same the whole time.

With the formula distance equals speed times time you can work out a lot. A train that travels at 100 km/h for 2 hours covers 200 kilometres. If a bike goes at 20 km/h and a car at 60 km/h, the car is 40 km/h faster, or three times as fast. In physics **metres per second** are often used: you divide km/h by 3.6, so 36 km/h becomes 10 m/s.

In Switzerland there are general **speed limits**: 50 km/h in built-up areas, 80 km/h outside them, 100 km/h on expressways and 120 km/h on motorways. In residential areas there are many **30 zones**, whose signs show a large 30. In shared zones the limit is just 20 km/h, and pedestrians have priority. The police check speeds with speed cameras.

A person walks at about 5 km/h, and jogging is often 10 km/h. By bike people usually ride at 15 to 25 km/h in everyday life. On slow **e-bikes** in Switzerland the motor assists up to 25 km/h, and on fast e-bikes up to 45 km/h. A cheetah can briefly reach about 100 km/h, and high-speed trains travel at over 300 km/h.

In a car the **speedometer** shows the current speed in km/h. It measures how fast the wheels are turning and works out the speed from that. On a bike this is done by a small bike computer or an app with GPS. In Great Britain and the USA, on the other hand, speedometers usually show miles per hour, abbreviated mph.

For huge speeds km/h is almost too small: sound travels at about 1200 km/h in air. The Earth moves round the Sun at about 107,000 km/h without our feeling it. Ships and aircraft often give their speed in **knots**; one knot is one nautical mile per hour, or about 1.85 km/h. A snail, on the other hand, manages only a few metres per hour.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much distance you cover in a certain time.
The highest speed allowed on a road.
Display in a vehicle that shows the speed.
Unit of speed in shipping and aviation, about 1.85 km/h.

gewusst: Because at 50 km/h you travel almost 14 metres every second, the braking distance is so much longer at higher speeds.
Light travels at about 1.08 billion km/h, which makes it the fastest thing there is.
A crash at 50 km/h is about as violent as a fall from a height of around 10 metres.

teile.einleitung: A candle is a piece of wax with a string in the middle that gives a calm flame when lit. In the past it was one of the most important sources of light; today it mainly creates atmosphere, for example during Advent. There is a surprising amount of physics and chemistry in a small candle flame.
wichtigste: Most candles are made of wax, for example paraffin wax, stearin or beeswax.
The string in the middle is called the wick.
The heat of the flame melts the wax, and the wick draws it upwards.
It is not the solid wax that burns, but its vapour.
A candle needs oxygen; under a glass it goes out.
You must never leave a burning candle alone.
During Advent one more candle is lit each week.

abschnitte.text: A **candle** consists of a fuel, usually **wax**, and a **wick** of braided cotton. Paraffin wax, which is made from crude oil, is often used. Stearin from plant or animal fats is also common. The wax for some candles comes from bees, which use it to build their honeycombs. Beeswax candles smell slightly of honey.

When you light the wick, the heat of the flame melts the wax at the top of the candle. The liquid wax rises up the wick, like water in blotting paper. In the heat it evaporates, and only this **wax vapour** burns with the **oxygen** in the air. This produces carbon dioxide, water vapour, heat and light. Over time there is less and less wax, until the candle has burnt down.

A candle flame has different zones. Down at the wick it glows bluish; there the gas burns with plenty of air. The bright yellow part comes from tiny glowing **soot particles**. The hottest part of the flame is over 1000 °C. When you blow out the candle, a thin thread of smoke rises; this is cooling wax vapour, which you can even light again with a match.

If you put a glass over a burning candle, it goes out after a short time because the oxygen in the glass is used up. Under a large glass it burns longer than under a small one, because there is more air in it. Around 1860 the English scientist **Michael Faraday** gave famous lectures for children about the candle. In them he showed how much science there is in a single flame. But experiments with fire should only be done with adults.

Long before there was electric light, candles and oil lamps were the most important sources of light in homes. Today people light candles mainly for a cosy atmosphere or for celebrations. During **Advent** one more candle is lit on the Advent wreath each week. In Switzerland **candle dipping** is popular in the weeks before Christmas: you dip a wick into liquid wax again and again. The important thing is: never leave a burning candle alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The string in the candle that carries the liquid wax to the flame.
A wax made from crude oil.
A gas in the air that every fire needs in order to burn.
Fine black carbon particles produced when burning is incomplete.

gewusst: The Advent wreath was invented in the 19th century by the Hamburg pastor Johann Hinrich Wichern for children in an orphanage.
In the past the night was sometimes divided up with candles that had marks for the hours scratched into them.
In the weightlessness of a space station a candle flame burns almost perfectly round and bluish.

teile.einleitung: An interferometer is a measuring device that overlaps light waves to measure tiny differences in length. This produces bright and dark fringes that react even to shifts of a fraction of a wavelength. Huge interferometers have even detected the trembling of space itself, gravitational waves.
wichtigste: An interferometer splits a beam of light into two beams and later brings them together again.
The component that splits the beam is called a beam splitter.
Depending on the path length, the waves reinforce or cancel each other, creating bright and dark interference fringes.
If one light path gets longer by half a wavelength, bright and dark swap places.
In 1907 Albert Michelson became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Physics, partly for his interferometers.
The Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 found no evidence of a luminiferous ether.
The LIGO detectors, with arms 4 kilometres long, detected gravitational waves for the first time in 2015.

abschnitte.text: Light behaves like a wave with crests and troughs. When two waves meet so that crest falls on crest, they reinforce each other; this is called **constructive interference**. When crest falls on trough, they cancel out; this is **destructive interference**. You can see something similar when water waves from two stones cross in a pond.

In the best-known setup, light hits a **beam splitter**, a half-silvered mirror. One beam goes straight on to a mirror, the other sideways to a second mirror. Both are reflected back and brought together again at the beam splitter. If you move one mirror by 1 micrometre with a wavelength of 500 nanometres, 4 **interference fringes** pass by, because the light path there and back becomes twice as long.

In the **Mach-Zehnder interferometer** a beam of light is sent along separate paths with two beam splitters and two mirrors and brought together again at the end. It was described in 1891 and 1892 by Ludwig Zehnder and Ludwig Mach. The **Fabry-Pérot interferometer** consists of two parallel, partly mirrored surfaces between which the light travels back and forth many times. This lets it distinguish wavelengths very finely, and it is used in lasers, for example.

In the 19th century many researchers believed that light needed an invisible substance, the **luminiferous ether**, to travel through. In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley in the USA wanted to measure how the Earth moves through this ether. But their interferometer showed no difference, however it was turned. This result later helped Albert Einstein with his **theory of relativity** of 1905.

The two **LIGO** detectors in the US states of Washington and Louisiana are huge Michelson interferometers with arms 4 kilometres long. In September 2015 they recorded **gravitational waves** for the first time, coming from two merging black holes. The arms changed their length by less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton. This discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017.

In factories, interferometers check whether lenses and mirrors are ground perfectly smooth. In **precision measurement** they measure lengths to within nanometres. In fibre optic networks, components based on the Mach-Zehnder principle control the light signals. Radio telescopes are also linked together into interferometers to get sharper pictures of the sky.

begriffe.erklaerung: Overlapping of waves in which they reinforce or cancel each other.
Half-silvered mirror that divides a beam of light into two parts.
Distance from one wave crest to the next.
Invisible substance once thought to carry light. It does not exist.
Tiny distortion of space and time that spreads out like a wave.

gewusst: The LIGO interferometers are so sensitive that they even have to filter out passing lorries and ocean waves on the coast.
With his measurements Albert Michelson also determined the speed of light more accurately than anyone before him.
The shimmering colours of soap bubbles come from the same interference that an interferometer uses.

teile.einleitung: A wedge is a block that comes to a point at the front, and it is one of humanity's oldest simple machines. It can be used to split, separate, clamp or lift things. Knives, axes, nails and even our front teeth work on the principle of the wedge.
wichtigste: A wedge is an object that narrows to an edge or point.
You can think of it as made up of two inclined planes.
A wedge redirects a force sideways, across the direction of the blow.
The slimmer a wedge is, the less force you need to split something.
Knives, axes, chisels, nails and ploughs work like a wedge.
A doorstop holds a door open by wedging itself in place.

abschnitte.text: A **wedge** is a block of wood, metal or stone that is wide on one side and narrows to a point on the other. The wide side is called the **back**, the pointed side the **edge**. You can think of a wedge as made up of two **inclined planes** lying back to back. It is one of the five classic simple machines, together with the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane and the screw. Simple machines help you achieve a lot with little force.

If you hit the back of a wedge with a hammer, the force pushes it forwards. The sloping sides redirect this force **sideways**, across the direction of the blow. In this way the wedge pushes the material apart, for example a piece of wood. A pointed wedge goes in more easily because the force is concentrated on a smaller area. The longer a wedge is compared with the width of its back, the less force you need to strike it with, but it has to go in further.

The kitchen **knife** is a thin wedge that cuts up bread or vegetables. A **nail** is pointed at the front so that it pushes the wood apart like a wedge. Our **front teeth** work like little wedges when we bite. In the slider of a zip, a tiny wedge separates the teeth when you open it. Pushed under a door, a doorstop holds it open, and wheel chocks secure parked lorries.

The **axe** and the splitting wedge help when splitting firewood, as foresters do in Swiss forests. Stone sculptors work with the **chisel**, which also acts as a wedge. The **plough** cuts open the soil with its wedge-shaped share and turns it over. The pointed bow of a ship also works like a wedge and pushes the water aside. Express trains and aircraft have a pointed shape so that they cut through the air more easily.

As early as the Stone Age people made sharp stone tools, such as the **hand axe**, which first appeared more than a million years ago. Stonemasons used to split large blocks of stone by hammering in wedges. To do this they drilled a row of holes and drove wedges into them until the stone broke along the line. This is how stone was obtained for houses, bridges and monuments. This method is still used in quarries today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device such as a lever or wedge that saves force or redirects it.
A sloping surface up which loads can be pushed with less force.
The wide side of a wedge, which you strike.
The sharp, pointed side of a wedge or knife.
A Stone Age stone tool that was held in the fist.

gewusst: In ancient Egypt stonemasons are said to have also used wooden wedges that swelled up with water and so split the stone.
You can also think of a screw as a wedge wound in a spiral around a rod.
A well-sharpened knife cuts better because its edge is a particularly narrow wedge.

teile.einleitung: ITER is a huge experimental reactor with which researchers from all over the world want to show that energy can be obtained from nuclear fusion. It is being built in southern France and is meant to fuse atomic nuclei in a similar way to the Sun. The name refers to the Latin word “iter”, which means “the way”.
wichtigste: ITER is being built in France, at Cadarache near the town of Aix-en-Provence.
ITER is a fusion reactor of the tokamak type.
The aim is to produce ten times more fusion power than is put in to heat the plasma.
The plasma is meant to reach about 150 million degrees Celsius.
Superconducting magnet coils produce strong fields with almost no electrical losses.
The project is supported by 7 members (as of 2025).
ITER will not feed electricity into the public grid, because it is an experimental facility.

abschnitte.text: In the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones and release tremendous energy; this is called **nuclear fusion**. ITER is meant to fuse the hydrogen types **deuterium** and tritium into helium. This also produces fast neutrons, which give off their energy as heat. Unlike nuclear fission, it does not create long-lived radioactive fuel waste.

A **tokamak** is a ring-shaped chamber that looks like a giant doughnut. Inside it the gas becomes so hot that it turns into a **plasma**, in which electrons and atomic nuclei fly around separately. No material could withstand 150 million degrees, so strong magnetic fields keep the plasma away from the walls. The idea of the tokamak came from the Soviet Union in the 1950s.

ITER's magnet coils are made of **superconductors**, which conduct current without resistance. For this they have to be cooled with liquid helium to about minus 269 degrees. So right next to the hottest place on Earth is one of the coldest. The whole tokamak facility weighs about 23,000 tonnes, roughly as much as three Eiffel Towers.

The **European Union**, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA take part in ITER. The members supply many components from their own factories, which are then assembled in France. The agreement was signed in 2006, and building work on the site began soon afterwards. The timetable has had to be postponed several times; according to the 2024 plan, research operation is to start around 2034.

With about 50 megawatts of heating power, ITER is meant to produce about 500 megawatts of **fusion power**, ten times as much. If this succeeds, it would be an important step towards later fusion power stations that actually supply electricity. Such a power station, often called **DEMO**, is to be built only after ITER. One day fusion energy could provide a lot of electricity without greenhouse gases.

Nuclear fusion is also researched in Switzerland. The **Swiss Plasma Center** at EPFL in Lausanne has its own tokamak, called TCV. There researchers study which shape of plasma is most stable. Swiss companies and institutes have also supplied components and expertise for ITER.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of light atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
Extremely hot gas in which electrons and atomic nuclei are separated.
Ring-shaped facility in which magnetic fields hold a hot plasma.
Material that, when very cold, conducts current with no resistance at all.
Heavy hydrogen, which is also found in sea water.

gewusst: The plasma in ITER is meant to become about ten times hotter than the inside of the Sun.
The word tokamak is a Russian abbreviation and means roughly “ring-shaped chamber with magnetic coils”.
Although the facility is huge, there are only a few grams of fuel in the plasma at any one time.

teile.einleitung: The degree Celsius, abbreviated °C, is the unit with which we measure temperature in Switzerland and almost everywhere in the world. At 0 °C water freezes, at 100 °C it boils. The unit is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius.
wichtigste: The symbol °C stands for degree Celsius.
The unit is named after the Swede Anders Celsius.
Between the freezing point and the boiling point of water there are 100 equal parts.
Temperatures below 0 °C are written with a minus sign, for example -5 °C.
In the USA temperature is usually measured in degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life.
In science the unit kelvin is often used, where 0 °C equals 273.15 kelvin.
The lowest temperature at a Swiss weather station was measured in La Brévine in 1987: -41.8 °C.

abschnitte.text: The degree Celsius is a **unit of temperature**. The scale is fixed at two points for water: the **freezing point** at 0 °C and the **boiling point** at 100 °C, each at normal air pressure at sea level. In between it is divided into 100 equal parts. That is why it used to be called the centigrade scale. A thermometer shows the temperature in degrees Celsius.

**Anders Celsius** lived from 1701 to 1744 and was an astronomer at the University of Uppsala in Sweden. In 1742 he proposed a temperature scale with 100 parts. The surprising thing is that in his scale the boiling point was at 0 and the freezing point at 100. Only shortly after his death was the scale turned round so that higher numbers mean warmer. Celsius also studied the northern lights and took part in an expedition to Lapland.

If it is 8 °C in the morning and 15 °C in the afternoon, it has become 7 degrees warmer. With temperatures below zero you have to be careful: if the temperature rises from -6 °C to 9 °C, it becomes 15 degrees warmer. If it is 3 °C and it gets 5 degrees colder, the thermometer shows -2 °C. Of several temperatures below zero, the one with the smallest number after the minus is the warmest, so -5 °C is warmer than -25 °C. The average of -2 °C, 4 °C and 7 °C is calculated like this: 9 divided by 3 gives 3 °C.

In the USA **degrees Fahrenheit** are mostly used in everyday life. There water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F. In physics the unit **kelvin** is used, whose zero point is absolute zero. Absolute zero lies at -273.15 °C; it cannot get any colder. A difference of 1 kelvin is exactly as large as a difference of 1 degree Celsius.

The lowest temperature at a weather station in Switzerland was measured on 12 January 1987 in **La Brévine** in the Neuchâtel Jura: -41.8 °C. That is why the village is also called the Siberia of Switzerland. The highest temperature was measured in the heatwave summer of 2003 in **Grono** in the canton of the Grisons, at 41.5 °C. So there are more than 83 degrees between these two records. A person's body normally has a temperature of about 37 °C.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how warm or cold something is.
A measuring device for temperature.
The temperature at which water turns into ice, 0 °C.
The temperature at which water boils, 100 °C at sea level.
The physics unit of temperature, which starts at absolute zero.

gewusst: At -40 degrees a Celsius and a Fahrenheit thermometer show exactly the same number.
On the summit of Mount Everest water boils at only about 70 °C, because the air pressure there is much lower.
Originally, on Anders Celsius's scale, the boiling point was at 0 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Jacob Bernoulli was a mathematician from Basel who lived from 1655 to 1705. He is regarded as one of the founders of probability theory and belonged to the famous Bernoulli family of scholars from Basel. Many numbers, curves and equations still bear his name today.
wichtigste: Jacob Bernoulli was born in Basel in 1655 and was professor of mathematics at the University of Basel from 1687.
His main work on probability, the “Ars Conjectandi”, appeared in 1713 after his death.
He formulated a first version of the law of large numbers.
The Bernoulli numbers appear in sums of powers of natural numbers.
The figure-of-eight curve lying on its side called the lemniscate is named after him.
In 1690 he set the problem of finding the shape of a freely hanging rope, the catenary.
In 1697 he also solved the brachistochrone problem, whose solution is the cycloid.

abschnitte.text: Jacob Bernoulli was born in **Basel** in 1655, the son of a merchant family. His father wanted him to study theology, but Jacob secretly taught himself mathematics. After travelling to France, the Netherlands and England, he became a professor at the **University of Basel** in 1687. He died in Basel in 1705, and his gravestone stands in the cloister of Basel Minster.

Over several generations the Bernoullis produced important mathematicians and physicists. Jacob's younger brother **Johann Bernoulli** also became a famous mathematician. The two brothers often argued fiercely about who had found the better solution. Johann's son **Daniel Bernoulli** is known for the Bernoulli equation about flowing liquids.

In the **Ars Conjectandi**, which means “the art of conjecturing”, Jacob studied games of chance and random experiments. An experiment with only two outcomes, such as heads or tails, is called a **Bernoulli trial** today. The probability of getting exactly two heads in three coin tosses is 3/8. The probability of throwing a die four times without a single six is about 48 per cent.

Jacob proved that over a very large number of trials the relative frequency gets closer to the probability. This **law of large numbers** is one of the foundations of statistics. If you roll a die 60 times, you expect 10 sixes on average. The more often you roll, the closer the share of sixes comes to one sixth.

The **lemniscate** looks like a figure eight lying on its side and is used today as the infinity symbol. The **catenary** describes how a chain or rope hangs between two points. In the brachistochrone problem, people asked along which path a ball rolls fastest from one point to a lower one; the answer is the cycloid. Jacob also studied the logarithmic spiral, which fascinated him particularly.

The **Bernoulli numbers** play an important part in number theory and in working with series. The Bernoulli differential equation has the form y' + p(x)·y = q(x)·yⁿ and can be solved with a trick. While studying compound interest, Jacob came across a number that is known today as **Euler's number** e. Without his work there would be neither modern insurance nor weather forecasts with probabilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number between 0 and 1 that shows how certain it is that an event will happen.
Curve in the shape of a figure eight lying on its side.
Shape that a chain hung from two points takes on.
Path of a point on a rolling wheel.

gewusst: Jacob wanted a logarithmic spiral on his gravestone, but the stonemason mistakenly carved a different kind of spiral.
His gravestone bears the Latin motto “Eadem mutata resurgo”, which means “Though changed, I shall arise the same”.
The Bernoulli family produced at least eight well-known mathematicians.

teile.einleitung: The law of the lever explains how you can move heavy loads with little force using a bar and a pivot. It says: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. The Greek scholar Archimedes already described it over 2200 years ago.
wichtigste: A lever is in balance when effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.
Archimedes was the first to describe the law of the lever precisely.
If you double the effort arm, the force needed is halved.
If you need only a quarter of the force, your hand has to move four times as far.
A lever saves force, but not work.
Seesaws, scissors, pliers, wheelbarrows and crowbars are levers.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid body, for example a bar, that can turn around a **pivot**. The distance from the pivot to the place where you push is called the **effort arm**. The distance from the pivot to the load is called the load arm. With a long effort arm you can move a heavy load with a small force.

The law of the lever says: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. If a load of 600 N hangs 0.2 metres from the pivot, only 100 N is needed on an effort arm 1.2 metres long. With 50 N on an arm 2 metres long you can hold 400 N on a load arm 25 centimetres long. The product of force and arm is called **torque**.

You want to lift a stone weighing 2800 N with a crowbar 1.5 metres long. If the pivot is 10 centimetres from the stone, the effort arm is 1.4 metres long. Then only 200 N is needed at the end, about as much as you need to hold 20 kilograms. In return, though, the end has to move 14 times as far as the stone.

A **seesaw** on the playground is a two-sided lever with the pivot in the middle. A lighter child can balance a heavier one if it sits further out. Scissors, pliers, nutcrackers, bottle openers and wheelbarrows are levers too. Even our forearm works like a lever, with the elbow as the pivot.

The Greek scholar **Archimedes** lived in the 3rd century BC in Syracuse in Sicily. He was the first to describe exactly how levers work. Famous is the saying attributed to him that with a fixed point and a long enough lever he could move the Earth. With this he recognised that levers can move almost any load.

A lever saves force, but not **work**. According to the golden rule of mechanics, whatever you save in force you have to add in distance. If you need only a quarter of the force, your hand moves four times as far as the load. Force times distance stays the same on both sides.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which a lever turns.
The distance from the pivot to the place where you apply the force.
The distance from the pivot to the load.
Force times lever arm, that is how strongly a force makes something turn.

gewusst: When you open a door you use a lever: it is much easier right at the outer edge by the handle than close to the hinges.
The big arm of a construction crane has heavy concrete weights at its short end so that the lever stays in balance.
The ancient Romans and Egyptians used levers to move huge blocks of stone.

teile.einleitung: A hydraulic press is a machine that uses a liquid to turn a small force into a huge force. It consists of two connected cylinders with pistons of different sizes. It is used to press sheet metal, forge metal or lift cars.
wichtigste: The increase in force comes from two pistons of different sizes.
The pressure in the liquid is the same under both pistons.
The forces are in the same ratio as the areas of the pistons.
With piston areas of 10 and 200 square centimetres, 50 newtons become a full 1000 newtons.
To gain force, the small piston has to travel a much longer distance.
Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in England in 1795.
The hydraulic car jack uses the same principle.

abschnitte.text: A hydraulic press has two **cylinders** that are connected at the bottom by a pipe and filled with oil. One cylinder holds a small piston, the other a large one. When you push the small piston down, oil is forced into the large cylinder and lifts the large piston. A valve stops the oil from flowing back.

**Pressure** is force divided by area, and it is the same throughout the liquid. So the force on the small piston divided by its area equals the force on the large piston divided by its area. If the small piston has 10 square centimetres and the large one 200, the area is 20 times larger, and 50 newtons become 1000 newtons. The other way round, with 5 and 100 square centimetres you need only 100 newtons on the small piston to get 2000 newtons on the large one.

The press does not give you any energy for free. What you gain in force, you lose in **distance**: if the large piston is 20 times larger, it rises by only 1 centimetre when the small one is pushed down by 20 centimetres. The work, meaning force times distance, stays the same on both sides. This principle is called the **golden rule of mechanics** and also applies to levers and pulleys.

The English inventor Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in 1795. He also invented a particularly secure lock and improved the flushing toilet. His press was based on Blaise Pascal's law about how pressure spreads in liquids. It became one of the most important machines of the Industrial Revolution.

In factories, giant presses shape car doors and roofs out of sheet steel. Scrap presses squash old cars into small cubes. Every garage has a hydraulic **car jack**, which lets you lift a car with little effort when changing a wheel. Hydraulic presses are also used to press fruit, oil seeds or waste paper.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a particular area.
Unit of force, abbreviated N.
Movable disc that slides up and down inside a cylinder.
Tool used to lift a car a little way.

gewusst: The largest hydraulic presses in the world reach forces of many tens of thousands of tonnes and forge aircraft parts in one piece.
With a small hydraulic car jack, even a child can lift a car a few centimetres.
The principle of the hydraulic press is based on a discovery by Blaise Pascal, after whom the unit of pressure is also named.

teile.einleitung: The high jump is an athletics event in which, after a run-up, you have to jump as high as possible over a bar. Since the 1960s almost all athletes have jumped backwards over the bar using the Fosbury flop. There is a lot of physics behind every jump.
wichtigste: In the high jump you jump over a horizontal bar after a run-up.
The high jump is part of athletics.
The best-known technique is the Fosbury flop, in which you jump backwards over the bar.
You land on a thick, soft mat.
If the bar falls down, the attempt does not count.
The men's world record is 2.45 m.
Every jumper comes down again, because gravity pulls them back.

abschnitte.text: The jumper runs towards the **bar** in a curve and takes off from one leg. Then he turns in the air and tries to cross the bar without knocking it off. He is allowed to land on a thick **mat**. If the bar falls down, the attempt does not count. An athlete has three attempts at each height, and anyone who fails three times in a row is out.

In the past people jumped with the **scissors** or the straddle, in which you rolled over the bar face down. The American **Dick Fosbury**, on the other hand, jumped backwards, with his back to the bar. With this technique he won the gold medal at the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City. The flop only became possible with soft foam mats, because you land on your back. Today almost all high jumpers use the **Fosbury flop**.

At take-off, part of the **kinetic energy** from the run-up is turned into height. After that, **gravity** inevitably pulls the jumper back down. A trick: in the flop the body bends like an arch over the bar. The **centre of gravity** can even pass just below the bar while the body slides over it bit by bit. In this way the jumper saves energy and gets higher.

The men's world record was set by the Cuban **Javier Sotomayor** in Salamanca in 1993 with 2.45 m. That is clearly higher than most ceilings. Many top jumpers are tall and have long legs. The best women also jump over 2 metres. In the **pole vault**, in which you catapult yourself upwards with a flexible pole, athletes even get over 6 metres high.

In Switzerland the high jump is done in many athletics clubs and in school sport. At the annual athletics meeting **Weltklasse Zürich** in the Letzigrund stadium, the best high jumpers in the world often compete. For children there are competitions with low bars and soft mats. Speed, jumping power and good technique are important. Those who practise early learn the right curved run-up most easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: The horizontal pole that you have to jump over in the high jump.
A technique in which you jump backwards over the bar with your back to it.
The point at which you can imagine the whole weight of a body being concentrated.
A sport with running, jumping and throwing.

gewusst: At first people smiled at Dick Fosbury, until he became Olympic champion with his backwards technique.
In the Fosbury flop the jumper's centre of gravity can stay below the bar.
The men's high jump world record has not been improved since 1993.

teile.einleitung: The Leibstadt nuclear power station is in the canton of Aargau, right on the Rhine at the border with Germany. It is the newest and most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland. Its huge cooling tower with its white plume of steam can be seen from far away.
wichtigste: Leibstadt is the Swiss nuclear power station with the highest electrical output.
It started up in the 1980s, in 1984.
It is in the municipality of Leibstadt in the canton of Aargau, on the Rhine.
The heat from the reactor is turned into mechanical energy in the steam turbine.
The tall cooling tower gives off the waste heat from the condenser into the air.
The white plume above the cooling tower consists of condensed water droplets, not smoke.
A 1200 megawatt power station running for 8000 hours a year supplies 9.6 terawatt hours of electricity.

abschnitte.text: The power station is in the north of the canton of **Aargau**, in the municipality of Leibstadt. Right beside it flows the **Rhine**, which forms the border with Germany here. The power station takes water from the Rhine for cooling. The Beznau nuclear power station and the interim store in Würenlingen are also nearby. The region is therefore an important centre of Swiss electricity production.

In the **reactor** atomic nuclei of the fuel uranium are split, producing a great deal of heat. Leibstadt is a **boiling water reactor**: the water boils directly in the reactor and turns into steam. The steam drives the **steam turbine**, in which the heat is turned into mechanical energy. The turbine turns a generator that produces electricity. Then the steam is cooled in the condenser and flows back into the reactor as water.

Leibstadt's cooling tower is about 144 metres high and one of the tallest structures in Switzerland. It gives off the **waste heat** from the condenser into the air so that the Rhine does not get too warm. Inside the tower warm water trickles down while cool air flows in from below. Part of the water evaporates. Above the tower the moist air cools down and tiny **water droplets** form, which you see as a white plume.

With an output of more than 1200 megawatts, Leibstadt is the most powerful power station in Switzerland. If a power station like this runs for 8000 hours a year, it supplies about 9.6 terawatt hours of electricity. This covers a considerable part of Switzerland's electricity needs. Together with the Beznau and Gösgen nuclear power stations, Swiss nuclear power stations supplied about a third of the country's electricity around 2025. Most of it comes from **hydropower**.

The safety of Swiss nuclear power stations is monitored by the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate, **ENSI**. Radioactive waste has to be stored safely for a very long time, and in Switzerland a site in the Nördlich Lägern area has been proposed for a deep geological **repository**. After the Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011, Switzerland decided not to build any new nuclear power stations. But the existing ones may keep running as long as they are safe. The future of nuclear power continues to be debated in Swiss politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of heavy atomic nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy as heat.
