A reactor in which the water is boiled directly into steam for the turbine.
A tall tower in which waste heat is given off with air and evaporating water.
A very large amount of energy: one billion kilowatt hours.

gewusst: The white cloud above the cooling tower is not smoke, just water vapour that has condensed into droplets.
In cold, damp weather the steam plume from Leibstadt is especially large and can be seen from far away.
Leibstadt celebrated 40 years of operation in 2024.

teile.einleitung: In nuclear fission a heavy atomic nucleus, for example uranium, is split into two smaller nuclei. This releases a great deal of energy. This discovery of 1938 changed the world: it made nuclear power stations possible, but also atomic bombs.
wichtigste: In nuclear fission a heavy atomic nucleus breaks up into two lighter nuclei.
It is usually triggered by a neutron hitting the nucleus.
Energy and two or three new neutrons are released.
The new neutrons can split more nuclei, creating a chain reaction.
Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission at the end of 1938.
Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the process in terms of physics.
In nuclear power stations the chain reaction is controlled to produce electricity.

abschnitte.text: When a slow **neutron** hits a nucleus of uranium-235, the nucleus becomes unstable. It wobbles like a drop of water and bursts into two medium-weight nuclei, such as barium and krypton. Two or three new neutrons fly out. The fragments together are slightly lighter than the original nucleus, and this missing mass becomes energy.

The neutrons released can split more uranium nuclei, and these in turn split others. This creates a **chain reaction**, which can spread at tremendous speed. To start it, a minimum amount of fissile material is needed, the **critical mass**. In a nuclear power station control rods capture extra neutrons so that the reaction stays steady.

In December 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin, after bombarding uranium with neutrons, surprisingly found the much lighter element barium. The physicist **Lise Meitner**, who had fled from the Nazis to Sweden, together with Otto Frisch interpreted this as the splitting of the nucleus. Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 1944 for it. Meitner was left out, which is often criticised today.

In a **nuclear power station** the energy from fission heats water, and its steam drives turbines and generators. The first nuclear reactor was started in Chicago in 1942 under the direction of Enrico Fermi. In Switzerland the Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt power stations produce electricity in this way. The used fuel rods are highly radioactive and must be stored safely.

If the chain reaction runs unchecked, a tremendous explosion happens in a fraction of a second. In the Second World War, in 1945, atomic bombs were dropped on the Japanese cities of **Hiroshima** and Nagasaki, killing a great many people. Since then many countries have worked for nuclear disarmament. International negotiations on disarmament are held again and again in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: Particle with no charge in the atomic nucleus.
Heavy metal whose nuclei can be split.
Each splitting triggers new splittings.
Minimum amount of fissile material for a chain reaction to keep going by itself.

gewusst: The chemical element meitnerium is named after Lise Meitner.
In Gabon in West Africa there were natural nuclear reactors in uranium deposits about two billion years ago.
A single fission releases many millions of times more energy than burning one carbon atom.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Hertz was a German physicist who was the first to produce and detect electromagnetic waves. With this he laid the foundation for radio, television, mobile phones and Wi-Fi. The unit of frequency is named after him: the hertz.
wichtigste: Heinrich Hertz was born in Hamburg in 1857.
In Berlin he studied under the famous physicist Hermann von Helmholtz.
At the Technical College in Karlsruhe he detected electromagnetic waves.
He produced the waves with sparks across a spark gap.
Along the way he discovered that ultraviolet light makes it easier for sparks to jump.
Heinrich Hertz died in 1894 at the age of only 36.
Shortly afterwards Guglielmo Marconi used the waves Hertz had studied for wireless telegraphy.

abschnitte.text: **Heinrich Hertz** was born in Hamburg on 22 February 1857. Even as a child he was interested in technology and built his own devices. At first he wanted to become an engineer, but then he chose physics. In Berlin he studied under **Hermann von Helmholtz**, one of the most important physicists of his time. In 1880 he completed his doctorate.

The Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell had predicted that **electromagnetic waves** must exist. Hertz wanted to test this at the Technical College in Karlsruhe. From 1886 he made strong sparks jump between two metal balls, a **spark gap**. This produced waves that spread out through the room. As a result, small sparks jumped in a ring of wire a few metres away, and the proof was there.

Hertz showed that the waves behave like light: they are reflected and refracted and spread out very quickly. This made it clear that light is also an electromagnetic wave. Along the way he noticed that sparks jump more easily when ultraviolet light falls on the metal balls. This was the discovery of the **photoelectric effect**, which Albert Einstein later explained. In 1889 Hertz moved to the University of Bonn.

Heinrich Hertz fell seriously ill and died in Bonn on 1 January 1894. He was only 36 years old. His family produced other important researchers. His nephew **Gustav Hertz** received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1925 together with James Franck. Hertz himself did not live to see the great consequences of his discovery.

Just a few years later the Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** used the waves for wireless telegraphy. From this came radio, television, radar, mobile networks and Wi-Fi. In honour of Hertz, the unit of **frequency** is now called the hertz, abbreviated Hz. 1 hertz means one oscillation per second. A radio station on 100 megahertz sends out waves that oscillate 100 million times a second.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wave of electric and magnetic fields, for example light or radio waves.
A gap between two metal parts across which an electric spark jumps.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
Light knocks electrons out of a metal.

gewusst: Hertz is said to have claimed that his waves probably had no practical use.
Every time you read a screen's refresh rate in hertz, you come across his name.
The Wi-Fi in your home transmits at several billion hertz.

teile.einleitung: The kinetic theory of gases explains why gases behave the way they do. It pictures a gas as a huge number of tiny particles flying about wildly and constantly colliding. This makes it easy to understand the pressure and temperature of a gas.
wichtigste: A gas consists of a very large number of small particles moving quickly and randomly.
The pressure of a gas comes from the particles hitting the wall of the container.
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles.
If you double the absolute temperature, the average speed increases by a factor of the square root of 2.
At the same temperature all gas particles have the same kinetic energy on average, but light particles are faster.
The speeds of the particles follow the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
In 1738 the Basel scholar Daniel Bernoulli was one of the first to explain gas pressure through the movement of particles.

abschnitte.text: The **kinetic theory of gases** says that a gas consists of an unimaginable number of tiny particles, **atoms** or **molecules**. These particles fly through space in straight lines until they hit another particle or a wall. There is a lot of empty space between the particles, which is why gases are easy to compress. The word kinetic comes from Greek and means roughly “to do with movement”.

Every time a particle hits the wall, it pushes against it a tiny bit. Because there are billions and billions of such collisions every second, you feel an even **pressure**. If you pump more air into a balloon, more particles hit the skin and the pressure rises. If you heat the gas, the particles fly faster and hit harder, and the pressure rises then too.

According to the kinetic theory of gases, **temperature** is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The hotter a gas, the faster its particles move. Nitrogen molecules, which make up most of the air, fly at about 517 m/s on average at 300 K, roughly room temperature. That is faster than sound. If you double the absolute temperature, the average speed rises by a factor of the square root of 2, about 41 per cent.

At the same temperature, helium and oxygen particles have the same kinetic energy on average. Because helium atoms are much lighter, they have to fly faster. Helium atoms at 4 g/mol are on average about 2.8 times faster than oxygen molecules at 32 g/mol, because the square root of 8 is about 2.8. But not all particles are equally fast; the spread of speeds is described by the **Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution**.

As early as 1738 the Basel scholar **Daniel Bernoulli** explained gas pressure with moving particles in his book “Hydrodynamica”. In the 19th century Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell and Ludwig Boltzmann developed the theory mathematically. For a long time many researchers doubted whether atoms existed at all. Only when **Albert Einstein** explained Brownian motion with colliding molecules in 1905 was the theory generally accepted.

Under the microscope, tiny particles in water or air keep trembling back and forth. This **Brownian motion** was described in 1827 by the Scottish botanist Robert Brown. Einstein realised that the particles are pushed by invisible molecules hitting them unevenly from all sides. You see a similar effect when specks of dust dance in a sunbeam, although air currents usually help there too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smallest particle of a substance, made up of several atoms.
Force acting on an area; in gases it comes from the collisions of the particles.
Energy an object has because of its motion.
Trembling movement of small particles pushed by molecules.

gewusst: There are about 25 sextillion molecules in a single litre of air, that is 25 followed by 21 zeros.
At room temperature every air molecule collides with other molecules several billion times a second.
Daniel Bernoulli came from a famous family of scholars in Basel that produced several important mathematicians.

teile.einleitung: A gravitational field is the invisible area around every mass in which other masses are attracted. The Earth, the Moon and the Sun are surrounded by such fields. Because the gravitational field exists, apples fall to the ground and the Moon circles the Earth.
wichtigste: Every body with mass creates a gravitational field around it.
Gravitational field strength shows how strongly one kilogram of mass is attracted; its unit is N/kg.
At the Earth's surface the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg, on the Moon only about 1.6 N/kg.
The field lines of a sphere such as the Earth point radially towards its centre.
As the distance grows, the field strength decreases with the square of the distance.
At the poles the acceleration due to gravity is slightly greater than at the equator.
The surface of equal gravitational potential that roughly corresponds to mean sea level is called the geoid.

abschnitte.text: A **field** describes what force would act on a body at every place in space. In a gravitational field this is the attractive force of the mass. The **gravitational field strength** is the force per kilogram and is measured in N/kg. It is equal to the acceleration due to gravity g in m/s²; the two units mean the same thing. On Earth, therefore, a force of about 9.81 newtons acts on a body with a mass of 1 kg.

Physicists show fields with **field lines**, which show in which direction the force acts. In the gravitational field of a sphere they run **radially** towards the centre, like the spokes of a wheel. Where the lines are close together, the field is strong. Close to the Earth's surface, in a small area such as a room, the lines run almost parallel. This is then called a uniform field, which is equally strong everywhere.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton realised that the attraction decreases with the square of the distance from the centre. So twice the distance means only a quarter of the force. At a height of two Earth radii above the ground you are three times as far from the centre of the Earth, so the field strength there is only a ninth. The **gravitational potential** of a point mass M at a distance r is -G·M/r, if it is set to zero at infinity. Inside a hollow spherical shell of even thickness, all the attractions cancel out exactly, and the field strength there is zero.

The Earth is not a perfect sphere, but is slightly flattened at the poles. At the poles you are therefore a little closer to the centre of the Earth than at the equator. In addition, the Earth turns, and at the equator this produces a small **centrifugal force** outwards. Together, these mean that the acceleration due to gravity is about 9.83 m/s² at the poles and only about 9.78 m/s² at the equator. Mountain ranges such as the Alps and rock of different densities underground also change the gravitational field a little.

If you join up all the points with the same gravitational potential, you get an irregularly wavy surface, the **geoid**. It roughly corresponds to mean sea level, imagined as continuing under the continents. The geoid is important for giving heights, for example in the phrase “metres above sea level”. The Federal Office of Topography swisstopo calculates its own precise geoid model for Switzerland. Satellites such as GRACE have measured the gravitational field of the whole Earth.

In 1687 Newton described gravitation in his work “Principia” as a force between masses. Albert Einstein, who lived in Bern and Zurich for several years, reinterpreted it in 1915 in the **general theory of relativity**. For him gravitation is a curving of space and time by mass. For everyday life and for the orbits of satellites, Newton's description is usually quite enough.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which one kilogram is attracted at a place, measured in N/kg.
An imaginary line that shows in which direction the force acts in the field.
A surface of equal gravity that roughly corresponds to mean sea level.
A measure of how much energy one kilogram has at a particular place in the field.

gewusst: On the Moon you weigh only about a sixth as much as on Earth, because its gravitational field is much weaker.
You yourself also have a tiny gravitational field, but it is far too weak to feel.
On Earth there are measurable differences in gravity from place to place, which geologists use to search for raw materials.

teile.einleitung: Thin-film interference is the reason why soap bubbles and oil patches shimmer in all the colours of the rainbow. Light is reflected at the front and at the back of a very thin layer, and the two light waves overlap. Depending on the thickness of the layer, certain colours are reinforced and others cancelled out.
wichtigste: Light is reflected at the front and back of a thin layer and interferes.
Depending on the thickness of the layer, different colours are reinforced, which is why soap bubbles shimmer.
When light is reflected from an optically denser medium, there is a phase shift of half a wavelength.
A soap film that is much thinner than the wavelength looks black.
Anti-reflective coatings on glasses use destructive interference.
An anti-reflective coating with a refractive index of 1.38 must be about 100 nanometres thick for 550 nanometres.
A curved lens on a glass plate produces Newton's rings.
The shimmering blue of some morpho butterflies comes from interference in fine scale structures.

abschnitte.text: The skin of a soap bubble is only a few hundred **nanometres** thick, much thinner than a hair. Part of the light is reflected at its outer surface, another part at its inner surface. The two light waves travel paths of different length and overlap. Because the skin is of different thickness in different places and the water flows, the colours keep moving.

White light contains all colours with different **wavelengths**. At a particular thickness of the layer, crest meets crest for one colour, and that colour is reinforced. Other colours, on the other hand, partly cancel out. The **phase shift** also matters: when light is reflected from an optically denser material, the wave shifts by half a wavelength.

Shortly before a soap bubble bursts, its skin often turns black at the top. There the layer is much thinner than the wavelength of light. Because of the phase shift at the outer surface, the two reflected waves then cancel out for all colours. A soap film with a refractive index of 1.33 and a thickness of 100 nanometres, on the other hand, reinforces green light of 532 nanometres.

Spectacle lenses and camera lenses carry a very thin **anti-reflective coating**. Its thickness is chosen so that the light reflected at its top and bottom surfaces cancels out. With a coating of refractive index 1.38 and green light of 550 nanometres, this needs a thickness of about 100 nanometres, a quarter of the wavelength in the material. As a result the lenses reflect less and let more light through; they often shimmer slightly violet or greenish.

A thin film of oil on a wet road shimmers in colours because light interferes at its top and bottom surfaces. Some **morpho butterflies** from Central and South America glow blue even though their wings contain hardly any blue pigment. Their scales have fine layered structures in which light interferes. If you place a slightly curved lens on a glass plate, **Newton's rings** appear, named after Isaac Newton, who studied them closely.

begriffe.erklaerung: One millionth of a millimetre.
Sudden shift of a wave when it is reflected.
Number that shows how strongly a material slows light down.
Thin coating that reduces unwanted reflections.

gewusst: The colours of a morpho butterfly are called structural colours, because they come from tiny structures and not from pigments.
From the colour of a soap film you can estimate its thickness to within a few nanometres.
The shimmer of mother-of-pearl in seashells also comes from light interfering in many thin layers.

teile.einleitung: Electrostatic induction is a shift of charge in a metal that happens when you bring an electrically charged object close to it. You do not even have to touch the metal. Electrostatic induction explains why charged objects also attract uncharged pieces of metal.
wichtigste: Electrostatic induction is the shift of charge in a conductor caused by an external electric field.
If you bring a negatively charged rod close, positive charge forms on the side of the metal facing it.
The total charge of an insulated conductor stays zero.
An uncharged metal ball is attracted because the opposite charge is closer to the rod.
By briefly earthing a conductor, you can charge it permanently by induction.
In insulators the similar process is called dielectric polarisation.
An electroscope deflects as soon as you just bring a charged rod near it.
The Wimshurst machine produces high voltages through repeated induction.

abschnitte.text: Metals contain many freely moving **electrons**. If you bring a negatively charged rod close, these electrons are repelled and move to the far side. The near side is left with a lack of electrons, so it becomes positive. Overall the conductor stays neutral; the charges have only been shifted.

The positive side of the metal is closer to the negatively charged rod than the negative side. Because electrical forces get weaker with distance, the attraction is greater than the repulsion. That is why an uncharged metal ball or a light ball of aluminium foil is attracted by the rod. With scraps of paper or hair, which are not conductors, the charges shift only within the molecules; this is called **dielectric polarisation**.

You can charge a conductor permanently by induction. To do this, bring a negatively charged rod close and briefly connect the ball to **earth**, for example with your finger. The repelled electrons flow away. If you remove the earth connection and only then take the rod away, the ball stays positively charged.

An **electroscope** is a simple measuring device with a metal rod and a light, movable pointer or two thin leaves. If you bring a charged rod near it without touching it, charges are shifted into the pointer. Pointer and rod then carry the same charge and repel each other, so the electroscope deflects. When you take the rod away, the pointer drops back again.

The **Wimshurst machine** from the late 19th century has two discs with metal plates that rotate in opposite directions. Through repeated induction it produces such high voltages that sparks jump across. Induction also explains the **Faraday cage**: in a closed metal shell the charges shift so that there is no electric field inside. That is why you are fairly well protected in a thunderstorm inside a car or a metal cable car cabin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material in which electric charges can move freely, for example metal.
Conducting connection to the ground through which charge can flow away.
Device that makes electric charge visible.
Metal shell with no electric field inside.

gewusst: The German word for this effect, Influenz, comes from the Latin influere, which means to flow in.
A balloon that has been rubbed on your hair sticks to the wall because of polarisation.
An aeroplane also acts like a Faraday cage, which is why passengers are protected if lightning strikes.

teile.einleitung: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure that a liquid at rest exerts because of its own weight. The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you and the greater the pressure becomes. You can already feel this in your ears when diving in a swimming pool.
wichtigste: Hydrostatic pressure is calculated with p = ρ · g · h.
It depends only on the density of the liquid, gravitational acceleration and depth.
At the surface of a liquid at rest, the hydrostatic pressure is zero.
In water the pressure rises by about 1 bar every 10 metres.
At the deepest point of Lake Zurich, 136 metres down, it is around 13 bar.
In the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the oceans, it is around 1100 bar.
The shape of the container makes no difference to the pressure at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: Water is heavy: one cubic metre weighs about 1000 kilograms. That is why every layer of water presses on everything beneath it. This pressure in a liquid at rest is called **hydrostatic pressure**. It acts equally in all directions, so downwards, sideways and also upwards.

It is calculated with p = ρ · g · h. Here ρ (pronounced rho) is the **density** of the liquid, g is gravitational acceleration and h is the depth. At a water depth of 3 metres this gives around 29.4 kilopascals. At a sea depth of 20 metres it is around 201 kilopascals, or about 2 bar, because salt water is denser.

In fresh water the pressure rises by roughly 1 **bar** every 10 metres. At the deepest point of Lake Zurich, 136 metres below the surface, it is around 13 bar. In the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 metres deep, it is about 1100 bar. In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first to reach the sea floor there in the submersible Trieste, which had been developed by his father Auguste Piccard.

Because pressure increases with depth, **dams** are much thicker at the bottom than at the top. The Grande Dixence dam in Valais, at 285 metres, is the tallest gravity dam in the world. At its foot the water presses against the concrete with enormous force. Water towers also use hydrostatic pressure to get water up to the top floors of houses.

Even at a depth of 2 to 3 metres you feel the pressure in your ears, because the water presses on your **eardrum**. Divers equalise the pressure by gently pushing air into their ears. With mercury, which is much denser than water, the pressure is already around 66 kilopascals at a height of just 0.5 metres. That is why mercury used to be used in barometers to measure air pressure with a short column.

The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the liquid, not on the shape of the container or the amount in it. This surprising fact is called the **hydrostatic paradox**. In the 17th century the Frenchman Blaise Pascal is said to have burst a barrel with a long, thin tube by pouring water into the top of the tube. The unit of pressure, the pascal, is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on an area, measured in pascals or bar.
How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example 1000 kg per cubic metre for water.
A unit of pressure: 1 bar is roughly the air pressure at sea level.
The unit of pressure: one newton per square metre.
The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the liquid, not on the shape of the container.

gewusst: In the Challenger Deep the water presses on every square centimetre as hard as more than a tonne of weight.
A snorkel cannot be as long as you like, because even at a depth of one metre the water pressure makes breathing in very difficult.
Deep sea fish have no air-filled cavities that could be crushed, which is why they survive the enormous pressure.

teile.einleitung: The threshold of hearing is the quietest sound that a person can just about hear. It is not the same for all pitches: some sounds we hear even when they are extremely quiet, while others have to be much louder. Doctors measure the threshold of hearing in a hearing test.
wichtigste: The threshold of hearing is the smallest sound pressure at which a sound can just be heard.
At 1 kHz it corresponds roughly to the reference value of 0 decibels.
The reference sound pressure in air is 20 micropascals, and the reference intensity is 10 to the power of minus 12 watts per square metre.
Young, healthy people hear from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
For low sounds such as 50 Hz, the threshold of hearing is much higher than at 1 kHz.
In old age, hearing of high sounds gets worse first.
Noise damage first shows up as a rise in the threshold of hearing around 4 kHz.
In a hearing test the threshold of hearing is shown in an audiogram.

abschnitte.titel: What the threshold of hearing is
abschnitte.text: Sound consists of tiny changes of pressure in the air. The **threshold of hearing** tells you how large these changes must be at least for our ear to perceive them. At 1000 hertz it is about 20 micropascals, which is roughly five billion times less than normal air pressure. So our ear is an incredibly sensitive measuring device.

Loudness is given in **decibels** (dB). The value 0 dB is defined so that it roughly matches the threshold of hearing at 1 kHz, that is 20 micropascals of sound pressure or 10 to the power of minus 12 watts per square metre of sound intensity. A whisper has about 30 dB, a normal conversation about 60 dB. Each increase of 10 dB means ten times the sound intensity.

Young people hear sounds from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The ear is most sensitive roughly between 2 and 5 kHz, where important parts of speech also lie. Very low sounds, for example 50 Hz, have to be much louder for us to hear them at all. Curves that join up all the sounds that seem equally loud are called **equal-loudness contours**.

In a hearing test you wear headphones and hear sounds of different pitches one after another, getting quieter and quieter. As soon as you hear a sound, you press a button or raise your hand. The device for this is called an audiometer, and the result is recorded as an **audiogram**. In it you can see at a glance at which pitches someone hears less well.

abschnitte.titel: When the threshold of hearing rises
abschnitte.text: As people get older they hear high sounds less well; this is called **age-related hearing loss**. Loud music, concerts or machine noise can permanently damage the fine hair cells in the inner ear. Such noise-induced hearing loss first shows up as a dip in the audiogram at about 4 kHz. That is why it is worth wearing ear protection in loud noise and not turning headphones up too loud.

begriffe.erklaerung: The quietest sound that you can just about hear.
A unit of measurement for loudness, abbreviated dB.
A diagram that shows how well someone hears different pitches.
A line joining all the sounds that seem equally loud.
The unit for pitch, that is vibrations per second.

gewusst: Some teenagers can still hear very high beeps that adults can no longer perceive.
At the threshold of hearing the eardrum moves less than the size of an atom.
The threshold of pain is at about 120 to 130 dB, that is millions of times higher in sound pressure than the threshold of hearing.

teile.einleitung: Primary colours are colours from which many other colours can be made by mixing, but which cannot themselves be mixed from other colours. Which colours are primary colours depends on whether you are mixing light or paints. In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often named; on a screen they are red, green and blue.
wichtigste: Primary colours cannot be mixed from other colours.
In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often called primary colours.
Screens put together all colours from the light colours red, green and blue.
Colour printers use cyan, magenta and yellow as well as black.
If you mix two primary colours, you get a mixed colour.
In the paintbox green is not a primary colour; you mix it from yellow and blue.
With at least three primary colours you can mix a great many colours.

abschnitte.text: **Primary colours** are the starting colours of a colour system. A great many other colours can be made from them by mixing, but they themselves cannot be mixed from other colours of the system. You need at least three primary colours to get a wide variety of colours. Colours mixed from two primary colours are called **mixed colours**.

In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often considered the primary colours. Yellow and blue make green, yellow and red make orange, red and blue make violet. So green is not a primary colour, but a mixed colour. This division also goes back to the colour wheel of the Swiss artist **Johannes Itten**.

A screen consists of tiny dots that glow red, green and blue, **RGB** for short. When red and green glow together, you see yellow; when all three glow brightly, you see white. This kind of mixing is called **additive colour mixing**, because light is added. With a magnifying glass you can see the small coloured dots on some screens.

A colour printer uses the colours cyan, magenta and yellow as well as black, **CMYK** for short. Printing inks absorb part of the light and reflect only the rest. That is why this is called **subtractive colour mixing**: the more ink you mix, the darker it gets. Black is used as well because the three colours together give only a dirty dark brown, and black is cheaper for text.

In the retina of the eye there are three kinds of **cones**, which are sense cells for colours. They react especially to red, green and blue light. From the mixture of their signals the brain creates all the colours we see. That is why three suitable primary colours are enough to show us a great many colours.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colour mixed from two or more primary colours.
Red, green and blue, the light colours of screens.
Cyan, magenta, yellow and black, the printing colours.
Sense cells in the eye that recognise colours.

gewusst: On a screen yellow is made from red and green light, although in the paintbox red and green rather give you brown.
The K in CMYK stands for key, the key colour black.
Some animals, such as many birds, have four kinds of cones and can even see ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: Gravitation, also called gravity, is the force of attraction between all bodies that have mass. It makes a ball thrown up into the air fall down again, keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth and the Earth in its orbit around the Sun. Although it is the weakest of the fundamental forces, it shapes the whole universe.
wichtigste: Gravitation is the force with which all masses attract each other.
The greater the masses, the stronger the attraction.
If you double the distance, the force falls to a quarter.
Isaac Newton described gravitation in 1687 in his law of gravitation.
In 1797 and 1798 Henry Cavendish was the first to measure the attraction between two masses in the laboratory.
Gravitation keeps the planets in their orbits around the Sun.
To leave the Earth completely, you need about 11.2 kilometres per second.

abschnitte.text: Everything that has mass attracts everything else: you, your dog, a mountain and the Earth. Between small things this **gravitation** is so tiny that you cannot feel it. Only very large masses such as the Earth pull noticeably. That is why a ball thrown up always falls down again and we stand safely on the ground.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** published his law of gravitation in 1687. It says that the attraction grows with the masses and decreases with the square of the distance. So if you double the distance between two bodies, the force falls to a quarter. Newton realised that the same force makes an apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth.

Because the attraction between everyday objects is so weak, it was hard to measure for a long time. In 1797 and 1798 the Englishman **Henry Cavendish** succeeded with a sensitive torsion balance. Small lead balls hung from a wire and were pulled a tiny distance by large lead balls. From his measurements it was later even possible to calculate the mass of the Earth.

As early as 1609 and 1619 **Johannes Kepler** described the orbits of the planets in three laws. The third says that the squares of the orbital periods are in the same ratio as the cubes of the semi-major axes, so distant planets take much longer for one lap. Newton was able to explain these laws with gravitation. Geostationary satellites circle above the equator at a height of about 35,800 kilometres and seem to stand still in the sky.

The Moon pulls much more weakly than the Earth; its acceleration due to gravity is only about 1.62 m/s². An astronaut with a mass of 60 kg has a weight of about 97 N there, while on Earth it would be almost 590 N. The Moon in turn pulls on the Earth's oceans and so causes the **tides**, that is ebb and flood. At the seaside you can observe this every day.

Albert Einstein, who worked in Bern for several years, presented his general theory of relativity in 1915. In it, gravitation is a curving of space and time by masses. This theory also predicted **gravitational waves**, which were first measured in 2015. Anyone who wants to fly into space and leave the Earth completely must reach the escape velocity of about 11.2 kilometres per second.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for gravitation, the attraction between masses.
Shows how quickly a falling body keeps getting faster; on Earth about 9.81 m/s².
The minimum speed needed to escape completely from the pull of a body in space.
The regular rise and fall of the sea level, caused mainly by the Moon.
A body in space with gravity so strong that not even light escapes.

gewusst: You also pull on the Earth, but it hardly moves because of its huge mass.
Without air resistance a feather and a hammer fall equally fast, as an astronaut showed on the Moon in 1971.
Near a black hole gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

teile.einleitung: Capillary action is the way liquids behave in very narrow tubes or gaps. In them, water can rise upwards as if by itself, against gravity. That is why a sugar cube soaks up coffee and a wick draws up liquid wax.
wichtigste: A liquid rises in a capillary when adhesion to the wall is stronger than cohesion.
In a narrow, clean glass tube the surface of the water curves downwards.
Mercury stands lower in a narrow glass tube than outside.
According to Jurin's law, the height it rises is inversely proportional to the radius of the tube.
Ethanol rises about 5.7 cm in a glass capillary with a radius of 0.1 mm.
A candle wick draws liquid wax up to the flame by capillary action.
To stop damp rising by capillary action in walls, a damp-proof course is built in.

abschnitte.text: A **capillary** is a very narrow tube, as thin as a hair, because the Latin “capillus” means hair. If you put a glass tube like this into water, the water rises higher inside it than the water level outside. This effect is called **capillary action** or capillarity. The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid rises.

The particles of a liquid attract each other; this is called **cohesion**. At the same time they are attracted by the wall; this is **adhesion**. If the attraction to the glass wall is stronger, the water creeps up the wall and pulls the rest of the liquid with it. The surface then curves downwards; this shape is called a **meniscus**.

With mercury, cohesion is much stronger than adhesion to the glass. So it sinks in a narrow glass tube and stands lower than outside; this is called **capillary depression**. Its surface curves upwards like a little dome. For the same reason, water forms beads and runs off a waxed or greasy surface.

In 1718 the English doctor and natural scientist James Jurin described how the height the liquid rises is inversely proportional to the radius. If you halve the radius, the liquid rises twice as high. The height also depends on the **surface tension** and the density of the liquid. Ethanol, with a surface tension of 0.022 N/m, rises about 5.7 centimetres in a capillary with a radius of 0.1 mm.

A **wick** draws liquid wax or paraffin up to the flame. Kitchen roll, sponges and towels soak up water through many fine gaps. In walls, too, damp can rise from the ground by capillary action, which is why a **damp-proof course** is built in. You can watch the effect well with a sugar cube in coloured water.

Plants have fine vessels through which water flows upwards from the roots. But capillary action alone would only be enough for a few centimetres to a few metres. In tall trees it is mainly the **transpiration pull** that gets the water all the way up to the crown. Water evaporates from the leaves and pulls the water up from below as if on a thread.

begriffe.erklaerung: Very narrow tube, as thin as a hair.
Attraction between a liquid and a wall.
Attraction between the particles of a liquid.
Curved surface of a liquid in a tube.
Pull created when water evaporates from leaves.

gewusst: The finest blood vessels in your body are also called capillaries, because they are as thin as hairs.
If you hang a strip of kitchen roll with felt-tip dots in water, capillary action separates the colours into colourful bands.
Some redwood trees are more than 100 metres tall and still get water right up to the top.

teile.einleitung: The law of conservation of momentum is one of the most important laws of physics. It says that the total momentum of a system stays the same as long as no external forces act on it. It can be used to explain collisions, rockets and even processes inside atoms.
wichtigste: Without external forces the total momentum of a system is conserved.
This applies to elastic and to inelastic collisions.
If an object at rest breaks apart in an internal explosion, the total momentum of the fragments afterwards is zero.
In oblique collisions you calculate each direction separately.
According to Noether's theorem, conservation of momentum follows from the translation symmetry of space.
In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli predicted the neutrino, partly to save the conservation of momentum in beta decay.
Rockets fly by the recoil principle, which is based on the conservation of momentum.

abschnitte.text: The **law of conservation of momentum** says: in a closed system the sum of all momenta before and after an event is the same. Closed means that no external forces act. The parts of the system can push, slow down or speed up each other. What one object loses in momentum, the other gains exactly.

In an **elastic collision** objects bounce off without losing kinetic energy, as with snooker balls. In an **inelastic collision** the objects change shape or stick together, and part of the energy turns into heat. But in both cases momentum is conserved. If a trolley of 1 kilogram moving at 4 metres per second hits a stationary trolley of 3 kilograms and then stops, the second one moves on at about 1.3 metres per second.

Because momentum has a direction, movements in the opposite direction count as negative. If a trolley of 2 kilograms moves to the right at 3 metres per second and one of 1 kilogram moves to the left at 2 metres per second, the total momentum is 4 kg·m/s to the right. In an oblique collision on a flat surface you apply the law to each direction separately, so left to right and front to back. This also makes it possible to reconstruct road accidents.

An object at rest has zero momentum. If it bursts, the fragments fly apart in such a way that their total momentum is still zero. That is why you feel **recoil** when firing a gun and why a fire hose pushes backwards. A rocket pushes hot gases out backwards and so gains momentum forwards; this works even in the airless vacuum of space.

In 1918 the German mathematician **Emmy Noether** proved that every conserved quantity is linked to a symmetry of nature. Conservation of momentum follows from the fact that the laws of nature are the same everywhere in space, in other words from the **translation symmetry** of space. When energy and momentum seemed to be missing in radioactive beta decay, Wolfgang Pauli suggested an invisible particle in 1930. This **neutrino** was actually detected in 1956.

begriffe.erklaerung: Group of objects on which no force acts from outside.
Collision in which no kinetic energy is lost.
Movement in the opposite direction when something is thrown away.
Tiny, almost massless particle that hardly reacts with matter.

gewusst: When you step from a rowing boat onto the bank, the boat slides away backwards: that is conservation of momentum.
Wolfgang Pauli worked for many years as a professor at ETH Zurich.
With Newton's cradle, exactly as many balls fly off on the other side as you let go.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Rohrer was a Swiss physicist who invented the scanning tunnelling microscope together with Gerd Binnig. With this device it became possible for the first time to make individual atoms on a surface visible. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
wichtigste: Heinrich Rohrer was born in 1933 in Buchs in the canton of St Gallen.
He studied and gained his doctorate at ETH Zurich.
As a student he attended lectures by Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Scherrer.
In his doctoral thesis he dealt with superconductivity.
At the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon he invented the scanning tunnelling microscope with Gerd Binnig.
In 1986 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
His invention was a decisive step forward for nanotechnology; he died in 2013.

abschnitte.text: **Heinrich Rohrer** was born on 6 June 1933 in Buchs in the canton of St Gallen. Buchs lies in the St Gallen Rhine valley on the border with Liechtenstein. In 1951 he began studying physics at **ETH Zurich**. There he attended lectures by the famous physicists Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Scherrer. He was regarded as a modest researcher with a good sense of humour.

In his doctoral thesis at ETH, Rohrer worked on **superconductivity**. At very low temperatures, superconductors conduct electricity with no resistance at all. After that he did research at Rutgers University in the US state of New Jersey. He even used part of his honeymoon for this. In 1963 he returned to Switzerland and began working at the IBM research laboratory in **Rüschlikon** on Lake Zurich.

From 1978 Rohrer worked together with the German physicist **Gerd Binnig**. In 1981 they succeeded in building the first **scanning tunnelling microscope**. In it an extremely fine metal tip, which at the front consists of just a single atom, moves very closely over a surface. Because of the quantum physical **tunnelling effect**, a tiny current flows between the tip and the surface. From this current a computer calculates a picture on which you can see the individual atoms as small hills.

Just five years after the invention, in 1986, Rohrer and Binnig received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. The other half of the prize went to the German Ernst Ruska, who had invented the electron microscope. That was unusually quick, because researchers often wait decades for this honour. This made Rohrer one of Switzerland's Nobel Prize winners in physics. He died on 16 May 2013 in Wollerau in the canton of Schwyz.

The scanning tunnelling microscope opened the door to **nanotechnology**, the technology of the tiniest structures. With the fine tip you can not only see atoms but also move them one at a time. This led to further devices such as the atomic force microscope. Today such microscopes help in developing computer chips, new materials and medicines. In Rüschlikon a nanotechnology centre bears the names of Binnig and Rohrer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A microscope that scans surfaces atom by atom with a fine tip.
A quantum effect in which particles get through a barrier that they should not really be able to cross.
A state in which a material conducts electricity without resistance at very low temperatures.
Technology with tiny structures only a few millionths of a millimetre in size.

gewusst: An atom is so small that about ten million of them fit side by side in a millimetre.
IBM researchers later wrote the company's name on a surface using individual atoms.
Rohrer and Binnig received the Nobel Prize only five years after their invention.

teile.einleitung: The hydrostatic paradox is a surprising observation: the pressure of a liquid at the bottom of a container depends only on how high it is filled, not on the shape of the container. A thin, tall tube can therefore press on the bottom just as hard as a wide vat. This sounds contradictory, but physics can explain it exactly.
wichtigste: The pressure on the bottom depends only on the filling height, not on the shape of the container.
The pressure is calculated as density times gravitational acceleration times height.
Simon Stevin described the paradox in the 16th century.
Blaise Pascal is said to have burst a wooden barrel with a little water in a long, thin tube.
With the same base area and filling height, the force on the bottom is the same in all containers.
In containers that are wide at the top, the sloping side walls carry part of the weight of the water.
In containers that are narrow at the top, the force on the bottom is greater than the weight of the liquid.

abschnitte.text: Imagine three containers: one shaped like a cylinder, one wide at the top like a vase and one narrow at the top like a bottle. All have a base area of 20 square centimetres and are filled with water to a height of 30 centimetres. Although they hold different amounts of water, the water in all three presses on the bottom with about 5.9 newtons. This astonishing fact is called the **hydrostatic paradox**.

The **gravitational pressure** in a liquid comes from the weight of the column of water above. It is calculated with the formula pressure equals density times gravitational acceleration times height. The width of the container does not appear in this formula. In a container that is wide at the top, part of the water presses down on the sloping walls, so a scale shows more than the force on the bottom. In a container that is narrow at the top, the walls push back, and the force on the bottom is greater than the weight of the water.

The French scholar Blaise Pascal is said to have put a long, thin tube upright into a closed wooden barrel. When he filled the tube with only a little water, the barrel burst. With a tube 10 metres high and a cross section of 1 square centimetre, an extra force of around 49 kilonewtons acts on a lid measuring 0.5 square metres. That is equal to the weight of about five tonnes.

The Flemish scholar **Simon Stevin** described the hydrostatic paradox as early as the 16th century. He lived in what are now the Netherlands and Belgium and worked on mathematics, mechanics and hydraulic engineering. Stevin also helped make decimal fractions better known in Europe. Later Pascal studied the pressure of liquids more closely, which is why the unit of pressure is called the pascal.

The paradox is important for building **dams**. The water pressure on a dam depends only on the depth of the lake, not on how long or wide the lake is. So a narrow, long reservoir presses just as hard as a wide lake of the same depth. That is why dams like the Grande Dixence in Valais are much thicker at the bottom than at the top, because that is where the pressure is greatest.

begriffe.erklaerung: Statement that at first sounds impossible but is nevertheless true.
The study of liquids at rest and their pressure.
Pressure that a liquid exerts because of its own weight.
Unit of pressure, named after Blaise Pascal.

gewusst: For every 10 metres of water depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar, roughly the whole of the air pressure.
It is not certain whether Pascal really carried out the barrel experiment himself.
For divers too, depth is what matters most: in a narrow mountain lake the water pressure at 10 metres is almost the same as in the open sea.

teile.einleitung: A horseshoe magnet is a permanent magnet bent like a U or a horseshoe. Its two poles lie side by side at the open ends, which is why it can hold iron especially firmly. It is one of the best-known images of magnetism of all.
wichtigste: The horseshoe magnet is called that because it looks like the horseshoe that horses wear under their hooves.
It looks like the letter U.
You can think of it as a bent bar magnet.
The north pole and south pole lie at the two open ends.
It holds especially well because both poles pull together.
To store it, you lay a piece of iron across the ends.
It is usually made of metal, for example steel or a special alloy.

abschnitte.text: A horseshoe magnet is like a **bar magnet** that has been bent in the middle into a U. It is usually made of magnetised steel or of special alloys such as Alnico, which contain aluminium, nickel and cobalt. Often one arm is painted red and the other green or blue. At school, red usually marks the north pole.

Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**. In a horseshoe magnet they lie close together at the two open ends. Between the poles the magnetic field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. In this gap in particular, the magnetic field is especially strong and even.

If you lay a piece of iron across both ends, both poles pull on it at the same time. The field lines can then run almost completely through the iron, which creates a closed loop. As a result a horseshoe magnet holds much more strongly than a bar magnet of the same size, which pulls with only one pole. That is why this shape is also used for holding magnets and lifting magnets.

To store it, you lay a piece of iron, the **keeper**, across the two ends. In this way the magnetic field stays enclosed in the iron and the magnet loses its strength more slowly. You should not drop a magnet or heat it strongly, because knocks and heat weaken it. It is better to keep electronic devices and bank cards away from strong magnets.

If you sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper above a horseshoe magnet, you can see the field lines as a pattern. In physics lessons a wire carrying a current is often hung in the gap to watch how it moves. This **Lorentz force** is the principle of every electric motor. In the past, horseshoe magnets were also found in telephone receivers, bicycle dynamos and measuring instruments.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place on a magnet where the pulling force is strongest.
The invisible area around a magnet in which it exerts forces.
A piece of iron laid across the poles of a horseshoe magnet to protect it.
Imaginary lines that show the shape of a magnetic field.

gewusst: The image of a red horseshoe magnet is used all over the world as a symbol of magnetism, although quite different shapes are mostly used today.
If you break a magnet, you get two new magnets, each with a north and a south pole.
A real iron horseshoe is attracted by the horseshoe magnet, but if it is made of soft iron it does not become a permanent magnet itself.

teile.einleitung: The Hall effect describes how a small voltage arises in a thin plate carrying a current when it lies in a magnetic field. This voltage appears at right angles to the current and to the magnetic field. Hall sensors can therefore measure magnetic fields, and today they are found in cars, mobile phones and laptops.
wichtigste: The American physicist Edwin Hall discovered the effect in 1879.
The Hall voltage appears at right angles to the current and the magnetic field.
The cause is the Lorentz force, which pushes moving charge carriers to the side in a magnetic field.
Hall sensors are mainly used to measure magnetic fields.
The sign of the Hall voltage reveals whether the charge carriers are positive or negative.
In semiconductors the Hall voltage is much greater than in metals, because there are fewer free charge carriers there.
Klaus von Klitzing received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985 for discovering the quantum Hall effect.

abschnitte.text: When **current** flows through a thin plate, charge carriers move inside it, usually electrons. If the plate lies in a **magnetic field**, the moving charges are deflected sideways by the **Lorentz force**. They gather at one edge of the plate, and at the other edge they are missing. This creates a voltage between the two edges, the Hall voltage. It is at right angles to the direction of the current and to the magnetic field.

**Edwin Hall** was a doctoral student at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore in the USA. In 1879 he found out that a magnetic field affects the current in a thin gold leaf. He was able to measure the tiny voltage at right angles to the current. At that time people did not even know that electrons existed. They were only discovered about 20 years later.

The Hall voltage is greater the stronger the current and the magnetic field are. It is smaller the more free **charge carriers** the material has and the thicker it is. In metals such as copper there are very many free electrons, so the voltage is tiny. With 10 amperes, 1 tesla and a metal plate 0.1 mm thick, it is only about 6 microvolts. In **semiconductors** there are far fewer free charge carriers, so the voltage there is much greater and easier to measure.

**Hall sensors** are small chips made of semiconductor material. In a smartphone they help as an electronic compass. In a laptop they notice whether the lid is closed, because a small magnet sits in it. In a car they measure, for example, how fast the wheels are turning for the anti-lock braking system. They are also used in electric motors, bike computers and current meters.

In 1980 the German physicist **Klaus von Klitzing** studied the Hall effect at very low temperatures and in strong magnetic fields. He found that the electrical resistance did not rise evenly but in exact steps. These steps depend only on constants of nature and are exactly the same everywhere in the world. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1985. Today the effect is used to measure electrical resistance extremely precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that a magnetic field exerts on moving electric charges.
Particles that carry electric charge, for example electrons.
A material such as silicon that conducts electricity better than an insulator but less well than a metal.
What drives electric current, measured in volts.

gewusst: When your laptop goes to sleep as you close it, a Hall sensor has often noticed.
Edwin Hall made his most important discovery while still a student.
With Hall sensors you can measure current without cutting open the cable.

teile.einleitung: A cable is a line that carries electricity or signals from one place to another. Cables run inside our walls, lie under the roads and even connect continents under the sea. To make them safe, they have a protective plastic sheath.
wichtigste: A power cable consists of metal wires, usually copper, and an insulating sheath.
The individual wires have different coloured coverings so that they can be told apart.
The protective wire for earthing is always green and yellow.
Inside, a cable often consists of many thin wires so that it is flexible.
A cable reel must be fully unwound before you plug in a powerful device.
In towns many power cables lie underground; across the country there are often high-voltage lines on pylons.
Besides power cables there are data cables, for example fibre optic cables for the internet.

abschnitte.text: Inside a power cable are metal **conductors**, usually made of copper because it conducts electricity very well. Each conductor is surrounded by a plastic covering, the **insulation**. It stops current getting out or two wires touching each other. Around everything there is also an outer sheath that protects the cable from damage. Flexible cables contain many fine wires called strands, whereas rigid cables in house walls often have a single thick wire.

So that electricians do not mix anything up, the wires are marked in colours. The **earth wire** is green and yellow, and the neutral wire is blue. The wires that carry the voltage are usually brown, black or grey. If there is a fault, the earth wire carries the current away safely so that nobody gets an electric shock.

You should not put cables under a carpet, because they can be damaged there and get hot without anyone noticing. A **cable reel** must be fully unwound before you plug in a powerful device such as a fan heater. Otherwise the wound-up cable can heat up strongly and even melt. Damaged cables with cracks in the sheath should be replaced straight away. And you never pull on a cable to take a plug out.

In towns and villages most power cables lie under the ground as **underground cables**. Over long distances electricity is often carried by **high-voltage lines** that hang high up on large pylons. These overhead lines are cheaper than underground cables and easier to repair. In Switzerland such lines also cross the Alps to exchange electricity between north and south.

Not every cable carries electricity to run devices. A **fibre optic cable** carries light signals and brings fast internet into the home. Huge submarine cables lie on the sea floor and connect Europe with America and Asia. The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was laid as early as 1858.

With a **charging cable** you charge your mobile phone, and with an extension cable you can reach a socket further away. A multi-socket adapter shares the power between several devices but must not be overloaded. Modern charging cables such as USB-C can carry power and data at the same time. Headphones, televisions and computers often need their own cables for sound and picture.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material through which current can flow well, for example copper.
Protective plastic covering that does not let current through.
Green and yellow wire that safely carries current into the ground if there is a fault.
Bundle of many thin wires that makes a cable flexible.

gewusst: A single fibre optic cable can carry so much data that millions of people could watch videos at the same time.
More than 95 per cent of internet traffic between continents runs through submarine cables and not via satellites.
A cable reel that is still wound up can heat up so much that the plastic melts.

teile.einleitung: Wood chip heating is a heating system that burns chopped-up wood to warm houses, school buildings or whole villages. Wood chips are finger-length pieces of wood that machines make from branches and leftover wood. In Switzerland, with its many forests, this kind of heating is especially common.
wichtigste: Wood chips are wood chopped up by machine.
The wood usually comes from leftover wood from forest care and sawmills.
A screw conveyor automatically carries the chips from the store into the boiler.
Dry chips give more heat than wet ones, because no water has to be evaporated.
Heating with wood from sustainable forestry is considered largely CO2-neutral.
A district heating network supplies many buildings from a central heating plant.
Fine dust is the most important pollutant and is held back with filters.

abschnitte.text: Wood chips are produced when a wood chipper cuts branches, treetop wood or thin trunks into small pieces. The pieces are usually a few centimetres long. The wood comes mainly from forest care, from sawmills and from looking after hedges and riverbanks. In this way wood is used that is not suitable for boards or furniture.

The chips are stored in a large **silo** or bunker next to the boiler room. A turning **screw conveyor** pushes them automatically into the boiler, rather like a mincer moves meat along. In the boiler the wood burns, and the heat warms water. This warm water flows through pipes to the radiators and also heats the water for showers.

Fresh wood contains a lot of water. When it burns, this water has to evaporate first, and energy is lost doing so. That is why the chips are left to dry beforehand, so that they give more usable heat. Dry wood also burns more cleanly and produces less smoke.

Often a large wood chip plant heats not just one house but a whole neighbourhood or village. Such a system is called a **district heating network**. The hot water flows through well-insulated pipes in the ground to the connected buildings. In Switzerland there are many such networks, especially in rural municipalities with their own forest.

A tree takes in carbon dioxide from the air as it grows. When it is burned, roughly the same amount of **CO2** is released again, which is why wood from sustainable forestry is considered largely CO2-neutral. Sustainable means that no more wood is cut than grows back. One problem is **fine dust**, which modern systems hold back with electrostatic filters or fabric filters.

About a third of the area of Switzerland is covered with forest. After hydropower, wood is one of the country's most important home-grown renewable sources of energy. Many municipalities heat school buildings, gyms and old people's homes with chips from their own forest. In this way the money for energy stays in the region instead of flowing abroad for imported heating oil.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wood chopped up by machine for heating.
A turning spiral that pushes loose material such as wood chips along.
A network that supplies many buildings with heat from a central heating plant.
Tiny particles in the air that you breathe in and that can harm the lungs.
Overall, no extra carbon dioxide gets into the air.

gewusst: A single lorry full of wood chips can often heat a family house for a large part of the winter.
The ash from clean wood contains minerals and used to be used as fertiliser.
A screw conveyor works on the same principle as the Archimedes screw, which lifted water even in ancient times.

teile.einleitung: The kilogram is the unit of mass used to say how heavy something is. One litre of water weighs about one kilogram, and a packet of sugar in the shop often weighs exactly that. The kilogram is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units.
wichtigste: Kilograms measure how heavy something is, in other words its mass.
One litre of water weighs about one kilogram.
One kilogram has 1000 grams; half a kilogram is 500 grams.
A six-year-old child weighs about 20 kilograms.
The prototype kilogram, which all kilograms were based on, was kept near Paris.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by a constant of nature, the Planck constant.
The symbol for kilogram is kg.

abschnitte.text: The kilogram is the **unit of mass**, abbreviated kg. The prefix “kilo” comes from the Greek word for thousand, so a kilogram is 1000 grams. For large masses the **tonne** is used, which equals 1000 kilograms. The kilogram is one of the seven base units of the **International System of Units**, SI for short.

A packet of sugar or flour often weighs exactly 1 kilogram, and so does a litre of water or milk, roughly. A large **watermelon** weighs several kilograms, a bar of chocolate only 100 grams. A bag of potatoes weighing 2 kg and a bag of carrots weighing 3 kg weigh 5 kg together. A six-year-old child weighs about 20 kilograms, an adult usually between 50 and 100.

After the French Revolution, France wanted to introduce the same measures for everyone. The kilogram was first defined as the mass of one litre of water. In 1889 a cylinder of **platinum-iridium** was made, the **International Prototype Kilogram**. It was kept in a safe in Sèvres near Paris under three glass bell jars, and all the scales in the world were based on it.

Measurements showed that the mass of the prototype kilogram had changed by tiny millionths of a gram compared with its copies. So it was decided to define the kilogram by an unchanging constant of nature, the **Planck constant**. This new definition has applied worldwide since 20 May 2019. With a special balance, the **Kibble balance**, the kilogram can now be reproduced anywhere.

In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern makes sure that scales measure correctly. It has also developed its own Kibble balance. Scales in shops, at market stalls or in pharmacies are checked regularly so that nobody gets too little. In everyday speech people often say “kilo” instead of kilogram, for example when buying apples.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
One thousandth of a kilogram.
Metal cylinder near Paris that defined the kilogram until 2019.
Unit of measurement agreed worldwide, such as the metre, second or kilogram.

gewusst: The prototype kilogram is only about 4 centimetres high, smaller than a drinks can.
The kilogram was the last base unit still tied to an object before it was defined by a constant of nature in 2019.
On the Moon you weigh less, but your mass in kilograms stays the same.

teile.einleitung: The ideal gas is a simplified model that physicists use to describe how gases behave. The gas particles are imagined as tiny points that whizz around, collide and otherwise do not affect each other. Surprisingly many real gases such as air or helium behave almost exactly like this.
wichtigste: In the model the particles take up no volume of their own and do not attract each other.
Pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature are linked by the equation p times V equals n times R times T.
The universal gas constant R is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin.
Real gases behave most like an ideal gas at high temperature and low pressure.
At room temperature helium comes particularly close to an ideal gas.
For an ideal gas the compressibility factor is exactly 1.
An ideal gas never becomes liquid, but a real gas does.
The van der Waals equation describes real gases more accurately.

abschnitte.text: A gas consists of unimaginably many particles moving quickly and randomly. For an **ideal gas** you assume that these particles take up no space themselves and do not attract each other. They just bump into each other elastically now and then, like perfect snooker balls. **Gas pressure** arises because the particles keep hitting the walls of the container.

For an ideal gas the **ideal gas law** applies: pressure times volume equals amount of substance times gas constant times temperature. The temperature must be given in kelvin, which starts at absolute zero at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The gas constant R is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin. One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and normal air pressure.

In the 17th century Robert Boyle and Edme Mariotte found that at the same temperature the volume halves when you double the pressure. Around 1800 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac studied how gases expand when heated. These laws were later combined into the ideal gas law. In 1910 the Dutchman Johannes Diderik van der Waals received the Nobel Prize for his equation for **real gases**.

Real gas particles have a small **volume of their own** and attract each other weakly. At high temperature and low pressure this hardly matters, and the gas behaves almost ideally. Helium is a good example, because its atoms are small and hardly attract each other. If you cool a real gas strongly and compress it, it becomes liquid, which never happens with an ideal gas.

A bike tyre gets warm when you pump it up, and a balloon shrinks when you put it in the fridge. On a plane, sealed crisp packets puff up because the cabin pressure is lower than on the ground. In air at a pressure of 100 kilopascals, oxygen makes up about 21 per cent, so its **partial pressure** is about 21 kilopascals. Weather balloons and diving cylinders are also calculated with the gas law.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit for a very large number of particles, about 602 sextillion of them.
Temperature unit that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
The share of a single gas in the total pressure of a gas mixture.
Actual gas whose particles take up space and attract each other.

gewusst: If you close an empty plastic bottle at the top of a high Swiss pass, it gets squashed by the higher air pressure down in the valley.
There are more gas particles flying around in one litre of air than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.
No gas is truly ideal; the model is a useful simplification.

teile.einleitung: A lever is a simple machine: a rigid bar that can turn around a pivot. With a lever you can move heavy things with little force. You can find levers everywhere, on the playground, in the kitchen and even in your own body.
wichtigste: A lever is a bar that turns around a fixed pivot.
With a long lever you need less force.
The seesaw on the playground is a lever.
On a seesaw, a heavy child has to sit closer to the pivot so that it balances.
Scissors, pliers, wheelbarrows and bottle openers are levers.
Your arm also works like a lever, with the elbow as the pivot.
A door is easiest to open if you push far away from the hinges.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid bar or board that rests on or is fixed to a fixed point. This point is called the **pivot**. If you press on one side, the other side moves the opposite way or lifts a load. Levers are among the oldest tools of humankind.

The seesaw on the playground is a perfect example of a lever. The pivot is in the middle, and a child sits on each side. If one child is much heavier, its side sinks down. To make it work anyway, the heavier child sits **closer to the pivot** and the lighter one further out.

Many tools are levers: a pair of **scissors** consists of two levers with a screw as the pivot. Pliers, nutcrackers, bottle openers and crowbars work in the same way. The easiest way to open the tight lid of a paint tin is to push a screwdriver under the rim as a lever. The **wheelbarrow** lifts heavy loads with a lever, with the wheel acting as the pivot.

An important principle is: the further from the pivot you push, the less force you need. That is why the door handle is placed far away from the hinges. Try pushing a door open right next to the hinges; it is much harder work. In return you have to move further at the long end.

Your body is also full of levers. In the **arm** the elbow is the pivot, and the biceps muscle pulls on the forearm to lift it. When you chew, your lower jaw works as a lever, and when you walk, your feet lift onto your toes like levers. The bones are the bars, and the joints are the pivots.

People were already using levers in ancient times to move heavy stones for buildings. The Greek scholar **Archimedes** explained over 2200 years ago exactly how levers work. He is said to have claimed that with a fixed point and a long lever he could move the world. In Switzerland levers were used, for example, in old wine presses and well pumps.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fixed point around which the lever turns.
The heavy thing that is to be moved with the lever.
The distance from the pivot to the place where you push.
The distance from the pivot to the load.

gewusst: With a crowbar two metres long, a child can lift a stone that it could never move with its bare hands.
A pair of tweezers is also a lever, but it makes movements smaller and more precise.
Piano keys also move a hammer through levers, and the hammer strikes the string.

teile.einleitung: A hot-air balloon is an aircraft that rises into the sky using heated air. A gas burner heats the air in the large envelope, and underneath hangs a basket for the passengers. Because it can only drift with the wind, every balloon flight is a small adventure.
wichtigste: A hot-air balloon rises because the warm air in the envelope is lighter than the cooler air around it.
The air is heated with a gas burner.
During the flight the people stand in a basket.
If the air in the envelope cools down, the balloon sinks.
A hot-air balloon travels with the wind and cannot be steered directly.
The Montgolfier brothers built one of the first hot-air balloons in France in 1783.
A large balloon festival takes place every winter in Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud.

abschnitte.text: Warm air expands and is therefore lighter than the same amount of cold air. If you fill a large envelope with warm air, **buoyancy** is created, similar to a cork in water. If the buoyancy is greater than the weight of the envelope, basket and passengers, the balloon rises. If the air cools down, the buoyancy becomes smaller and the balloon sinks.

The **envelope** is made of light, strong fabric such as nylon or polyester and is often as tall as a house with several storeys. Below it sits the **burner**, which burns propane gas and blows a long flame into the envelope. The basket is usually made of woven willow, because it is light, sturdy and springy. At the top of the envelope there is an opening through which the pilot can let warm air out.

A hot-air balloon has no engine and no rudder. It **travels with the wind**, which is why in German people say they “drive” a balloon rather than fly it. The pilot can only change the height, by heating or letting air out. Because the wind often blows from different directions at different heights, she can influence the direction of travel a little in this way.

The French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne **Montgolfier** sent up one of the first hot-air balloons in 1783. In September 1783 a sheep, a duck and a cockerel travelled as the first passengers at Versailles. In November 1783 people flew in a hot-air balloon for the first time, in Paris. That is why hot-air balloons are also called **montgolfières**.

In the Vaud village of **Château-d'Oex** a large international balloon festival takes place every winter in January. Dozens of colourful balloons then float over the snowy mountains. In 1999 the Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and the Briton Brian Jones were the first to fly round the Earth non-stop in a balloon. Their balloon, the Breitling Orbiter 3, was a mixture of gas and hot-air balloon and took off from Château-d'Oex.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes upwards when something is lighter than the air or water it pushes aside.
The device that heats the air in the envelope with a gas flame.
The large fabric bag of the balloon that is filled with warm air.
Another word for a hot-air balloon, after the Montgolfier brothers.

gewusst: The first passengers of a hot-air balloon were a sheep, a duck and a cockerel.
After a balloon flight it is an old tradition to celebrate the passengers with a balloonists' christening.
Bertrand Piccard later also flew round the world in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse.

teile.einleitung: A concave mirror is a mirror curved inwards that can gather light at one point. This point is called the focal point, because with sunlight even paper can start to burn there. Concave mirrors are found in torches, satellite dishes, make-up mirrors and large telescopes.
wichtigste: A concave mirror is curved inwards, like the inside of a spoon.
Light that arrives in parallel is gathered at the focal point.
The focal length is about half the radius of curvature.
If a lamp sits at the focal point, a parallel beam of light is produced.
In a make-up mirror you see yourself enlarged if your face is within the focal length.
The Olympic flame is lit in Greece with a concave mirror.
Reflecting telescopes gather the light of distant stars with large concave mirrors.

abschnitte.text: A **concave mirror** is curved inwards on its reflecting side. Its opposite is the convex mirror, which is curved outwards, like the traffic mirrors at blind junctions. A simple example of a concave mirror is the shiny inside of a spoon. If you hold the spoon at arm's length, you see yourself in it smaller and upside down.

When parallel light, such as sunlight, hits a concave mirror, it is reflected so that it meets at the **focal point**. The distance from the mirror to the focal point is called the **focal length**. For a mirror curved like a sphere, it is about half the radius of curvature, so with a radius of 40 centimetres it is about 20 centimetres. Only a mirror in the shape of a **parabola** gathers the light at exactly one point.

At the focal point of a concave mirror pointing at the sun, it gets very hot. If you hold a dark piece of paper there, it can catch fire. This is also how the **Olympic flame** is lit at Olympia in Greece, with sunlight and a concave mirror. Huge solar furnaces use the same principle to reach temperatures of over 3000 degrees.

The path of the light also works the other way round. If a lamp sits exactly at the focal point, the concave mirror sends a **parallel beam of light** forwards, as in torches, headlamps and lighthouses. In a make-up or shaving mirror you see yourself enlarged, because your face is within the focal length. Dentists also use small concave mirrors to look at teeth enlarged.

A **satellite dish** is also a concave mirror, but for invisible radio waves rather than light. Its curved shape gathers the weak signals of a satellite at the focal point. That is exactly where the receiver sits, which picks up the signals. Large radio telescopes also work on this principle.

In a **reflecting telescope** a large concave mirror gathers the faint light of distant stars and galaxies. The first usable reflecting telescope was built by Isaac Newton in the 17th century. The bigger the mirror, the more light it gathers and the fainter the objects you can see. The largest telescopes in the world have mirrors many metres across, made up of individual segments.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point at which a concave mirror gathers parallel light.
The distance between the mirror and the focal point.
Curved inwards, like a bowl.
A concave mirror in the shape of a parabola, which gathers light at exactly one point.
The radius of the sphere that the mirror surface is part of.

gewusst: A legend says that Archimedes set enemy ships on fire with mirrors, but whether that is true is much disputed.
