In Odeillo in the French Pyrenees there is a huge solar furnace whose concave mirror covers the front of a whole building.
A spoon also shows you upright on its back and upside down on its inside.

teile.einleitung: The half-life is the time after which only half of a radioactive substance is left. The other half of the atomic nuclei has decayed during this time. Depending on the substance, this takes fractions of a second or billions of years.
wichtigste: The half-life tells you after what time half of the nuclei have decayed.
After two half-lives a quarter is left, after three an eighth.
After ten half-lives only about a thousandth is left.
You cannot predict when a single nucleus will decay.
Iodine-131 has a half-life of about 8 days.
Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years.
Heat or pressure hardly change the half-life at all.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are **unstable** and decay by themselves, giving off radiation as they do so. This process is called radioactive decay. The **half-life** is the time after which half of the nuclei in a sample have decayed. Every radioactive substance has its own fixed half-life.

After each half-life the amount halves again. If a sample contains 800 nuclei with a half-life of 10 minutes, after 40 minutes there are 400, 200, 100 and finally 50 left. Of 64 mg of iodine-131, with a half-life of about 8 days, 8 mg are still there after 24 days. After ten half-lives only about a thousandth remains, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1024.

Nobody can predict exactly when a single nucleus will decay; only the **probability** is known. With a very large number of nuclei, chance evens itself out, which is why the half-life is known very precisely. It cannot be speeded up: strong heating, cooling or pressure leave it practically the same. This is because decay happens inside the nucleus.

Iodine-131 has a half-life of about 8 days, carbon-14 of about 5730 years. **Uranium-238** takes about 4.5 billion years, which is roughly the age of the Earth. That is why about half of the uranium-238 that was present when the Earth formed is still there today. Other substances, on the other hand, decay in fractions of a second.

With carbon-14, researchers can work out the age of bones, wood or fabrics; this is called **radiocarbon dating**. In medicine, substances with a short half-life are used so that they disappear from the body quickly. With radioactive waste from nuclear power stations, the long half-life is a problem: it has to be stored safely for a very long time. In Switzerland, Nagra is planning a deep geological repository for it.

Around 1900 the physicist **Ernest Rutherford** observed that the radiation of a radioactive gas always fell by half at fixed intervals of time. With this he introduced the idea of the half-life. Rutherford received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908. Today the term half-life is also used in biology and medicine, for example for how medicines are broken down in the body.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of unstable atomic nuclei of decaying by themselves and giving off radiation.
The tiny core at the centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
Working out age with the help of carbon-14.
A store deep in the rock for radioactive waste.

gewusst: The age of the glacier mummy Ötzi, about 5300 years, was worked out with the help of carbon-14.
Some radioactive substances have half-lives much longer than the age of the whole universe.
Caffeine also has a half-life of a few hours in the body.

teile.einleitung: A climbing frame is a piece of playground equipment made of bars, ropes or nets on which children climb, swing and do gymnastics. Climbing involves many ideas from physics: force, weight, balance and stable shapes. To keep them safe, climbing frames are built to precise rules.
wichtigste: When climbing you need a lot of strength in your arms, because you pull up your own weight.
When climbing, three of your four hands and feet should always have a hold.
Climbing frames are often built from triangles, because triangles are very stable.
A large climbing frame does not tip over because it is firmly anchored in the ground.
Under the frame there is sand, gravel or bark chips to make a fall softer.
Take off your cycle helmet for climbing, and there should be no cords hanging down from your jacket.
When jumping down, it is best to land with bent knees.

abschnitte.text: A climbing frame is a piece of **playground equipment** on which you can climb up high. There are frames made of wooden beams, metal bars, ropes or nets. Well-known shapes include the **climbing dome**, the rope spider's web, monkey bars and climbing walls with holds. Almost every Swiss school and neighbourhood playground has at least one.

When climbing you pull your whole **body weight** upwards, so you need a lot of strength in your arms and hands. You can push off with your legs to take the load off your arms, because the leg muscles are much stronger. Your **centre of gravity** also matters; it should stay as close as possible to the wall or frame. That way climbing takes less strength and you do not lose your balance so easily.

A square made of bars can easily be pushed into a slanted diamond. A **triangle**, on the other hand, cannot change its shape as long as the bars stay the same length. That is why many climbing frames, bridges and cranes are made of triangles; such structures are called **trusses**. In addition the frame is firmly **anchored** in the ground with concrete foundations so that it does not tip over even with many children on it.

Under the frame there is **impact protection** made of sand, gravel, bark chips or soft rubber mats, which cushions falls. In Europe there are standards that say how playground equipment must be built and tested. In Switzerland the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention, **BFU**, advises municipalities and schools on building safe playgrounds. Gaps are designed so that heads and fingers cannot get stuck.

Follow the **three-point rule**: three of your four hands and feet always have a hold, and only one moves. Take off your cycle helmet and make sure no cords, scarves or strings are hanging down, because they can get caught. If you jump down, land with bent knees so that your legs cushion the impact. Only climb as high as you feel safe, and look out for smaller children.

begriffe.erklaerung: Point where you can imagine the whole weight of a body to be concentrated.
Way of building with rods joined into stable triangles.
Soft ground under play equipment that cushions falls.
When climbing, three hands or feet always have a hold.

gewusst: Climbing trains not only the muscles but also balance and spatial thinking.
Many climbing domes in playgrounds are made entirely of triangles, rather like a geodesic dome.
Sport climbing has been an Olympic sport since 2021.

teile.einleitung: Work done in lifting is the work you do when you lift an object upwards against gravity. It depends only on the mass, the height and the gravitational field strength. The energy is not lost; afterwards it is stored as potential energy in the lifted body.
wichtigste: Work done in lifting is calculated as mass times gravitational field strength times height.
If you lift 5 kg by 2 m, the work done in lifting, with g = 10 N/kg, is 100 joules.
Whether you lift quickly or slowly makes no difference to the work done in lifting.
After being lifted, a body has extra potential energy.
An inclined plane does not save work done in lifting, only force.
Like all work, work done in lifting is measured in joules.

abschnitte.text: The Earth pulls all bodies downwards with its **gravity**. If you want to lift something up, you have to work against this force. This work is called **work done in lifting**. It is greater the heavier the body and the higher you lift it.

Work done in lifting is calculated with W = m · g · h, that is mass times gravitational field strength times height. The **gravitational field strength** g is about 9.81 N/kg in Switzerland; for calculations people often use 10 N/kg. Lifting a 1 kg bag of flour 1 metre high therefore takes 10 joules. A crane that lifts a concrete beam weighing 1000 kg 15 metres high does 150,000 joules of work, that is 150 kilojoules.

If you know the work done in lifting, you can also work out the height. If a box weighing 20 kg is lifted with 600 joules, it went up 3 metres. If you lift a 2 kg dumbbell 1.5 metres ten times, that adds up to 300 joules. All that matters is the height, not the route by which you bring the body up.

The work done in lifting does not disappear; it is stored as **potential energy**. If the body falls down again, this energy is turned into kinetic energy. In Switzerland this is used in **pumped storage power stations**. There, water is pumped into a reservoir high up and later allowed to flow back down through turbines to produce electricity.

Whether you lift a box quickly or slowly, the work done in lifting stays the same. Only the **power** changes, that is how much work is done per second. Someone who runs up the stairs produces more power than someone who walks up at leisure, but does the same work in lifting. An inclined plane or a pulley system does not save work done in lifting either; it only spreads it over a longer distance.

When you climb stairs, you lift your own body. A child weighing 40 kg who climbs 3 metres to the next floor does about 1200 joules of work in lifting. Mountaineers, lifts and cable cars also do work in lifting. A cable car up to a mountain summit has to use a great deal of energy for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: The work needed to lift a body against gravity.
Tells you how strongly the Earth pulls on one kilogram, about 9.81 N/kg on Earth.
The energy a body has because it is higher up.
Work divided by time, measured in watts.
The unit of work and energy.

gewusst: On the Moon the work done in lifting the same box would be only about a sixth as much as on Earth.
One joule is roughly enough to lift a small 100 gram bar of chocolate one metre.
The energy in a bar of chocolate would be enough to lift a person several kilometres into the air.

teile.einleitung: A hydrant is an outlet where you can draw water directly from the public water main. Above all the fire brigade needs hydrants to get large amounts of water for firefighting quickly. In Switzerland they stand in almost every street, often unnoticed at the roadside.
wichtigste: Hydrants are used above all by the fire brigade.
A hydrant is connected to the water main under the street.
In Switzerland you find many hydrants at the roadside.
There are pillar hydrants above the ground and underground hydrants under a cover in the ground.
The fire brigade connects a hose and opens the hydrant with a hydrant key.
The water has a lot of pressure because it comes from storage tanks high up.
You must not park in front of a hydrant, so that the fire brigade can reach it quickly.

abschnitte.text: When a house is on fire, the fire brigade needs a great deal of water in a short time. A fire engine has only a limited supply on board. That is why the fire brigade connects a **hose** to the nearest hydrant and so has a constant supply. Hydrants are also used for cleaning streets, on building sites or at markets, but only with permission.

A **pillar hydrant** is a column that sticks out of the ground at the roadside. An **underground hydrant** lies hidden under a metal cover in the road or on the pavement, and a sign on a house wall shows where it is. The fire brigade puts a standpipe on it, to which it connects the hoses. They open both kinds with a special **hydrant key**.

Hydrants are connected to the drinking water network that runs under the streets. The water is stored in **reservoirs**, which often lie on hills or on mountain slopes above the village. Because the water flows down from there, it is under high pressure in the pipes, usually several bar. This principle is based on hydrostatic pressure: the higher the reservoir, the greater the pressure.

In winter, water in a hydrant could freeze and burst it. That is why the valve of a pillar hydrant lies deep in the ground, where it does not freeze. After use, the remaining water drains out of the column through a small opening. This is very important, especially in the Swiss mountains with their cold winters.

No car may be parked and no bike left in front of a hydrant, because in an emergency every second counts. Snow should not be shovelled onto hydrants either. Children and adults must never open a hydrant themselves. Opening one without permission can damage the pipes and leave the fire brigade short of water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A connection point on the water main where a lot of water can be drawn.
A hydrant that lies under a cover in the ground.
A pipe that the fire brigade puts onto an underground hydrant.
A large water store, usually high up, that supplies the pipe network.

gewusst: The word hydrant comes from the Greek hydor, which means water.
A single hydrant can deliver so much water per minute that a bath would be full in a few seconds.
The fire brigade checks hydrants regularly so that they work reliably in an emergency.

teile.einleitung: Joule heating is the heat produced when electric current flows through a conductor. It makes a toaster glow and a kettle get hot. It is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule.
wichtigste: Joule heating happens because electrons collide with the building blocks of the metal lattice.
The heating power is calculated as current squared times resistance.
If the current doubles, the heating power becomes four times as large.
If 2 A flow through 5 Ω for one minute, 1200 J of heat are produced.
In a toaster, Joule heating is exactly what it is useful for.
In a light bulb only the thin wire glows, because it has a much greater resistance than the leads.
If you shorten a heating wire at a fixed voltage, its heating power increases.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, many **electrons** move through the metal. They keep colliding with the atoms of the **metal lattice** and give off energy. As a result the atoms vibrate more strongly and the wire gets warm. In this way electrical energy is turned into heat.

James Prescott Joule was an English brewery owner and scientist from the area around Manchester. Around 1841 he found out how the heat produced depends on current and resistance. He also showed that heat and work are two forms of the same **energy**. In his honour, the unit of energy is now called the **joule**.

The heating power is P = I² · R, in other words current times current times **resistance**. At a fixed voltage P = U² : R also applies, so a smaller resistance then gives more heat. An immersion heater of 46 ohms at 230 volts therefore has 1150 watts and gives off 345 kilojoules in 5 minutes. A 100 ohm resistor weighing 2 grams, through which 0.1 amperes flow for 10 seconds, warms up by about 6.3 kelvin if it gives off no heat.

In many devices, heat is exactly what you want. **Toasters**, hairdryers, irons, kettles and electric heaters all work with heating wires or heating coils. In a light bulb the thin tungsten wire gets so hot that it shines brightly. The **fuse** also uses the effect, because its wire melts if the current is too high and breaks the circuit.

Joule heating is often a **loss**, for example in power lines, chargers or computer chips. That is why electricity is carried over long distances at high voltage, because at high voltage less current is needed and less heat is produced. Computers and mobile phones need fans or heat sinks so that the chips do not overheat. Overloaded cables can get so hot that a fire starts, so you should not plug too many devices into one multi-socket adapter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how strongly a material holds back current, measured in ohms.
Unit of energy and heat.
Energy per second, measured in watts.
Safety part with a thin wire that melts if there is too much current.

gewusst: Superconductors have no electrical resistance, so no Joule heating at all happens in them.
An old light bulb turns only about 5 per cent of the energy into light; the rest becomes heat.
In many cars the rear window is defrosted with thin heating wires that work on the same principle.

teile.einleitung: A high-voltage power line is a line that transports electrical energy at very high voltage over long distances. Usually its cables hang from tall pylons right across the landscape. They connect power stations with towns, villages and factories.
wichtigste: Electricity is transported over long distances at very high voltage so that less energy is lost.
The highest voltage in the Swiss transmission grid is 380,000 volts.
The Swiss transmission grid for extra-high voltage is run by Swissgrid.
High-voltage lines hang from tall steel frameworks, the pylons.
Insulators separate the line electrically from the pylon.
A bird can sit safely on a single line, because no current flows through it.
You must not fly kites under high-voltage lines, because there is a risk of electric shock.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a long cable, it warms up and some of the energy is lost. These losses depend strongly on the **current**. For the same power, the higher the **voltage**, the less current you need. That is why electricity is transported over long distances at hundreds of thousands of volts. Near the houses the voltage is lowered step by step in **transformers** to 230 volts for the socket.

The transmission grid of Switzerland works at 380,000 and 220,000 volts. It is run by the national grid company **Swissgrid**, based in Aarau. The grid is several thousand kilometres long and connected with the neighbouring countries. A lot of electricity comes from hydroelectric power stations in the Alps and has to reach the Central Plateau. Switzerland is also an important hub for the exchange of electricity in Europe.

The conductor cables hang from tall steel **pylons**, which are often over 50 metres high. The cables themselves are usually made of aluminium with a steel core. Between cable and pylon sit long **insulators** made of glass, porcelain or plastic. They stop the current from flowing through the pylon into the ground. Right at the top of the pylon there is often a thinner earth wire, which protects the line from lightning.

A bird on a single line touches only one cable, so no current flows through it. It only becomes dangerous if it touches two cables at once, or a cable and the pylon. For people, high-voltage lines are life-threatening even without touching them. At such high voltage the current can jump through the air in an **electric arc**. That is why you must not fly kites or drones under the lines and must never climb pylons.

Instead of hanging them from pylons, high-voltage lines can also be laid in the ground as **underground cables**. Then you cannot see them, and the landscape stays clear. But underground cables are much more expensive and harder to repair than overhead lines. In Switzerland, therefore, it is mainly especially sensitive sections, for example in villages or beautiful landscapes, that are put underground. In damp weather you can sometimes hear crackling and humming from overhead lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: What drives electric current, measured in volts.
A device that raises or lowers the voltage of alternating current.
A component that does not conduct electricity and so separates the line and the pylon.
The network of extra-high-voltage lines that distributes electricity over long distances.

gewusst: 380,000 volts is over 1600 times the voltage in a socket.
The crackling on high-voltage lines comes from tiny discharges in the air around the cables.
Some pylons in the Alps have to be built by helicopter.

teile.einleitung: Hooke's law describes how a spring behaves when you pull on it or press on it. It says that the restoring force of a spring is proportional to its displacement. Thanks to this law, spring balances and force meters work.
wichtigste: The law is named after the English natural scientist Robert Hooke.
The restoring force of a spring is proportional to its displacement.
Double the force means double the stretch.
The formula is F = D · s.
D is the spring constant; it tells you how stiff a spring is.
The law only applies as long as the spring is not overstretched.
Spring balances and force meters are based on this law.

abschnitte.text: If you hang a weight on a spring, it gets longer. If you hang on twice the weight, it is stretched twice as much. This is called **proportional**: force and stretch grow in the same ratio. The force with which the spring pulls back is called the **restoring force**.

The law is written as F = D · s. F is the force in newtons, s the displacement, that is how far the spring is stretched or squeezed. D is the **spring constant** in newtons per metre. A stiff spring, for example in a car, has a large spring constant, and a soft spring in a ballpoint pen has a small one.

**Robert Hooke** was an English natural scientist who lived from 1635 to 1703. In 1676 he first published his law as a coded letter puzzle, so that nobody could steal the idea. In 1678 he revealed the answer: “ut tensio, sic vis”, which means roughly “as the stretch, so the force”. Hooke was also one of the first to describe cells under the microscope.

Because the stretch grows exactly with the force, you can use a spring as a measuring device. A **force meter** has a scale on which you can read off the force in newtons directly. In the past, traders at markets weighed fish or vegetables with spring balances. At school you study the law by hanging different weights on a coil spring and measuring its length.

Hooke's law only applies in the **elastic range**, that is as long as the spring returns to its old shape afterwards. If you pull too hard, the spring is overstretched and stays bent. Then the law no longer holds. Rubber bands also follow the law only roughly.

Springs are found in mattresses, trampolines, ballpoint pens, clothes pegs and bike saddles. In cars and mountain bikes they cushion bumps. Mechanical watches, for which Switzerland is famous, also use a fine **hairspring**, the balance spring, for an even beat. Even bridges and tall buildings behave rather like springs under small loads.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two quantities grow in the same ratio: twice as much of one means twice as much of the other.
The force with which a stretched spring tries to return to its starting position.
A number that tells you how stiff or soft a spring is.
A body is elastic if it returns to its old shape after being deformed.

gewusst: No portrait of Robert Hooke that is certainly genuine has survived.
Hooke coined the word “cell” for the small chambers he discovered in cork.
A trampoline also stores energy in springs when you jump in and gives it back when you bounce up.

teile.einleitung: An isobaric process is one in which a gas changes while its pressure stays the same. The Greek “isos” means equal and “baros” means weight. If a gas is heated at constant pressure, it expands and does work as it does so.
wichtigste: In an isobaric process the pressure stays constant.
On a p-V diagram it appears as a horizontal line.
For an ideal gas the volume grows in the same proportion as the absolute temperature.
The heat supplied equals the change in enthalpy.
For an ideal gas the difference between the molar heat capacities Cp minus Cv equals the gas constant R.
One mole of ideal gas does about 83 J of work when heated by 10 K.
With a monatomic ideal gas, 40 per cent of the heat is given off as work.

abschnitte.text: A gas is described by the **state variables** pressure, volume and temperature. In an isobaric change the pressure stays the same while volume and temperature change. Imagine a cylinder closed at the top by a piston that moves easily. If you heat the gas inside, it pushes the piston upwards, but the pressure always stays the same.

Around 1802 the French researcher Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac showed that gases expand evenly at constant pressure. For an **ideal gas**, the volume divided by the absolute temperature in kelvin is constant. So if a gas is heated from 300 K to 450 K, its volume grows by half. On a **p-V diagram** this process is drawn as a horizontal line.

When the gas expands, it does **expansion work**, which is calculated as pressure times change in volume. 2 litres of gas at 150 kilopascals, heated from 300 K to 450 K, grow to 3 litres and do 150 joules of work. The heat supplied has to both warm the gas and provide this work. That is why at constant pressure it equals the change in **enthalpy**.

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is called Cp, and the one at constant volume Cv. Cp is larger because part of the heat is lost as work; for an ideal gas it is larger by exactly the **gas constant** R of about 8.31 J per mole and kelvin. A monatomic ideal gas has a Cp of about 20.8 J/(mol·K), so 1 mole needs about 208 J of heat for 10 K. Of this, about 83 J, or 40 per cent, is given off as work.

Most processes in the open air are roughly isobaric, because the **air pressure** stays almost the same. A hot air balloon fills with warm air, which expands and therefore becomes lighter. When cooking in an open pan, the pressure is also that of the surroundings. Chemists, too, usually measure heats of reaction at constant pressure, which is why enthalpy is so important to them.

Isobaric steps occur in many machines. In the **Brayton cycle** of a gas turbine, such as the ones that work in aircraft engines, heat is supplied at constant pressure. In the idealised model of a diesel engine the combustion is also isobaric. Besides the isobaric process there are isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes.

begriffe.erklaerung: At constant pressure.
Simplified model of a gas that is easy to calculate with.
Energy quantity whose change equals the heat at constant pressure.
Temperature unit that starts at absolute zero. 0 °C is about 273 K.

gewusst: On weather maps, lines of equal air pressure are also called isobars.
In 1804 Gay-Lussac rose to a height of over 7000 metres in a gas balloon to take air samples.

teile.einleitung: A hypothesis is a reasoned guess that can be checked with observations or experiments. Researchers put forward hypotheses to answer a question or explain something. Only when a hypothesis passes many tests does it become established knowledge.
wichtigste: Hypothesis is the technical word for a scientific guess.
A good hypothesis must be testable with an experiment or an observation.
The word comes from Greek and means “supposition” or “assumption”.
A hypothesis can turn out to be right or wrong.
Even a disproved hypothesis moves research forward.
Well-tested hypotheses can become part of a theory.

abschnitte.text: A **hypothesis** is a guess based on knowledge and observations. It is more than just guessing, because you can give reasons why you put it forward. It is often phrased as an if-then sentence. For example: if a plant gets no light, then it grows less well. This statement can be tested.

Research usually starts with a **question**, for example: why do leaves fall in autumn? Then you put forward a hypothesis. With an **experiment** or careful observations you test whether the guess is right. Then you analyse the results and draw conclusions. This often leads to new questions and new hypotheses.

You can test a hypothesis yourself. Your hypothesis is: cress seeds do not sprout without water. Put seeds on two plates with cotton wool and moisten only one of them. Everything else stays the same, so it is a fair **experiment**. After a few days you will see whether your hypothesis was confirmed or disproved.

In the 20th century the philosopher **Karl Popper** stressed that it must be possible to disprove a scientific hypothesis. This property is called **falsifiability**. The statement “Tomorrow it will rain or it will not rain” is always true, but it tells you nothing. A good hypothesis, on the other hand, makes a clear prediction that could also fail. If an experiment disproves the hypothesis, you have still learnt something important.

If a hypothesis is confirmed again and again by many researchers, it gains trust. Several well-tested hypotheses can together form a **theory** that explains many observations. One example is Copernicus's idea that the Earth goes round the Sun. At first it was disputed; today it is confirmed by countless measurements. But in science everything stays open to new findings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reasoned guess that can be checked.
Planned test used to check a guess.
Well-tested explanation for many observations.
The property of a statement that it could be disproved by a test.

gewusst: In everyday life “theory” often means a mere guess, but in science a theory is very well supported.
Detectives also work with hypotheses when they think about who the culprit might be and then check it.

teile.einleitung: The Chapel Bridge is the famous wooden bridge in Lucerne that has crossed the River Reuss since the 14th century. It shows how people centuries ago could build stable and long-lasting structures out of wood. At the same time it is an example of how vulnerable wood is to fire.
wichtigste: The Chapel Bridge is the famous covered wooden bridge in Lucerne.
It was built around 1365 and crosses the River Reuss where it flows out of Lake Lucerne.
The bridge rests on wooden piles driven into the riverbed.
A roof protects the wood from rain and therefore from rot.
In 1993 a fire destroyed large parts of the bridge.
Next to the bridge stands the octagonal stone Water Tower.

abschnitte.text: The **Chapel Bridge** is the best-known landmark of Lucerne. It links the old town with the area on the other bank of the River Reuss. At just over 200 metres long, it is one of the longest covered wooden bridges in Europe. It was built around 1365 as part of the town's fortifications. It gets its name from the nearby St Peter's Chapel.

Wood is light, easy to work with and can still carry heavy loads. But a big problem is **rot**, because wet wood is broken down by fungi. That is why the Chapel Bridge has a **roof** that keeps the beams dry. In this way a wooden bridge can last for centuries, as long as it is looked after. Switzerland has many other covered wooden bridges, for example over the Rhine or the Emme.

The Chapel Bridge rests on many trestles, groups of upright **piles** that were driven deep into the riverbed. Cross beams lie on the piles, and on top of them the long beams for the walkway. The weight of the bridge and of the people is carried through the piles into the ground. Wood that is always under water hardly rots, because little oxygen gets to it there. That is why such piles often last a very long time.

Wood consists mainly of substances that contain carbon, so it burns well. During the night of 17 to 18 August 1993, a fire broke out on the Chapel Bridge. Dry wood, plenty of air above the water and the long roof let the flames spread quickly. A large part of the bridge and many valuable gable paintings were destroyed. The fire brigade was only able to put out the fire after several hours.

After the fire the bridge was rebuilt true to the original with new wood. People were able to walk across it again as early as April 1994. Today there are extra measures for **fire safety**; for example, smoking on the bridge is banned. The stone **Water Tower** next to the bridge survived the fire. The Chapel Bridge is once again one of the most visited structures in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Group of piles on which a section of a bridge rests.
Long tree trunk driven upright into the ground.
Breakdown of wood by fungi and moisture.
Measures that prevent fires or slow down their spread.

gewusst: After the fire, some charred gable paintings were deliberately hung up again as a reminder of the disaster.
The Chapel Bridge was originally longer than today, because the lakeshore used to lie further inland.

teile.einleitung: Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in space and time that arise when very heavy bodies in space such as black holes circle each other and merge. Albert Einstein predicted them more than 100 years ago. Only in 2015 did scientists succeed in measuring them directly, one of the greatest discoveries of modern physics.
wichtigste: Gravitational waves were predicted in theory by Albert Einstein.
They travel at the speed of light.
A gravitational wave stretches and squeezes space across its direction of travel.
In 2015 they were detected directly for the first time, caused by the merging of two black holes.
Detectors such as LIGO measure them with laser interferometers that record tiny changes in length.
Even before that, the shrinking orbit of a double pulsar provided indirect proof.
With LISA, ESA is planning a gravitational wave observatory in space.

abschnitte.text: According to Einstein's **general theory of relativity**, heavy masses curve space, rather as a ball makes a dent in a stretched sheet. When very heavy bodies move violently, ripples arise in this space: **gravitational waves**. They travel through space at the speed of light. As they do so, they alternately stretch and squeeze space across their direction of travel.

**Albert Einstein**, who had worked for several years at the patent office in Bern, predicted gravitational waves in 1916. But he believed they were far too weak ever to be measured. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a **double pulsar**, that is two neutron stars circling each other. Their orbit shrank exactly as the loss of energy through gravitational waves requires, and for this they received the Nobel Prize in 1993.

A **laser interferometer** such as LIGO in the USA has two tubes kilometres long, set at right angles to each other. A laser beam is split, runs through both arms and is brought together again. When a gravitational wave passes through, one arm becomes a tiny bit longer and the other shorter. This change is much smaller than an atomic nucleus, which is why the devices are built to be extremely sensitive.

On 14 September 2015 both LIGO detectors picked up a signal that came from two merging **black holes**. The event was about 1.3 billion light years away. The signal had the typical shape of a **chirp**, in which frequency and strength rise rapidly just before the merger. In 2017 Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

Today LIGO, the European detector Virgo in Italy and other facilities regularly measure gravitational waves. In 2017 the merger of two neutron stars was observed for the first time with both gravitational waves and light. ESA is planning the space observatory **LISA**, with three satellites flying millions of kilometres apart. Researchers at ETH Zurich are also working on this project.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein's theory that explains gravity as a curving of space and time.
A body in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.
A measuring device that overlays light waves to detect tiny differences in length.
A signal that gets faster and higher and higher, like a short chirp.
The extremely dense remains of a large star that has exploded.

gewusst: If you turn the first measured signal into a sound, it sounds like a short chirp.
The gravitational wave of 2015 had been travelling for over a billion years before it reached the Earth.
The arms of the LIGO detectors are each 4 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Static friction is the force that stops an object at rest from starting to slide. Without it we could neither walk nor ride a bike, and every book would slide off a sloping desk. It is usually greater than the friction when sliding.
wichtigste: Static friction stops an object at rest from starting to slide.
It is greater than sliding friction, which is why getting something moving is the hardest part.
The greatest force of static friction is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force.
The coefficient of static friction has no unit.
The size of the contact area hardly matters.
When walking, static friction between shoe and ground drives us forwards.
An anti-lock braking system makes use of the greater static friction when braking.

abschnitte.text: When a crate lies on the floor, tiny bumps in the two surfaces catch on each other. If you want to move the crate, **static friction** acts against you. If you push with 100 N against a crate that does not move, the static friction is exactly 100 N. So it grows along with your push until it reaches its maximum, and then the crate starts to slide.

The greatest force of static friction is the **coefficient of static friction** times the **normal force**, that is the force with which the object presses on the surface beneath it. If a crate presses on the floor with 200 N and the coefficient of static friction is 0.5, the greatest force of static friction is 100 N. A crate of 50 kg has a weight of about 490 N; with a coefficient of static friction of 0.6 it starts to slide from about 294 N. The coefficient of static friction has no unit; it is simply a number.

It takes more force to get a heavy crate moving than to keep pushing it afterwards. The reason is that static friction is greater than **sliding friction**. The amazing thing is that the size of the contact area hardly matters. If you slowly tilt a board with a book on it more and more steeply, the book suddenly starts to slide at a certain angle.

When walking, the foot pushes off backwards, and static friction pushes us forwards. On black ice it is almost completely missing, which is why you slip. A rolling car tyre also transfers the driving force to the road through static friction, because the part touching the ground is standing still at that moment. On dry tarmac the coefficient of static friction of rubber is much greater than on snow or ice.

If the wheels lock when braking, the car slides with only the smaller sliding friction and can no longer be steered. An **anti-lock braking system** (ABS) releases the brake again and again for a very short time so that the wheels keep rolling. In this way the car uses the greater static friction, the braking distance often becomes shorter and you can still steer. When a lorry brakes, static friction acts on a crate on the loading area against the direction of travel and holds it in place.

In the Swiss winter, winter tyres, snow chains and grit help to increase static friction. Climbing shoes have a particularly grippy rubber sole. But sometimes you want to reduce friction, for example with oil in machines or with wax under skis. Leonardo da Vinci was already studying how friction works about 500 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which a body presses at right angles on the surface beneath it.
A number that shows how well two substances grip each other.
The friction when a body is already sliding.
A technology in cars that stops the wheels from locking when braking.

gewusst: Without static friction every knot would come undone and every screw would fall out.
A bike can only go round a bend because static friction holds the tyres in place sideways.

teile.einleitung: Kepler's laws describe how the planets move around the Sun. The German astronomer Johannes Kepler found them more than 400 years ago by careful calculation with observation data. They still apply today and also explain the orbits of moons, comets and satellites.
wichtigste: There are three Kepler's laws about the motion of the planets.
The first law says: planets move in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.
The second law says: a planet moves faster when it is close to the Sun than when it is far away.
The third law links the time of an orbit with the size of the orbit.
The first two laws appeared in 1609 in the work “Astronomia nova”, the third in 1619 in “Harmonices mundi”.
Kepler recognised the elliptical shape from the orbit of the planet Mars.
Isaac Newton was later able to explain the laws with his theory of gravity.

abschnitte.text: **Johannes Kepler** lived from 1571 to 1630 and came from Weil der Stadt in Württemberg. He worked as a mathematician and astronomer in places including Graz, Prague and Linz. In Prague he received the very precise observations of the Danish astronomer **Tycho Brahe**. He calculated with this data for years until he found the true orbits of the planets.

In the past people believed that planets had to move in perfect circles. But Kepler noticed from the orbit of **Mars** that this did not fit the measurements. He realised that the orbits are **ellipses**, slightly stretched circles. An ellipse has two special points, the foci, and the Sun is at one of them.

The second law is also called the **law of areas**. If you draw an imaginary line from the Sun to the planet, this line sweeps out equal areas in equal times. This means that close to the Sun the planet moves faster, and far away more slowly. Behind this law lies the **conservation of angular momentum**, rather like a figure skater who spins faster when she pulls in her arms.

The third law states that the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. If you measure the orbital period in years and the distance in **astronomical units** (AU), simply T² = a³. A planet at 4 AU therefore takes 8 years, because 4³ = 64 = 8². Mars, at about 1.52 AU, takes about 1.9 Earth years, and a comet with an orbital period of 27 years has a semi-major axis of 9 AU.

Kepler did not yet know why his laws held. Only **Isaac Newton** showed at the end of the 17th century that they follow from his law of gravitation. Newton added the mass of the central body to the third law: T² = 4π²·a³/(G·M). With this, the mass of the Sun, planets or distant stars can even be worked out today.

Kepler's laws apply not only to planets but also to moons, comets and **satellites**. Space agencies use them to plan the paths of space probes. A NASA space telescope that discovered thousands of planets around other stars from 2009 onwards was named after Kepler. Kepler is regarded as one of the founders of modern natural science.

begriffe.erklaerung: Oval, stretched circle shape with two foci.
One of the two special points inside an ellipse.
Average distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.
Half the longest width of an ellipse, a measure of the size of the orbit.

gewusst: The Earth's orbit is almost a circle: its distance from the Sun varies by only about 3 per cent.
The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, in the middle of winter in the northern hemisphere.
Kepler also wrote one of the first stories about a journey to the Moon, the “Somnium”.

teile.einleitung: We call a low temperature at which we freeze and water turns into ice cold. In physics, cold is not a thing of its own but the absence of heat. The colder a substance is, the more slowly its particles move.
wichtigste: Cold means little heat energy; the particles move slowly.
Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.
An ice cube melts back into water in a warm room.
Ice floats because it is lighter than the same amount of water.
Freezing water expands and can burst a full glass bottle.
The lowest possible temperature is absolute zero at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
A fridge keeps food cold so that it stays fresh for longer.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny particles that are always moving. The warmer a substance, the faster they jiggle and whizz around. When it is cold, they slow down. So cold is really missing **heat**, and **temperature** is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius.

At 0 degrees Celsius water **freezes** into ice. When it gets warmer, the ice melts again, which is why an ice cube turns into water in a warm room. Amazingly, ice takes up more space than liquid water. That is why ice floats on top and a full glass bottle can burst in the freezer, and why freezing water can even split rocks in winter.

abschnitte.titel: Why lakes do not freeze solid
abschnitte.text: Water is heaviest at about 4 degrees Celsius. In winter this heavy water sinks to the bottom of a lake. At the top a layer of ice forms, which protects the water below like a blanket. This allows fish to survive the winter; this peculiarity is called the **anomaly of water**.

The lowest officially measured temperature in Switzerland was minus 41.8 degrees Celsius, recorded in January 1987 in La Brévine in the Neuchâtel Jura. That is why the valley is also called the “Siberia of Switzerland”. Worldwide, minus 89.2 degrees was measured at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983. It cannot get colder for ever: at **absolute zero**, minus 273.15 degrees, the particles almost stand still.

A **fridge** pumps heat from its inside to the outside. To do this, a refrigerant evaporates in pipes inside and takes up heat as it does so, just as sweat cools your skin when it evaporates. At the back of the fridge the heat is given off again, which is why it is warm there. In the cold, bacteria grow more slowly, so food stays fresh for longer.

abschnitte.titel: People and animals in the cold
abschnitte.text: Our body keeps a temperature of about 37 degrees. In the cold we shiver, because muscle movements produce heat, and we get goose bumps. Animals protect themselves with thick fur, feathers or a layer of fat, and marmots in the Alps go into a long **hibernation**. Clothes in several layers keep us warm, because the air between them insulates well.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measure of how warm or cold something is.
Temperature at which a liquid becomes solid; for water, 0 degrees Celsius.
Lowest possible temperature, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
Substance in a fridge that takes up heat when it evaporates.

gewusst: Salt on the road makes ice melt even below 0 degrees, because salt water only freezes at lower temperatures.
In the laboratory, physicists have already reached temperatures only billionths of a degree above absolute zero.
Because ice takes up more space than water, icebergs float, and only about a tenth sticks out of the sea.

teile.einleitung: Capacitance tells you how much electric charge a capacitor can store at a particular voltage. It is measured in farads, named after the scientist Michael Faraday. Capacitors are found in almost every electronic device, from mobile phones to camera flashes.
wichtigste: Capacitance is the stored charge divided by the voltage.
A capacitor that stores a charge of 1 mC at 5 V has 200 µF.
If you double the voltage, the capacitance stays the same; only the charge doubles.
Typical capacitors in circuits have capacitances from picofarads to millifarads.
Supercapacitors reach several thousand farads.
As a conducting sphere, the Earth has a capacitance of only about 0.7 mF.
A capacitive touchscreen detects your finger because it changes the capacitance at that spot.

abschnitte.text: In its simplest form a **capacitor** consists of two metal plates separated by a thin layer. If you apply a voltage, positive **charge** collects on one plate and negative charge on the other. The capacitance tells you how much charge is stored per volt. It depends only on how the capacitor is built, not on the voltage applied.

C = Q : U, in other words capacitance equals charge divided by voltage. The unit is the **farad**; one farad equals one coulomb per volt. A 47 microfarad capacitor stores a charge of 564 microcoulombs at 12 volts. The larger the plates and the smaller the gap between them, the greater the capacitance, and a **dielectric** between the plates increases it further.

A farad is a very large unit, so people usually work with **picofarads**, nanofarads, microfarads and millifarads. Even the whole Earth, seen as a conducting sphere with a radius of 6371 kilometres, has only about 0.7 millifarads. **Supercapacitors**, also called double-layer capacitors, are quite different: they reach several thousand farads. They use an extremely thin layer of charge on a huge inner surface.

In the **touchscreen** of a mobile phone there is a fine grid of transparent conducting tracks under the glass. Your finger conducts a little current and changes the capacitance at the spot you touch, and the chip measures this. In a camera flash a capacitor charges up slowly and then releases the energy in a flash. Capacitors also smooth voltages in power supplies and store braking energy in some buses.

One of the first capacitors was the **Leyden jar** from the middle of the 18th century. It was a glass vessel coated with metal inside and out. Researchers could use it to collect electric charge and make powerful sparks. In the 19th century the Englishman **Michael Faraday** studied how different materials between the plates change the storage capacity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Component that stores electric charge.
Unit of capacitance, named after Michael Faraday.
Electrical property of particles, measured in coulombs.
Non-conducting layer between the plates of a capacitor.

gewusst: Even two cables lying side by side form a tiny capacitor.
Some buses and trams store energy in supercapacitors when braking and use it again when moving off.
A touchscreen does not react to normal gloves, because they hardly change the capacitance.

teile.einleitung: A refrigerating machine moves heat from a cold place to a warmer one, and it needs work or energy to do so. The fridge in the kitchen is the best-known example. Air conditioners, chest freezers and heat pumps work on the same principle.
wichtigste: A refrigerating machine uses work to move heat from a colder place to a warmer one.
A household fridge gives off the heat at the condenser, usually on its back.
In a compression refrigerator the expansion valve lowers the pressure of the refrigerant before the evaporator.
Absorption refrigerators are driven mainly by heat, for example waste heat or solar heat.
If the warm side is used for heating, the machine is called a heat pump.
A fridge with its door open in a closed room makes the room warmer.
CFCs as refrigerants were gradually banned by the Montreal Protocol of 1987, because they damage the ozone layer.

abschnitte.text: On its own, heat always flows from warm to cold, never the other way round. A refrigerating machine forces the heat in the other direction and needs **energy** to do so, usually electricity. It works like a pump that carries heat uphill instead of water. For this it uses a special working fluid, the **refrigerant**.

In a fridge the refrigerant flows round in a circle through four important parts. In the **evaporator** inside, it evaporates at low pressure and takes heat from the food as it does so. The **compressor** sucks in the vapour and squeezes it together, which makes it hot. In the condenser at the back it gives off the heat to the kitchen and becomes liquid again; then the expansion valve lowers the pressure, and everything starts again.

A **heat pump** is a refrigerating machine whose warm side is used for heating. It takes heat from the outside air, the ground or groundwater and passes it to the heating system. In Switzerland heat pumps are now very often installed in new buildings. They use much less electricity than the heat they deliver, because they only move heat rather than producing it.

The **absorption refrigerator** needs no compressor but is driven mainly by heat. It can use waste heat from factories, district heating or solar heat. Small absorption fridges run almost silently and are therefore used in hotel rooms and caravans. Some of them can even be run with a gas flame.

In the 1870s the German engineer **Carl von Linde** built one of the first reliable compression refrigerating machines, at first for breweries. Later he developed the **Linde process**, which can be used to liquefy air. It uses the Joule-Thomson effect, in which a gas cools down when it expands through a throttle. This is still how liquid nitrogen and oxygen are obtained today.

In the past **CFCs** were often used; they are not poisonous, but they destroy the protective ozone layer. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 led to them being banned step by step. Many replacement substances also strengthen the greenhouse effect, so today natural refrigerants such as isobutane, propane, ammonia or carbon dioxide are used more and more. Old fridges must be disposed of properly so that no refrigerants escape.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substance that evaporates and condenses in the cycle and so carries heat.
Pump that squeezes a gas together.
Part in which the refrigerant evaporates and takes up heat.
Device that takes heat from the surroundings and uses it to heat a house.
Chlorofluorocarbons, once common refrigerants that damage the ozone layer.

gewusst: The back of a running fridge feels warm because that is where the heat from inside is given off.
Anyone who leaves the fridge door open in summer to cool the kitchen actually makes it warmer.
In 1930 Albert Einstein and Leo Szilard jointly patented a fridge with no moving parts.

teile.einleitung: In physics, momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity. It describes how much “oomph” there is in a movement. Momentum is a conserved quantity: in a closed system it is never lost.
wichtigste: Momentum is mass times velocity, as a formula p = m · v.
Its unit is kilograms times metres per second.
Momentum has a direction, namely the direction of motion.
In a closed system the total momentum always stays the same.
In collisions momentum is transferred from one object to another.
Rockets fly thanks to recoil, which is explained by the conservation of momentum.
At the same speed, a heavy lorry has much more momentum than a bike.

abschnitte.text: A rolling lorry is much harder to stop than a football, even if both are moving at the same speed. This is because of **momentum**, which is calculated from mass and velocity. The formula is p = m · v. A bike with its rider, 80 kg together, travelling at 5 m/s, has a momentum of 400 kg·m/s.

Momentum is a **directed quantity**, in other words a vector. It always points in the direction in which the object is moving. Two cars of equal weight driving towards each other at the same speed have a total momentum of zero. That is why you always have to pay attention to direction in calculations.

The **law of conservation of momentum** is one of the most important laws of physics. It says that the total momentum in a closed system stays the same, whatever happens inside it. If in snooker a ball hits a stationary ball straight on, it can stop while the other rolls on at almost the same speed. The momentum has simply been passed on.

If you stand on a skateboard and throw a heavy ball forwards, you roll backwards yourself. This is called **recoil**. Rockets use exactly this principle: they push out hot gases backwards at high speed and are driven forwards as a result. That is how propulsion works even in the airless vacuum of space.

To change an object's momentum you need a force acting over a certain time. The longer this time, the smaller the force needed. That is why **airbags**, seat belts, cycle helmets and gym mats make the braking time longer and impacts gentler. When you catch a ball, too, you let your hands give a little so that it hurts less.

As early as the 17th century the French philosopher René Descartes spoke of a “quantity of motion” that is conserved. **Isaac Newton** put momentum at the centre of his laws of motion in 1687. Today we know that light also has momentum. The idea of solar sails for space probes is based on this.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, the force behind a movement.
Quantity that always stays the same in a closed system.
Quantity with size and direction, often drawn as an arrow.
Movement in the opposite direction when you push something away from yourself.

gewusst: With Newton's cradle and its hanging steel balls, exactly as many balls fly off at the other end as you let go on one side.
A squid swims by recoil, pushing water forcefully out of its body.
A rifle also produces recoil when it is fired, which you feel in your shoulder.

teile.einleitung: Embodied energy, called grey energy in German, is the energy you cannot see in a product: it was used for making, transporting, storing, selling and disposing of it. A smartphone, for example, has already cost a lot of energy before you switch it on for the first time. Anyone who saves embodied energy protects the climate and the environment.
wichtigste: Embodied energy lies in the making, transporting and disposing of a product.
You do not see it on your own electricity bill, because it was used before you bought the product.
A smartphone usually needs most of its energy when it is being made.
Strawberries flown in during winter contain especially large amounts of embodied energy.
Per kilogram of goods, the aeroplane usually causes the most embodied energy.
Cement needs a particularly large amount of energy to make.
Repairing and recycling save a lot of embodied energy.

abschnitte.text: **Embodied energy** is the name for all the energy needed for a product to reach us and later to be disposed of again. This includes mining the raw materials, the factory, packaging, transport, storage, sale and disposal. In German it is called grey energy because it is hidden and you cannot see it directly. It does not appear on your own electricity bill, because it was used before you bought the product.

With a **smartphone**, most of the energy over its whole lifetime is usually used when it is made. Chips, screen and battery need rare raw materials and very complex factories. Charging it at home, by comparison, uses little electricity. Anyone who uses a device for longer or has it **repaired** therefore saves a lot of embodied energy, because no new one has to be made.

Strawberries that come by **aeroplane** from faraway countries in winter contain especially large amounts of embodied energy. Per kilogram of goods, the aeroplane needs much more energy than a ship, a train or a lorry. Vegetables from heated greenhouses can also contain a lot of embodied energy. Seasonal and regional food is therefore often the better choice.

In building, a great deal of embodied energy lies in the materials. For **cement**, limestone is burned in large kilns at over 1400 degrees, which needs an enormous amount of energy. Steel, glass and aluminium are also energy-intensive. That is why it can be more climate-friendly to renovate an old house than to demolish it and build a new one. Wood from Swiss forests, on the other hand, needs comparatively little energy.

In **recycling**, new materials are made from old ones. Melting down aluminium from drinks cans again needs only about 5 per cent of the energy needed for new aluminium from ore. In Switzerland glass, paper and PET can also easily be returned at collection points. But even better than recycling is using things for a long time and passing them on.

Switzerland imports many goods, which is why a large part of the embodied energy of what we consume is used abroad. You can make a big difference: wearing clothes and using appliances for longer, having things repaired or buying second-hand. When shopping, seasonal calendars help you choose fruit and vegetables from the region. Sharing, borrowing and swapping also save embodied energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hidden energy for making, transporting and disposing of a product.
Reusing used materials.
A natural material such as ore, wood or oil from which products are made.
Harvested at the right time of year.

gewusst: A new smartphone has often already used more energy than you need for charging it over many years.
A recycled aluminium can may be back on the shelf as a new can after just a few weeks.
Cement production is one of the largest sources of CO2 in the world.

teile.einleitung: A hairdryer, called a Föhn in German, blows out warm air so that wet hair dries quickly. It is a small appliance full of physics: a motor drives a fan, and a heating wire makes the air warm. In German it is named after a warm wind from the Alps.
wichtigste: A hairdryer blows out warm air.
A fan sucks in air and blows it out again at the front.
An electric heating wire makes the air warm.
Warm air makes the water in hair evaporate faster.
The German name Föhn comes from the warm foehn wind in the Alps.
Electricity and water are life-threatening, which is why a hairdryer never belongs near a full bath.
After use you should unplug the hairdryer and let it cool down before putting it away.

abschnitte.text: Inside a hairdryer there is a small **electric motor** that turns a fan. The fan sucks in air at the back and blows it out through the nozzle at the front. In between lies a **heating wire**, which glows when current flows through it. The air flowing past is warmed up. A grille at the back stops hairs or fluff from being sucked in.

Wet hair dries because the water **evaporates** and goes into the air as water vapour. Warm air can take in much more water vapour than cold air. In addition, the stream of air carries the damp air straight away from the hair. In this way new, dry air can keep flowing in. That is why hair dries much faster with a hairdryer than in the air.

The **foehn** is a warm, dry downslope wind that blows from the mountains into the valley. In Switzerland it is known especially in the Reuss valley, the Rhine valley and the canton of Glarus. Because the hairdryer also blows warm air, in German it was named after this wind. “Fön” was originally a brand name of the German firm AEG. Today many people use the word for all hairdryers.

**Electricity** and water together are life-threatening, because water conducts electricity. That is why you must never use a hairdryer near a full bath or a full washbasin. In Swiss bathrooms, **residual current circuit breakers** protect people by switching off the current in a flash if there is a fault. Many hairdryers also have overheating protection, which switches the appliance off if it gets too hot. After use you unplug the hairdryer and let it cool down before putting it away.

You can also use a hairdryer to dry a steamed-up mirror. Some people use it to remove labels or to dry wet shoes carefully. Household hairdryers usually have a **power** of about 1000 to 2000 watts. This means a hairdryer uses more electricity than many other household appliances. Air that is too hot can dry out the hair, which is why there are often several temperature settings and a cold setting.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water slowly turns into invisible water vapour without boiling.
A wire that gets warm when current flows through it.
A warm, dry downslope wind in the Alps.
A safety device that switches off the current at once if it flows the wrong way.

gewusst: When the foehn is strong, it can suddenly become as warm as spring in Alpine valleys in winter.
The heating wire in a hairdryer can get several hundred degrees hot.
The first hairdryers were heavy and were often fixed to the wall or built as a hood.

teile.einleitung: A kaleidoscope is a tube in which mirrors and coloured pieces create beautiful star-shaped patterns. Every turn makes a new picture that almost never comes back. It was invented about 200 years ago in Scotland.
wichtigste: A kaleidoscope contains mirrors and coloured pieces.
When you look in, you see colourful, regular patterns like a star.
If you turn the kaleidoscope, the pattern changes.
You almost never see the same pattern again.
The word kaleidoscope means roughly “seeing beautiful shapes”.
The kaleidoscope was invented about 200 years ago by David Brewster.
When you look into it, it is best to hold it up to the light.

abschnitte.text: A kaleidoscope is an **optical toy** shaped like a tube with a peephole at one end. Inside there are two or three long **mirrors** set at an angle to each other. At the other end there is a chamber with small pieces of coloured glass, beads or bits of plastic. If you hold the tube up to the light and look in, a colourful pattern appears.

The mirrors reflect the image of the coloured pieces back and forth again and again. As a result a small piece is repeated many times and arranged all the way round. If two mirrors are at an angle of 60 degrees, you see the image six times; at 45 degrees, eight times. This creates a **symmetrical** pattern that looks like a star or a snowflake.

When you turn the kaleidoscope, the pieces tumble about and form a new pattern. Because they lie a little differently each time, you almost never see exactly the same picture again. There are so many possible arrangements that you could keep turning it all your life. In a **teleidoscope** there are no pieces; instead you see your surroundings through a lens as a pattern.

The Scottish physicist **David Brewster** invented the kaleidoscope in 1816 during experiments with light and mirrors. He patented it in 1817, but the toy was copied so quickly that he hardly earned anything from it. Within a few months hundreds of thousands of kaleidoscopes were sold. Brewster made up the name from the Greek words **kalos** for beautiful, eidos for shape and skopein for looking at.

Today there are kaleidoscopes as simple children's toys made of cardboard and as precious works of art made of brass and glass. Their patterns serve designers as models for fabrics, wallpapers and tiles. Kaleidoscope pictures can also be created on a computer. In a figurative sense people say “a kaleidoscope of impressions” when they mean many colourful, changing experiences.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mirror throws back the light and shows an image.
Regularity in which parts of a picture repeat exactly.
Legal right that reserves an invention for its inventor for a certain time.

gewusst: You can build a simple kaleidoscope yourself with three strips of mirror, a cardboard tube and a few coloured beads.
David Brewster also researched how light is refracted in crystals.

teile.einleitung: An integrated circuit, often just called a chip, is a tiny electronic circuit on a small wafer of silicon. Billions of components sit on just a few square centimetres. Chips are found in mobile phones, computers, cars and even washing machines.
wichtigste: An integrated circuit combines many components on a single piece of semiconductor.
Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit in 1958 and received the Nobel Prize in 2000.
The Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented the planar process for mass production in 1959.
The structures are transferred onto the wafer with light by photolithography.
EUV lithography works with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres.
Chips are made in clean rooms, because even tiny dust particles would destroy them.
The Intel 4004 of 1971 was the first commercially available single-chip processor.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer is called a die.

abschnitte.text: An **integrated circuit** (IC for short) contains transistors, resistors and conducting tracks on a single small piece. In the past, circuits were built from separate components that were soldered together with wires. In a chip, everything is built into one piece of **semiconductor**, usually silicon. This makes the circuit tiny, fast, cheap and reliable.

In 1958 the engineer **Jack Kilby** built the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in the USA, and in 2000 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. Soon afterwards Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor developed a chip made of silicon. This was made possible by the **planar process**, which the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented in 1959. It allowed chips to be made flat and in large numbers.

The starting point is a thin, round silicon disc, the **wafer**. With **photolithography** the circuit pattern is transferred with light through a mask onto a light-sensitive layer, as with a photo. For the finest structures, extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres is used. Then the wafer is sawn into many separate pieces called dies, and each goes into a protective casing.

Because the structures are a thousand times thinner than a hair, even a single grain of dust would destroy a conducting track. That is why chips are made in **clean rooms**, where the air is filtered all the time. The workers wear full-body suits, hoods and masks. The air there is much cleaner than in an operating theatre.

In 1971 Intel brought out the **4004**, the first commercially available microprocessor on a single chip, with about 2300 transistors. Today's processors contain many billions of transistors. As early as 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double regularly. This prediction is called **Moore's law** and held up astonishingly well for decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny electronic switch that can turn current on and off.
Material such as silicon that conducts current or not, depending on conditions.
Thin silicon disc on which many chips are made at the same time.
Process that transfers circuit patterns onto the wafer with light.

gewusst: A modern mobile phone chip contains more transistors than there are people on Earth.
Jean Hoerni, the inventor of the planar process, was born in Geneva in 1924.
Silicon is obtained from quartz sand, one of the most common materials in the Earth's crust.

teile.einleitung: The golden rule of mechanics says: what you save in force, you must add in distance. Whether a lever, a block and tackle or a ramp, no simple machine saves work. It only shares the work out differently between force and distance.
wichtigste: What you save in force, you must add in distance.
In a simple machine without friction, the work stays the same.
Work is force times distance and is measured in joules.
One joule is one newton times one metre.
Behind the golden rule lies the law of conservation of energy.
Friction means that in reality you have to put in more work.

abschnitte.text: The **golden rule of mechanics** applies to all simple machines such as levers, pulleys, blocks and tackles and inclined planes. It says that with these aids you can save force, but in return you have to cover a longer distance. The product of force and distance, the **work**, stays the same without friction. So you can lift a heavy load with little force, but you have to pull or push for longer.

Mechanical work is calculated as force times distance. Its unit is the **joule**, named after the Englishman James Prescott Joule. One joule is one newton times one metre. To lift a load of 500 N by 2 metres, you need 1000 joules without friction, whatever aid you use.

A ramp is a good example of the golden rule. If you want to raise a crate weighing 300 N by 1.5 metres, the work is 450 joules. If you push it up an **inclined plane** 6 metres long, you need only 75 N without friction. The distance is four times as long, but the force is four times smaller.

In a **block and tackle** a rope runs over several pulleys. If you use it to lift 400 N by 3 metres and pull with only 100 N, you have to pull 12 metres of rope. The same applies to the lever: the long arm of the lever moves a long way, the short arm only a little. Such blocks and tackles have been used on building sites and sailing ships for centuries.

Behind the golden rule lies the **law of conservation of energy**: energy cannot come from nothing. That is why no machine can give out more work than you put in. In reality, friction always produces some heat, and you have to put in more work. The ratio of useful work to work put in is called **efficiency**.

Even in ancient Greece people knew levers, pulleys and wedges. Archimedes and later Hero of Alexandria described how to move large loads with them. Around 1600 Galileo Galilei clearly recognised that simple machines do not save work. The name golden rule shows how important this principle is for mechanics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force times distance, the amount of energy needed to move or lift something.
The unit of work and energy: one newton times one metre.
An aid such as a lever, pulley or ramp that changes force or direction.
How much of the work put in is really used in the end.
Energy is never lost and never comes from nothing; it is only converted.

gewusst: Mountain roads with many hairpin bends, such as on the Gotthard, are a huge inclined plane that saves force but makes the distance longer.
A perpetual motion machine that runs for ever without a supply of energy is impossible because of the conservation of energy.
A bike in a low gear also uses the golden rule: pedalling is easier, but you have to pedal more often.

teile.einleitung: A suspension bridge is a bridge whose path hangs from strong ropes or chains. The supporting cables are firmly anchored at both ends and sag lowest in the middle. Suspension bridges exist as swaying footbridges in the mountains, on playgrounds and as huge road bridges over sea inlets.
wichtigste: In a suspension bridge the path hangs from cables that carry the weight of the bridge and the people.
Strong anchorages hold the cables firmly at both ends.
A suspension bridge sags lowest in the middle.
Because it hangs from cables, a suspension bridge wobbles when you walk across it.
If several children jump in the same rhythm, the bridge swings more and more strongly.
The calmest way to cross a wobbly suspension bridge is to walk slowly and steadily.
The Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge in the canton of Valais is almost 500 metres long.

abschnitte.text: A suspension bridge consists of **supporting cables**, a footpath or roadway and firm anchorages. On large bridges the main cables run over tall towers, the **pylons**. Vertical cables hang down from the main cables and carry the roadway. At the ends the cables are anchored in mighty concrete blocks or in the rock. Simple footbridges in the mountains, on the other hand, hang directly between two rocks.

The cables of a suspension bridge are loaded under **tension**, which means they are pulled tight. Steel cables can withstand huge pulling forces, which is why they can span very long distances. Under their own weight the cables sag in a graceful curve and are lowest in the middle. The towers, on the other hand, are squeezed together and carry the load into the ground. Because the whole structure hangs from cables, it can move and sways slightly.

Every bridge has a natural frequency at which it most likes to swing. If several people jump exactly in this rhythm, the bridge rocks more and more strongly. This is called **resonance**. That is why soldiers should not march across a bridge in step. In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the USA collapsed because the wind set it swinging more and more violently.

The **Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge** near Randa in the canton of Valais is 494 metres long and was opened in 2017. It hangs up to 85 metres above a valley and lies on the Europaweg between Grächen and Zermatt. Also well known is the Trift Bridge in the Bernese Oberland, which hangs high above a glacier gorge. Such bridges attract many hikers. You do need a bit of courage, though, and should have a head for heights.

One of the most famous suspension bridges is the **Golden Gate Bridge** in San Francisco, which was opened in 1937. Its main span between the towers is about 1280 metres long. The bridge with the longest span today is the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey, at over 2000 metres. It was opened in 2022 and crosses the strait of the Dardanelles. Giant bridges like these are constantly monitored with sensors.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strong cable from which the path or roadway of the bridge hangs.
The firm fixing of the cables in rock or in a concrete block.
A tall tower over which the main cables of a large bridge run.
A swinging movement building up when you push in the right rhythm.

gewusst: When it opened, the Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge was the longest pedestrian suspension bridge in the world.
The Millennium Bridge in London had to be closed again shortly after it opened in 2000 because it swayed strongly under the footsteps of pedestrians.
The main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge are made of tens of thousands of individual steel wires.

teile.einleitung: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. It is also called energy of motion. The heavier and above all the faster something is, the more kinetic energy it has.
wichtigste: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.
Potential energy, on the other hand, is stored energy of position, for example due to height.
The formula is E = ½ · m · v².
Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy.
It is measured in joules.
Energy can be turned from one form into another, for example in a pendulum or on a roller coaster.
That is why a car's braking distance gets much longer at higher speed.

abschnitte.text: Everything that moves has **kinetic energy**. The word comes from the Greek “kinesis”, movement. A rolling ball, a flying bird and a moving bike all have it. If something is standing still, its kinetic energy is zero.

Kinetic energy is calculated with E = ½ · m · v², where m is the mass and v the speed. Because the speed is squared, it has a particularly large effect. At twice the speed the energy is four times as large, and at three times the speed even nine times. The unit is the **joule**.

**Potential energy** is stored energy of position: a stone on a rock has it because it can fall down. When it falls, the potential energy is turned into kinetic energy. In a pendulum this happens back and forth all the time. On a **roller coaster**, too, the car is first pulled up and then races down with growing kinetic energy.

Because the energy grows with the square of the speed, speed in traffic is so dangerous. A car at 50 km/h has about four times as much kinetic energy as one at 25 km/h. When braking, this energy has to be turned into heat, which is why the **braking distance** gets much longer. That is why many Swiss residential areas have 30 km/h zones.

People have long used the kinetic energy of wind and water. **Wind turbines** turn the movement of the air into electricity; in the past windmills drove millstones. In Switzerland river power stations on the Rhine and the Aare produce electricity from flowing water. Electric cars can store part of the kinetic energy back in the battery when braking.

As early as the 17th century the scholar Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz realised that mass times speed squared is an important quantity. He called it “living force”. The term **energy** in today's sense only became established in the 19th century. At that time researchers also discovered that energy is never lost, only turned into other forms.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy an object has because of its motion.
Stored energy, for example due to the height of an object.
Unit of energy.
Energy is never lost; it is only turned into other forms.

gewusst: A bullet is tiny, but because of its high speed it has a great deal of kinetic energy.
Meteorites hit the ground at many kilometres per second and can therefore make huge craters.
On the ramp a ski jumper turns potential energy into kinetic energy and reaches about 90 km/h at take-off.

teile.einleitung: Terminal velocity is the highest speed a falling body can reach in air or water. It is reached when air resistance brakes just as strongly as gravity pulls. That is why raindrops, skydivers and snowflakes do not keep getting faster.
wichtigste: A falling body reaches terminal velocity when air resistance and weight are equal.
At terminal velocity the acceleration is zero, and the body keeps falling at a steady speed.
