A skydiver lying on their stomach falls at about 200 km/h.
Large raindrops fall at most about 30 km/h.
Heavy, compact bodies have a higher terminal velocity than light, bulky ones.
In thin air the terminal velocity is much higher than in dense air.
Small animals such as mice often survive falls unhurt, because their terminal velocity is very low.

abschnitte.text: At the start of a fall, **weight** pulls the body down, and it keeps getting faster. The faster it falls, the more strongly **air resistance** brakes it. This grows roughly with the square of the speed, so at twice the speed it becomes four times as large. At some point the two forces are equal and cancel each other out. From this moment the body no longer accelerates and falls at a constant speed, the **terminal velocity**.

What matters are the mass, the shape and the area the body presents to the air. An iron ball and a wooden ball of the same size have the same air resistance, but the iron ball is much heavier. That is why the iron ball reaches a higher terminal velocity. A flat feather or a sheet of paper, on the other hand, falls very slowly. The **density of the air** also plays a part: in thin air high up, the resistance is smaller.

A skydiver lying on their stomach with arms spread out falls at about 200 km/h. If they dive head first, they present much less area to the air and become much faster. When they open the parachute, the area suddenly becomes huge and the terminal velocity falls to a few metres per second. In this way they can land gently. In Switzerland the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland is known for BASE jumpers who jump from rock faces.

In 2012 the Austrian **Felix Baumgartner** jumped from a capsule under a balloon at a height of almost 39 kilometres. At this height the air is very thin and hardly brakes at all. That is why he became faster than sound in free fall and reached over 1300 km/h. Further down, where the air becomes denser, air resistance slowed him down strongly again. In the end he landed safely with his parachute.

Large **raindrops** fall at most about 30 km/h, and small drizzle drops much more slowly still. Snowflakes sink gently to the ground because of their large, loose shape. Small animals such as mice or insects have a large surface area in relation to their weight. Their terminal velocity is so low that they often survive a fall from a great height unhurt. Plant seeds such as those of the dandelion also make use of this to fly a long way on the wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: A braking force that arises when a body moves through the air.
The force with which the Earth pulls a body downwards.
How quickly the speed of a body changes.
A layer of air high above the clouds, where the air is very thin.

gewusst: Without air resistance, a raindrop falling from a height of 1000 metres would hit the ground at over 500 km/h.
Wingsuit flyers slow down their fall with a suit that has fabric surfaces between the arms and legs.
In a vacuum there is no terminal velocity; there a feather and a hammer fall equally fast.

teile.einleitung: Tipping over is when an object falls over an edge. Whether a tower, a chair or a lorry tips over depends on the centre of gravity and the base. Anyone who understands this can set things up more safely and knows why the Leaning Tower of Pisa is still standing.
wichtigste: An object tips over when the vertical line from its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
A wider base makes an object more stable.
A low centre of gravity prevents tipping.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa stands because the vertical line from its centre of gravity still falls inside its base.
The turning effect that tries to make an object fall over is called the tipping moment.
Lorries with tall loads tip over more easily on tight bends.
Wind acting high up can easily blow things over because of the long lever arm.

abschnitte.text: Every object has a **centre of gravity**, the point where you can imagine all its weight to be concentrated. The **base** is the area on which the object rests. If you draw a vertical line downwards from the centre of gravity, the **plumb line**, what matters is where this line meets the ground. If it lies inside the base, the object stays standing; if it lies outside, it tips over.

If a block stands on a base 10 cm wide and its centre of gravity is exactly above the middle, the edge is 5 cm away. So you can move the centre of gravity 5 cm sideways until its plumb line reaches the edge. After that a small push is enough and the block falls. The higher the centre of gravity, the less you have to tilt the object before this happens.

The famous bell tower in Pisa in Italy began to lean while it was still being built in the 12th century, because the ground beneath it is soft. Today it leans by about 4 degrees. It still stands because the plumb line from its centre of gravity still falls inside its base. From around 1990 to 2001 it was stabilised at great effort by carefully removing soil from under one side.

A **lorry** with a tall load has a high centre of gravity. On a tight bend centrifugal force pushes it outwards, and the **tipping moment** becomes large. That is why such vehicles have to drive slowly on bends. Tractors on steep slopes can also tip over, which is why farmers in the Swiss mountains drive with special care.

When you **rock back on your chair**, you are standing on just a narrow edge, and the centre of gravity is close to the edge, so you easily fall backwards. Heavy books go on the bottom shelf so that the centre of gravity of the bookcase is low. You close an open sunshade in strong wind, because the wind acts high up with a long lever arm. Tall cupboards are often fixed to the wall so that they do not fall over if a child climbs up them.

Engineers calculate precisely whether buildings and machines are safe from tipping. Cranes have heavy **counterweights** and wide supports so that they can lift large loads. Racing cars are built low to have a low centre of gravity. A roly-poly toy works exactly the other way round: its centre of gravity is so low in its round base that it always stands up again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Point where you can imagine the whole weight of an object to be concentrated.
Area on which an object stands, up to its outer edges.
Vertical line downwards, here from the centre of gravity to the ground.
Turning effect of a force that tries to knock an object over.

gewusst: After the repair work, the Leaning Tower of Pisa even straightened up again a little.
You cannot knock over a roly-poly toy, because a heavy weight at the very bottom keeps its centre of gravity very low.
A rucksack on a cargo bike makes it wobblier than the same load low down in the transport box.

teile.einleitung: The hertz is the unit of frequency, that is of how often something repeats itself per second. One hertz means one oscillation per second. This unit is needed for sounds, electricity, radio waves and computers.
wichtigste: The hertz, abbreviated Hz, is the unit of frequency.
1 hertz means one event per second.
The unit is named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz.
The alternating current from a Swiss socket has 50 hertz.
People hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.
Large frequencies are given in kilohertz, megahertz or gigahertz.
Sound waves and radio waves are also described by their frequency in hertz.

abschnitte.text: The **frequency** tells you how often an event repeats itself per second. If a swing goes back and forth once a second, it has a frequency of 1 hertz. If a heart beats 60 times a minute, that is also 1 hertz. The symbol for the unit is **Hz**.

The unit is named after the German physicist **Heinrich Hertz**, who lived from 1857 to 1894. Around 1886 to 1888 he was the first to prove that electromagnetic waves exist. With this he laid the foundation for radio, television, mobile phones and Wi-Fi. The name hertz was fixed internationally for the unit in 1930.

Sound consists of vibrations of the air. The higher the frequency, the higher a note sounds. The concert pitch A, to which orchestras tune their instruments, usually has 440 hertz. People hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz; bats and dogs also hear much higher sounds, known as **ultrasound**.

In Switzerland and in Europe the socket supplies **alternating current** at 50 hertz. This means the current changes direction back and forth 50 times a second. In the USA it is 60 hertz. The railway in Switzerland uses a frequency of 16.7 hertz for its own power network.

For very high frequencies there are prefixes: 1 kilohertz is 1000 hertz, 1 megahertz a million and 1 **gigahertz** a billion hertz. FM radio stations broadcast between 87.5 and 108 megahertz. Wi-Fi transmits at 2.4 or 5 gigahertz. A computer processor works at a clock speed of several gigahertz, that is billions of calculation steps per second.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of oscillations or repetitions per second.
A regular back-and-forth movement, for example of a pendulum.
Current that regularly changes its direction.
Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: Depending on the species, a hummingbird beats its wings about 50 times a second, that is at around 50 hertz.
Elephants communicate with very low sounds below 20 hertz, which people cannot hear.
A screen with 120 hertz shows 120 pictures a second, which makes movements look especially smooth.

teile.einleitung: When an object blocks light, a shadow forms behind it. But not all shadows are the same: there are completely dark areas, the umbra, and lighter ones, the penumbra. These two kinds of shadow can even explain solar and lunar eclipses.
wichtigste: An umbra is an area that no light from any light source reaches.
A penumbra is lit by only part of the light source or light sources.
A single point-like lamp produces just a sharp shadow without a penumbra.
Two lamps produce an umbra and two penumbras behind an object when the shadows overlap.
Large, flat lamps produce shadows with soft, blurred edges.
In a total lunar eclipse the Moon is in the Earth's umbra.
A total solar eclipse can only be seen in the Moon's umbra.

abschnitte.text: Light travels in straight lines. When it hits an object it cannot see through, it cannot pass, and a **shadow** forms behind the object. With a very small, point-like lamp the shadow is equally dark everywhere and has a sharp edge. If you hold your hand closer to the lamp, its shadow on the wall gets bigger.

The **umbra** is the area that no light reaches at all. That is why it is the darkest. When two lamps light up a rod, the umbra forms exactly where the shadows of both lamps overlap. The smaller and further away the light source is, the more clearly the umbra can be seen.

A **penumbra** is an area that only part of the light reaches. It is therefore lighter than the umbra but darker than the lit surroundings. With two lamps, two penumbras form next to the umbra, because one lamp still shines into each of them. A large, flat lamp acts like many small points of light, so its shadow gets a soft, blurred edge.

In a **lunar eclipse** the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line, and the Moon moves through the Earth's shadow. In a total lunar eclipse it is completely in the umbra. Even so, it does not disappear but often glows copper red. This is because the Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight into the Earth's shadow, which is why people also call it a blood moon.

In a **solar eclipse** the Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth. Its umbra hits only a narrow strip of the Earth's surface, and only there can you see a total solar eclipse. In the much larger penumbra people see a partial eclipse, in which the Sun is only partly covered. A total solar eclipse is very rare at any particular place, on average only about once every few hundred years.

In everyday life you come across umbras and penumbras all the time. Under a ceiling lamp with a large shade, objects have soft shadows, whereas in the light of a small torch they have hard ones. Photographers use large light surfaces to create soft shadows on faces. And in **shadow puppet theatre** the size of the figures depends on how close they are to the lamp.

begriffe.erklaerung: Darkest part of a shadow, which no light reaches at all.
Part of a shadow that only some of the light reaches.
Very small lamp that produces sharp shadows without a penumbra.
Event in which one celestial body moves into the shadow of another.

gewusst: During a total solar eclipse the Moon's umbra on the Earth is usually only about 100 to 200 kilometres wide.
A total lunar eclipse can be seen from anywhere the Moon is in the sky at the time, whereas you often have to travel far for a total solar eclipse.
In the middle of a total solar eclipse it gets so dark in the middle of the day that you can see bright stars.

teile.einleitung: Seasons are parts of the year in which weather, temperature and the length of the day change in a typical way. Here they are spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth's axis is tilted while the Earth travels round the Sun for a year.
wichtigste: There are seasons because the Earth's axis is tilted.
Here we have spring, summer, autumn and winter.
Astronomical spring begins around 20 March, autumn in September.
When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia.
At the equator there is often a rainy season and a dry season instead of summer and winter.
The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, not in summer.
A year has 365 days, a leap year 366 days.

abschnitte.text: The Earth travels once round the Sun in a year. Its **axis** is tilted by about 23.4 degrees and always points in the same direction in space. That is why sometimes the northern hemisphere and sometimes the southern hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun. In summer the Sun is high in our sky, its rays hit the ground steeply and the days are long.

Many people think the Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. That is not true: it is closest at the beginning of January, in the middle of our winter. What matters is the **angle** at which the Sun's rays arrive. When they arrive at a slant, the warmth is spread over a larger area, like the light of a torch held at an angle.

According to the calendar of the stars, **spring** begins around 20 March, when day and night are the same length. Summer begins around 21 June with the longest day, and autumn around 22 or 23 September. Winter begins around 21 December with the shortest day. Weather experts, on the other hand, use **meteorological seasons**, which begin on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December.

In the southern hemisphere the seasons are the other way round: when it is summer here, it is winter in Australia. People there often celebrate Christmas on the beach. In many countries near the **equator** it is warm all year round, and instead they have a rainy season and a dry season. Near the poles the Sun stays in the sky for weeks in summer, while in winter there is the **polar night**.

In spring trees come into leaf and migratory birds return. In summer fruit and grain grow, and in autumn the leaves change colour and fall. In winter animals such as the marmot **hibernate**, while others grow a thick winter coat. For a long time people also arranged their lives around the seasons, for example for sowing and harvesting.

In Switzerland the seasons shape life strongly, especially in the mountains. In early summer farmers take their cows up to the alpine pastures, and in autumn they bring them back down in the **Alpabzug**. In winter there is often snow in the Alps, and many people go skiing or sledging. Customs such as the Sechseläuten in Zurich, where the Böögg is burnt, celebrate the end of winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.
Imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.
Time when the Sun does not rise for days near the poles.
Year with 366 days, because 29 February is added.

gewusst: Without a tilted axis there would be practically no seasons on Earth.
Because one orbit of the Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours, a leap year with 366 days is needed almost every four years.
On Mars each season lasts almost twice as long as on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A climbing pole is an upright pole made of metal or wood that you can climb up and slide back down. You find them in gyms and in playgrounds. When climbing, force, friction and gravity work together, which makes the climbing pole an exciting piece of hands-on physics.
wichtigste: A climbing pole is a smooth, upright pole for climbing.
The best way up is to pull with your arms and grip with your legs.
Without friction between your hands, legs and the pole you could not hold on.
A smooth metal pole has less friction than a rough tree trunk.
Sliding down is much easier than climbing up, because gravity helps.
When you slide down fast, friction produces heat in your hands.
In some fire stations firefighters slide down a pole.

abschnitte.text: A climbing pole is an upright **pole**, usually three to five metres high. In gyms there are often several poles side by side, fixed to the ceiling and the floor. In playgrounds they are often part of a climbing frame. Unlike a **ladder**, the pole has no rungs, which makes climbing it harder.

If you want to climb up, you pull yourself up with your **arms** and then grip the pole between your feet or lower legs. This technique is often called the **leg clamp**. While your legs hold on, your hands reach further up. In this way arms and legs take turns, like a caterpillar pushing itself along.

The reason you do not just slide down a pole is **friction**. The tighter you grip the pole, the greater the friction force. A smooth metal pole offers less friction than a rough tree trunk with bark. If you slide down fast, part of the kinetic energy is turned into **heat** by friction, which is why your hands get hot.

When climbing up you have to work against **gravity** and lift your own body weight. When sliding down, gravity pulls you down by itself. You only have to loosen your grip a little and brake with friction. That is why sliding down is much easier than climbing up.

Some fire stations have a **fire pole** that firefighters use to get down quickly from the upper floor when the alarm goes. The idea comes from the USA in the 19th century. Sliding is faster than the stairs. Today, though, many new stations no longer install poles, because people can get hurt on them.

Many climbers rub their hands with white **chalk** powder so that they stay dry and grippy. There are usually thick mats under climbing poles in gyms. In winter you should never touch an ice-cold metal pole with your tongue, because the moist tongue freezes to it immediately. The metal conducts the heat away from the tongue very quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force produced when two surfaces rub against each other, which slows down a movement.
Force with which the Earth pulls everything downwards.
White powder (magnesium carbonate) that absorbs sweat and makes hands grippy.
Climbing technique in which you grip the pole between your legs.

gewusst: The first fire pole is said to have been installed in a fire station in Chicago around 1878.
The chalk is the same powder that gymnasts use on the high bar and sport climbers on rock faces.
A cold metal pole feels colder than a wooden rod at the same temperature, because metal conducts heat away from your hand faster.

teile.einleitung: In an implosion an object is suddenly squashed inwards by pressure from outside. It is the opposite of an explosion, in which something flies apart outwards. Implosions happen when the pressure inside is much lower than outside.
wichtigste: In an implosion an object is pushed inwards by pressure from outside.
The cause is low pressure inside, for example from cooling steam.
A drinks can filled with hot steam gets crushed when you dip it upside down into cold water.
A sealed tank wagon that cools down can be crushed by air pressure.
Old tube televisions could implode when they broke, because their picture tube contained a vacuum.
Submarines cannot dive as deep as they like, because the water pressure could crush the hull.
The lid of a jar of jam filled while hot sits tightly because of the low pressure.

abschnitte.text: In an **implosion** a hollow object suddenly collapses inwards. This happens when the pressure from outside is much greater than the **pressure inside**. Air pressure at sea level is about 1 bar, which equals the weight of around 10 tonnes on every square metre. If there is no counter pressure inside, this force can crush thin metal or glass.

You heat a little water in an empty drinks can until steam forms. The **steam** pushes the air out of the can. Then you dip the can upside down into cold water so that no air can flow back in. The steam condenses in a flash into a few drops, and the air pressure outside crushes the can with a bang.

After being cleaned with hot steam, railway tank wagons can become dangerous. If they are sealed while the steam cools, **low pressure** forms and the air pressure crushes the huge steel tank. A PET bottle rinsed with hot water and sealed straight away also shrinks as it cools. As early as the 17th century Otto von Guericke showed with the Magdeburg hemispheres how enormous air pressure is.

Old televisions had a large glass **picture tube** with almost no air in it. If it broke, glass splinters could fly first inwards and then in all directions. For submarines, at great depth the water presses from outside with tremendous force. That is why they have a maximum diving depth that they must not exceed.

When **preserving**, you fill jars with hot jam and seal them straight away. As they cool, low pressure forms in the jar and the lid is sucked on tightly. This protects the jam from germs for a long time. When you open such a jar you often hear a pop, because air rushes in.

Huge stars can implode too. When their fuel is used up, their core collapses under its own gravity in a fraction of a second. This can create a neutron star or a black hole. The outer layers are flung away in a tremendous **supernova**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sudden inward collapse of an object caused by pressure from outside.
A pressure that is lower than the air pressure of the surroundings.
When steam cools and turns back into liquid water.
The pressure that the air of the Earth's atmosphere exerts on everything.

gewusst: When tower blocks are demolished with explosives, people often call it an implosion, because they are made to collapse inwards cleverly.
Air pressure presses on the palm of your hand with a force equal to about 100 kilograms; we just do not notice because it is pushed back equally hard from inside.
With the Magdeburg hemispheres, even teams of horses could not pull apart the hemispheres once the air had been pumped out.

teile.einleitung: Hornussen is a traditional Swiss team sport in which a small puck, the nouss, is struck far into the field with a long, flexible stick. The opposing team tries to catch it in the air with boards. The sport is closely linked with physics, because the nouss reaches enormous speeds.
wichtigste: Hornussen comes from Switzerland.
The small disc that is struck is called the nouss and weighs about 78 grams.
The name comes from the fact that the nouss buzzes like a hornet as it flies.
It is struck with a long, flexible stick.
The nouss can fly at up to about 300 km/h.
The team in the field catches the nouss with the board.
The playing field in which the nouss is caught is called the Ries.

abschnitte.text: **Hornussen** is a Swiss national sport played mainly in the canton of Bern, in the Emmental and in north-western Switzerland. Two teams play against each other and take turns. One team strikes, and the other stands in the field and defends. Together with Swiss wrestling and stone throwing, hornussen is one of the traditional Swiss sports.

The striker places the **nouss** on a launching ramp, the so-called Bock. With a swinging movement he strikes it with the stick as far as possible into the field and gets points for long strikes. In the **Ries**, the playing field, the opponents stand spread out and try to catch the nouss with their **boards**. If the nouss lands in the Ries without being caught, the defending team gets a penalty point, a so-called Nummer.

The nouss flies through the air so fast that it makes a whirring sound. It sounds similar to the buzzing of a **hornet**, which is Hornisse in German. That is how the game got its name. In the past the nouss was made of wood; today it is made of plastic and weighs about 78 grams.

The long **stick** bends a great deal during the swing. It acts like a spring that stores energy and releases it again at the right moment. In this way the nouss gets much more speed than with a rigid stick. It can reach up to about 300 km/h and often flies several hundred metres.

The defending players hold a flat board with a handle in their hands, called the Schindel. They often throw the **board** up into the air to stop the nouss in flight. Because the nouss is so fast, good reactions and teamwork are needed. The players therefore spread themselves out cleverly in the Ries so that as much area as possible is covered.

begriffe.erklaerung: The small, fast plastic disc that is struck in hornussen.
The long, flexible striking stick in hornussen, called the Stecken.
A board with a handle with which the nouss is caught.
The playing field in which the nouss has to be caught.
The launching ramp on which the nouss is placed before the strike.

gewusst: A nouss can fly as fast as a Formula 1 racing car.
Hornussen is one of the living traditions of Switzerland.
The nouss is lighter than a bar of chocolate, but it can fly hundreds of metres.

teile.einleitung: A yo-yo is a toy made of two discs joined by an axle with a string wound around it. If you let it fall, it unrolls and then climbs back up as if by magic. Behind it lies exciting physics of energy and rotation.
wichtigste: The string of a yo-yo is wound around the axle in the middle.
As it unrolls, potential energy turns into kinetic and rotational energy.
A yo-yo falls more slowly than a stone in free fall, because part of the energy goes into the spin.
At the bottom the spin winds the string back up, which is why the yo-yo climbs.
If you throw it down hard, it spins faster at the bottom.
In the trick called the “sleeper”, the yo-yo spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time.
There were already pictures of yo-yo-like toys on vases in ancient Greece.

abschnitte.text: A yo-yo consists of two round **discs** joined in the middle by a narrow **axle**. A string is wound around the axle, and its end is fixed to your finger with a loop. In the past yo-yos were mostly made of wood; today they are often made of plastic or metal. Modern models have a **ball bearing** so that they spin very easily.

When you hold the yo-yo up, it has **potential energy**. As it falls, this is turned into kinetic energy and **rotational energy**, because the yo-yo falls and spins at the same time. Because a large part of the energy goes into the spin, it falls much more slowly than a stone. Much as with a pendulum, potential and kinetic energy keep taking turns.

At the bottom, at the end of the string, the yo-yo keeps spinning very fast. This spin winds the string back up, so the yo-yo climbs upwards. Because some energy is lost through **friction**, it never quite reaches its starting height. That is why you always give a small tug with your hand to supply the missing energy.

In the **sleeper**, the yo-yo spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time, because the string lies only loosely around a ball bearing. Many other tricks build on this one, such as “Walk the Dog”, in which the yo-yo rolls along the floor. If you throw it down hard, it spins faster and sleeps longer. At yo-yo world championships, players from all over the world show difficult tricks.

Vases from **ancient Greece** already show children with yo-yo-like discs. Later the toy was popular in Asia and, in the 18th century, in France too. The name yo-yo probably comes from the **Philippines**. Pedro Flores, an immigrant from the Philippines, opened a yo-yo factory in California in the 1920s and made the toy famous in America.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that an object has because it is high up.
Energy contained in a spinning movement.
Part in the middle around which something turns.
Yo-yo trick in which it spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time.

gewusst: In 1985 astronauts took a yo-yo into space to see how it works in weightlessness.
Without gravity a yo-yo does not fall by itself; you have to throw it away hard.
Good yo-yos with ball bearings can spin on the spot for many minutes.

teile.einleitung: Calorimetry is the measurement of amounts of heat. With a calorimeter you can find out how much heat is released in a chemical reaction or how much energy there is in a food. The name comes from the Latin “calor” for heat.
wichtigste: A calorimeter is used to measure amounts of heat.
Many calorimeters have a double wall with a vacuum so that hardly any heat is lost.
The water equivalent shows how much water would have the same heat capacity as the vessel.
A bomb calorimeter is used to find the gross calorific value of substances.
One thermochemical calorie equals 4.184 joules.
Unlike the net calorific value, the gross calorific value includes the heat of condensation of the water vapour.
From the rise in temperature of the water, you can calculate the heat supplied.

abschnitte.text: A **calorimeter** is a well-insulated vessel, usually filled with water, with a thermometer and a stirrer. If heat is put in, the temperature of the water rises. So that as little heat as possible is lost, many calorimeters have a double wall with a **vacuum** in between, much like a Thermos flask. This strongly slows down conduction and convection.

The heat absorbed is the **heat capacity** times the rise in temperature. You have to take both the water and the vessel into account. A calorimeter with 210 J/K and 0.5 kg of water has 2300 J/K altogether, so with 9200 J of heat the temperature rises by 4 K. The heat capacity of the vessel is often expressed as a **water equivalent**, the mass of water that would absorb the same amount of heat.

In a **bomb calorimeter** a sample is burnt with pure oxygen in a thick steel container, the bomb. The bomb sits in a water bath that absorbs the heat released. This is how the **gross calorific value** of coal, wood, heating oil or food is found. The gross calorific value also includes the heat released when the water vapour produced condenses back into water; the net calorific value does not.

Food packaging shows how much energy the food provides, in kilojoules and in **kilocalories**. One thermochemical calorie equals 4.184 joules, so one kilocalorie is 4.184 kilojoules. The figures were originally based on measurements with calorimeters. Per gram, fat provides about twice as much energy as sugar or protein.

In the 18th century the Scottish chemist **Joseph Black** was one of the first to study how much heat substances absorb. Around 1782 Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace built an **ice calorimeter**. In it the heat from an experiment melted ice, and from the amount of meltwater they calculated the heat. With this device they even studied the heat given off by a live guinea pig.

begriffe.erklaerung: Well-insulated device used to measure amounts of heat.
How much heat an object needs to get 1 degree warmer.
Total heat released when a substance burns completely.
Old unit of heat, today mostly replaced by the joule.

gewusst: Water has a particularly large heat capacity, which is why it is so good for calorimeters.
Modern condensing boilers also use the heat from the water vapour in the exhaust gases and so save energy.
With the guinea pig, Lavoisier and Laplace showed that breathing is a kind of slow burning.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold for hours. Many people simply call it a Thermos flask, after a well-known brand. Its secret is two walls with an almost airless space between them.
wichtigste: A vacuum flask keeps drinks warm or cold for a long time.
Another word for a vacuum flask is Thermos flask.
It has two walls, and there is almost no air between them.
The airless space, the vacuum, strongly slows down the transfer of heat.
The lid must be closed tightly, otherwise the heat escapes.
Hot tea does not stay hot for ever, but slowly cools down.
In summer the flask can also keep cold water cool.

abschnitte.text: A vacuum flask is a container that strongly slows down the **exchange of heat** between the drink and the surroundings. It has an inner wall and an outer wall that are joined only at the neck of the flask. The air between them has been almost completely pumped out, creating a **vacuum**. Modern flasks are usually made of stainless steel; older ones had a glass insert.

Heat can travel in three ways: by **conduction**, by the flow of air or liquid, and by radiation. In a vacuum there are hardly any particles that could pass on heat or flow around. To deal with heat radiation, the walls are often mirrored or shiny, so the radiation is reflected back. Because all three paths are slowed down, the flask works equally well for hot and cold drinks.

Around 1892 the Scottish scientist **James Dewar** built a double-walled glass vessel with a vacuum to store very cold, liquid gases. It is still called a **Dewar flask** after him. The German glassblower Reinhold Burger realised that the idea was also useful in everyday life and applied for a patent in 1903. Soon afterwards the flask went on sale under the brand name Thermos.

On a **winter hike** or when skiing, hot tea from a Thermos flask is especially welcome. In summer it keeps water or squash pleasantly cool on a bike ride. Many children take a small vacuum flask to school or on a school trip. If you warm the flask with hot water first, it keeps the drink warm even longer.

A vacuum flask is never perfect; a little heat always escapes through the **lid** and the neck. That is why tea slowly cools down and is often only lukewarm after a day. If the flask is dropped, the vacuum can be damaged, and then it insulates much less well. To clean it, use a brush and rinse it out well so that no smells remain.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space in which there is almost no air and no other particles.
Stop heat or cold from getting out or in quickly.
Passing on of heat from particle to particle, for example through a spoon in hot tea.
Double-walled vessel with a vacuum, named after its inventor James Dewar.

gewusst: In research laboratories, liquid nitrogen at almost minus 200 degrees is stored in large Dewar flasks.
A good vacuum flask can keep tea much warmer for many hours than an ordinary bottle.

teile.einleitung: Glow-worms are not worms but beetles that can glow with their abdomen. They are also called fireflies or, in German, St John's beetles. On warm summer nights in Switzerland you can see their small yellow-green lights in the grass and between bushes.
wichtigste: Glow-worms are beetles and belong to the firefly family.
They glow with a special organ on their abdomen.
Their light is cold; it is produced almost without heat.
In our part of the world glow-worms glow yellow-green.
They glow so that they can find each other in the dark.
The larvae like to eat snails.
A lot of artificial light at night disturbs glow-worms, which is why there are fewer of them.

abschnitte.text: Glow-worms are small, inconspicuous **beetles**, usually about a centimetre long. On their abdomen they have a **light organ** that gives off yellow-green light. In some species the females have no wings and look more like larvae. That is why people used to think they were worms.

The light is produced by a **chemical reaction**: the substance **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped by a protein called **luciferase**. In the process almost all the energy is turned into light and hardly any into heat. That is why the light of glow-worms is cold. An old light bulb, on the other hand, turns most of its energy into heat.

Glow-worms are active mainly in June and July, around **St John's Day** on 24 June, which is where the German name St John's beetle comes from. On warm nights the females glow in the grass, and the males fly around looking for them. So the light helps them to find each other. The adult beetles live only a few weeks and hardly eat anything during this time.

Glow-worms spend most of their lives as **larvae**, often for two to three years. The larvae can already glow. They hunt mainly snails, which are often much larger than themselves. They stun the snail with a bite and then digest it from the outside.

abschnitte.titel: Glow-worms in Switzerland and their protection
abschnitte.text: Three species are found in Switzerland; the best known are the **common glow-worm** and the **lesser glow-worm**. They live at the edges of woods, in gardens, hedges and natural meadows. Because many street lamps and lit gardens make the night bright, the animals see each other less well; this is called **light pollution**. Anyone who wants to help glow-worms switches off unnecessary lights at night and leaves wild corners in the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body with which an animal can produce light.
The substance that reacts with oxygen in the light organ and produces light.
The ability of living things to produce light themselves.
Too much artificial light at night, which disturbs animals and plants.

gewusst: The light of a glow-worm is one of the most efficient lights there is, much more economical than a light bulb.
Many animals in the deep sea can also produce light themselves, like glow-worms.
In some parts of Asia and America, thousands of fireflies flash at the same time in the same rhythm.

teile.einleitung: In a temperature inversion the air higher up is warmer than down at the ground, exactly the opposite of usual. The Latin word “inversio” means turning upside down. In Switzerland this weather situation brings grey high fog to the Central Plateau in winter and bright sunshine on the mountains.
wichtigste: Normally the air gets colder with height; in an inversion it is warmer above than below.
In winter, inversions often form with an area of high pressure.
On the Swiss Central Plateau an inversion often brings high fog and cold.
On mountains such as the Rigi you can then often see the sun above the sea of fog.
The warm layer acts like a lid, so exhaust fumes stay down below and the air quality is poor.
Together with the high fog, the cold bise often blows across the Central Plateau.
If it is 0 °C in Zurich and 8 °C at a height of 1500 metres, there is an inversion.

abschnitte.text: Normally the temperature drops by about half a degree to one degree for every 100 metres of height. In an inversion, though, there is a layer of air in which it gets warmer going up, the **inversion layer**. Beneath it lies cold, heavy air that cannot rise. That is why this weather situation is also called a **temperature reversal**.

In winter the nights are long, and the ground gives off a lot of heat to the clear sky. The air at the ground cools down strongly and collects in valleys and basins. In an **area of high pressure**, air also sinks from above and warms up as it does so. In this way a warm layer settles over the cold air near the ground, creating a **subsidence inversion**.

abschnitte.titel: Sea of fog over the Central Plateau
abschnitte.text: The Swiss Central Plateau lies like a tub between the Jura and the Alps. In an inversion a thick blanket of **high fog** often forms in the cold, damp air and can stay for days. From above, this cloud cover looks like a **sea of fog**, with the summits sticking out of it like islands. Popular viewpoints include the Rigi, Mount Pilatus, the Weissenstein and the Napf.

The **bise**, a cold, dry northeasterly wind, often blows beneath the blanket of fog. It is funnelled between the Jura and the Alps and blows particularly hard at Lake Geneva. The bise makes the temperatures in the fog feel even colder. While people are freezing in Bern or Zurich, it can be noticeably warmer and sunny at 1500 metres.

The warm layer of air acts like a lid on a pot. Exhaust fumes from traffic, heating and industry cannot escape upwards and collect near the ground. That is why the amount of **fine dust** in the air rises during long inversions. In big cities such as Milan, or London in the past, dense **smog** could form like this.

Inversions do not only happen in winter. On clear summer nights a thin **ground inversion** often forms by the morning and quickly disappears once the sun comes out. There are also inversions high up, which can slow down the rise of thunderclouds, for example. Glider and balloon pilots therefore pay close attention to such layers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reversal; here: it is warmer above than below.
Region with high air pressure, usually with calm, dry weather.
Fog that does not lie on the ground but hangs over the land like a low blanket of cloud.
Cold, dry wind from the northeast on the Swiss Central Plateau.
Mixture of smoke, exhaust fumes and fog that pollutes the air.

gewusst: In strong inversions it can be more than 10 degrees warmer in the mountains than in the valley below.
The word smog is made up of the English words “smoke” and “fog”.
Hikers and day trippers sometimes call sunny trips above the sea of fog “Nebelflucht”, German for escaping the fog.

teile.einleitung: The Beznau nuclear power station is on an island in the River Aare in the canton of Aargau. Its unit 1 started up in 1969 and is the oldest nuclear power station still running in the world. The plant belongs to the energy company Axpo and has supplied electricity for Switzerland for more than 50 years.
wichtigste: The Beznau nuclear power station is on an island in the Aare near Döttingen in the canton of Aargau.
Unit 1 is the oldest nuclear power station still running in the world.
The plant has 2 reactor units of the pressurised water reactor type.
It is operated by the company Axpo.
With 1130 MW of thermal power and 365 MW of electrical power, the efficiency is about 32 per cent.
In hot summers it sometimes has to reduce its output so that the Aare does not get too warm, to protect the fish.
Part of the waste heat heats municipalities in the lower Aare valley as district heating.

abschnitte.text: The power station stands on **Beznau Island** between the Aare and a canal, in the municipality of Döttingen in the canton of Aargau. A **hydroelectric power station** has stood on the same island since the beginning of the 20th century. Not far away are the Paul Scherrer Institute and the interim storage facility for radioactive waste in Würenlingen. The Aare supplies the cooling water for the nuclear power station.

Both units have a **pressurised water reactor**. In the reactor uranium nuclei are split, and the heat released heats water that is under high pressure and therefore does not boil. In a **steam generator** this water passes its heat to a second circuit, where steam is produced. The steam drives turbines and generators, which produce electricity.

Unit 1 started up in **1969**, and unit 2 followed in 1971. This made Beznau Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station. Mühleberg, Gösgen and Leibstadt were added later, though Mühleberg was shut down in 2019. Over the years Beznau has been upgraded several times to improve safety; it is supervised by **ENSI**, the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate.

Each unit produces about 1130 megawatts of heat but only about 365 megawatts of electricity, so the **efficiency** is about 32 per cent. Most of the heat goes into the Aare with the cooling water. Part of it, however, is supplied through the **Refuna** district heating network to municipalities in the lower Aare valley, where it heats houses. Because the Aare must not get too warm, Beznau sometimes has to run at lower output in hot summers.

After the nuclear accident at **Fukushima** in 2011, Switzerland decided not to authorise any new nuclear power stations, and voters confirmed this in 2017 with the Energy Strategy 2050. Existing plants may keep running as long as they are safe. Axpo has announced that it will shut down the two units for good in 2032 and 2033 (as of 2025). After that, the years-long **decommissioning** of the plant will begin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reactor in which water under high pressure takes up the heat without boiling.
Share of the energy that is turned into a useful form, here into electricity.
Heat delivered through pipes to many houses.
Gradual dismantling of a power station that has been shut down.

gewusst: Because Beznau has no cooling tower, you do not see a big cloud of steam there as at Gösgen or Leibstadt.
The hydroelectric power station on the same island is much older than the nuclear power station.

teile.einleitung: In physics, momentum is the force behind a movement, how much “oomph” it has. It depends on how heavy an object is and how fast it moves. A slow lorry can therefore have just as much momentum as a fast car.
wichtigste: Momentum is mass times velocity.
Its SI unit is kilograms times metres per second.
Momentum is a vector quantity, so it has a direction.
A ball of 0.16 kilograms moving at 25 metres per second has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.
A 10 tonne lorry at 1 m/s and a 1 tonne car at 10 m/s have the same momentum.
With the same momentum, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.
Close to the speed of light, momentum is greater than mass times velocity.
Light also has momentum, even though photons have no mass.

abschnitte.text: **Momentum** describes how much motion there is in an object. It is calculated as mass times velocity, and its symbol is usually p. The unit is kilograms times metres per second. A football of 0.16 kilograms flying at 25 metres per second has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.

Momentum is a **vector quantity**, so it always points in the direction of motion. If a ball of 0.3 kilograms hits a wall head on at 10 metres per second and bounces back just as fast, its momentum is reversed. The change in momentum is then not zero but 6 kg·m/s. That is why a wall feels a ball that bounces off more strongly than one that just drops.

A heavy, slow object can have as much momentum as a light, fast one. A lorry of 10 tonnes moving at 1 metre per second has the same momentum as a car of 1 tonne moving at 10 metres per second. But their **kinetic energy** is different: the faster, lighter car has ten times as much. Energy and momentum are therefore two different quantities.

Isaac Newton realised that a **force** changes the momentum of an object. The shorter the time in which the momentum changes, the greater the force. That is why airbags, cycle helmets and crumple zones protect you: they make the braking time longer and so reduce the force on the body. When landing after a jump you also bend your knees to cushion the impact.

Surprisingly, light also has momentum, even though **photons** have no mass. That is why solar sails in space can be driven by sunlight. If an object moves at almost the speed of light, the simple formula no longer applies. According to Albert Einstein's **theory of relativity**, the momentum is then greater than mass times velocity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, the force behind a movement.
Quantity that has a size and a direction.
Smallest particle of light.
Force times the time it acts; it equals the change in momentum.

gewusst: In German, momentum is called “Impuls”, while the English word impulse means rather the force times its duration.
An ocean ship moving slowly has such enormous momentum that it needs several kilometres to stop.
In 2010 Japan successfully tested a solar sail in space for the first time with the space probe IKAROS.

teile.einleitung: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and engineer who greatly improved the steam engine. His economical engines strongly drove the Industrial Revolution forward. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
wichtigste: James Watt lived from 1736 to 1819 and came from Scotland.
He greatly improved the steam engine.
A separate condenser made his engine much more economical.
With the businessman Matthew Boulton he founded a company making steam engines.
He introduced horsepower to compare engines with horses.
His engines strongly drove the Industrial Revolution forward.
The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

abschnitte.text: James Watt was born in Greenock in **Scotland** in 1736 and died near Birmingham in England in 1819. He first worked as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow. There, around 1763, he was asked to repair a model of a **steam engine** that worked on the principle of Thomas Newcomen. While doing so he noticed how much coal and heat this engine wasted.

In the old engine the cylinder was cooled with cold water at every stroke and then heated up again. In 1765 Watt had the idea of cooling the steam in a **separate condenser**. That way the cylinder stayed hot all the time, and the engine needed much less coal. In 1769 he received a patent for it.

From 1775 Watt built steam engines in Birmingham together with the businessman **Matthew Boulton**. He improved them further so that they could not only pump but also turn wheels. This meant his engines could drive spinning mills, mills and factories. A centrifugal governor made sure the engine ran at an even speed.

To sell his engines, Watt compared them with horses, which drove many pumps at the time. That is how he introduced the unit **horsepower**. In his honour, today's unit of power is called the **watt**, abbreviated W. One horsepower (in its metric form) equals about 735 watts. A motor that does 1200 joules of work in 60 seconds has a power of 20 watts.

Lamps, hairdryers and kettles show how many watts they have. The more watts, the more energy the device uses per second. A 60 watt lamp uses 600 watt hours in 10 hours, or 0.6 **kilowatt hours**. This is exactly the unit that is counted on the electricity bill.

The improved steam engine powered the **Industrial Revolution**, which began in Great Britain. Factories no longer had to stand by rivers with water wheels. Later this led to steam locomotives and steamships, like the ones that still sail on Lake Lucerne or Lake Geneva today. Watt's portrait, together with Matthew Boulton, appeared on a British 50 pound banknote.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine that produces movement using hot steam.
In a steam engine, a container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
How much work or energy is converted per second.
The right to be the only one allowed to use an invention.

gewusst: Watt is said to have had the idea of the separate condenser on a Sunday walk in Glasgow.
One horsepower was originally meant as the work a strong horse can keep up for a long time.
A modern high-speed train has a power of many thousands of kilowatts.

teile.einleitung: Every battery and every other voltage source has an internal resistance, a built-in electrical resistance inside itself. It causes the voltage to drop as soon as a current flows. That is why, for example, a car's headlights dim briefly when the engine is started.
wichtigste: Internal resistance is the resistance inside a voltage source.
With no current, you measure the full open-circuit voltage.
When current flows, the terminal voltage is lower by internal resistance times current.
A 1.5 volt battery with 0.5 ohms internal resistance still delivers 1.3 volts at 0.4 amperes.
Internal resistance limits the short-circuit current.
A source delivers the most power when the load resistance equals the internal resistance.
When a car starts, the voltage drops because of the high starter current, and the headlights dim.

abschnitte.text: A battery supplies current through chemical reactions inside it. The current also has to flow through the materials of the battery itself, and these slow it down a little. This built-in resistance is called **internal resistance**, and it is measured in ohms. So you can picture a battery as an ideal voltage source with a small resistance behind it.

With no device connected, no current flows, and you then measure the **open-circuit voltage**. As soon as current flows, part of the voltage is already lost inside. At the terminals only the **terminal voltage** is left: open-circuit voltage minus internal resistance times current. With a 1.5 volt battery and 0.5 ohms internal resistance, 1.3 volts remain at 0.4 amperes.

You can work out the internal resistance from two measurements. If a source shows 9.0 volts in open circuit and still 8.0 volts at 0.5 amperes, 1 volt has been lost inside. The internal resistance is therefore 1 volt divided by 0.5 amperes, which gives 2 ohms. If you connect two D cells of 1.5 volts and 0.3 ohms each in series to 2.4 ohms, exactly 1 ampere flows, because the voltages and internal resistances add up.

If you connect the terminals directly, only the internal resistance limits the current. A 12 volt car battery with 0.02 ohms internal resistance could then deliver about 600 amperes, enough to make cables glow. The car needs this low internal resistance for the **starter motor**, which draws a lot of current when starting. The voltage drops briefly, and the headlights dim.

A source delivers the greatest possible power to a device when the device's resistance is exactly as large as the internal resistance. This is called **impedance matching**. A source with 6 volts and 3 ohms internal resistance can then deliver at most 3 watts, but half of the energy is turned into heat in the source itself. Flat or cold batteries have a higher internal resistance, which is why mobile phone batteries struggle in winter when you go skiing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Voltage of a source when no current flows.
Voltage at the terminals when current flows.
Unit of electrical resistance.
Direct connection of the terminals with no device in between.

gewusst: A car starter battery has a much smaller internal resistance than a small torch battery.
Battery testers often measure the internal resistance indirectly to see how good a battery still is.
Because a battery heats up through its internal resistance at high current, rechargeable batteries get warm during fast charging.

teile.einleitung: A nuclear power station is a power station that produces electricity from the energy of atomic nuclei. It is also called an atomic power station. In Switzerland nuclear power stations supply a large share of the electricity, and at the same time their advantages and disadvantages have been debated for decades.
wichtigste: A nuclear power station gets energy by splitting uranium nuclei.
The heat turns water into steam, and the steam drives a turbine and a generator.
Nuclear power stations need large amounts of water for cooling.
The white cloud above a cooling tower is water vapour and not poisonous.
What is left is radioactive waste that gives off dangerous radiation for a very long time.
In 2026 there are nuclear power stations in operation at 3 sites in Switzerland: Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt.
Beznau is one of the oldest nuclear power stations still running in the world.

abschnitte.text: In the **reactor** the nuclei of **uranium** atoms are split. This releases a great deal of heat. This heat is used to turn water into steam, and the steam drives a turbine. The turbine turns a generator that produces electricity, rather like a bike dynamo. Then the steam is cooled again so that it can be used once more.

A nuclear power station needs huge amounts of water for cooling. That is why nuclear power stations often stand on large rivers, in Switzerland for example on the Aare and the Rhine. Some plants have a tall, round **cooling tower**. A white cloud rises from it, made of water vapour, just like the clouds in the sky.

In 2026 nuclear power stations are running at three sites in Switzerland. **Beznau** in the canton of Aargau has two reactors; the first started up in 1969 and is one of the oldest in the world. **Gösgen** is in the canton of Solothurn, and **Leibstadt**, on the Rhine in the canton of Aargau, is the largest Swiss nuclear power station. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down at the end of 2019 and is being dismantled. In recent years nuclear power stations have supplied about a third of Swiss electricity.

The used fuel elements are highly **radioactive**. They give off invisible radiation that is dangerous for living things. Some waste stays radioactive for hundreds of thousands of years. In Switzerland Nagra has been looking for decades for a safe **deep geological repository** deep in the rock, and the Nördlich Lägern area has been proposed as the site.

Nuclear power stations produce a lot of electricity, whether or not the sun is shining or the wind is blowing. While running they emit hardly any carbon dioxide, which harms the climate. On the other hand, radioactive waste is produced, and serious accidents such as **Chernobyl** in 1986 or **Fukushima** in 2011 can contaminate large areas. After Fukushima, Switzerland decided not to authorise any more new nuclear power stations, and voters confirmed this course in a vote in 2017.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a lot of energy.
Heart of the power station, where nuclear fission takes place under control.
Invisible radiation given off by certain substances that can harm living things.
Tall tower in which the cooling water is cooled with the help of the air.

gewusst: A uranium fuel pellet no bigger than a thimble provides about as much energy as around a tonne of coal.
The cooling tower at Gösgen is about 150 metres high and can be seen from far away.
Not every nuclear power station has a cooling tower: Beznau is cooled directly with water from the Aare.

teile.einleitung: A merry-go-round is a spinning platform on which you ride round in a circle, in the playground or at the funfair. In Switzerland the classic merry-go-round with wooden horses is also called a Rösslispiel. As it spins you feel exciting forces that physics can explain precisely.
wichtigste: A merry-go-round turns around an axis in the middle.
To start it turning, it needs a strong push or a motor.
On a fast-spinning merry-go-round you are pushed outwards; this force is called centrifugal force.
Right on the outer edge you are moving fastest.
In the middle you have to hold on least.
After the ride you feel dizzy because your organ of balance is confused.
It is safest to get off when the merry-go-round has stopped.

abschnitte.text: A merry-go-round consists of a round platform or frame that turns around an upright **axis**. In the playground you push a roundabout with your own strength; at the fair a motor drives the merry-go-round. There are carousels with horses, chair swing rides in which you fly through the air in seats on chains, and many other kinds. In Switzerland they are part of every **Chilbi**, the village fair, and of festivals such as the Knabenschiessen in Zurich.

When the merry-go-round spins, your body actually wants to fly straight on; this is called **inertia**. Because the merry-go-round forces you onto a circular path, you feel a pull outwards, the **centrifugal force**. The faster the merry-go-round spins and the further out you sit, the stronger it is. You have to hold on with your arms, which provide the necessary force towards the centre.

Every point on the merry-go-round takes the same time for one turn. But at the outer edge the path for one turn is much longer than near the middle. That is why you move fastest at the edge, while in the middle you hardly do more than turn on the spot. Physicists therefore distinguish between the **rotational speed** of the whole merry-go-round and the **linear speed** at a particular point.

In the **inner ear** is the organ of balance, with small curved canals filled with liquid. As you spin, the liquid starts moving and tells the brain you are turning. When the merry-go-round stops, the liquid keeps swirling for a little while. The brain then thinks you are still turning, while your eyes see something different, and you feel dizzy.

The word carousel comes from the French “carrousel” and the Italian “carosello”. Originally it meant splendid **riding tournaments** at royal courts, in which riders rode in a circle and carried out tests of skill. Later, turning frames with wooden horses were built on which children and ordinary townspeople could also “ride”. In the 19th century the first merry-go-rounds were driven by steam engines.

Always hold on well with both hands and stay seated during the ride. Only get off when the merry-go-round has **stopped** completely, otherwise you could fall. When pushing a playground roundabout, make sure no feet get under the platform. If you feel unwell, say so in good time so that the others spin it more slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force you feel pushing you outwards when spinning.
The property of objects that makes them want to keep moving as they are.
Part of the inner ear that senses the position and turning of the head.
Swiss German word for a merry-go-round with wooden horses.

gewusst: Figure skaters hardly get dizzy during fast spins, because they have trained for a long time.
The same centrifugal force acts in a salad spinner as on a merry-go-round; it flings the water off the leaves.
Astronauts also train in huge centrifuges, which work like an extremely fast merry-go-round.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, often called CO2 for short, is a colourless and odourless gas. It is produced when something burns, for example a candle, and also when we breathe. Plants need carbon dioxide to live, but too much of it in the air warms the climate.
wichtigste: Carbon dioxide consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Carbon dioxide is produced when a candle burns.
Humans and animals breathe out carbon dioxide.
Plants take in carbon dioxide and, with light, turn it into sugar and oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and contributes to global warming.
Frozen carbon dioxide is called dry ice.
The bubbles in sparkling mineral water are made of carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.text: **Carbon dioxide** is a chemical compound of carbon and oxygen. Its formula is **CO2**: one carbon atom is joined to two oxygen atoms. At normal temperatures it is a gas that you can neither see nor smell. It is about one and a half times as heavy as air and therefore tends to collect near the ground. The air contains only a very small share of it, about 0.04 per cent.

When wood, candle wax, petrol or natural gas burn, the carbon in them combines with the oxygen in the air. This produces carbon dioxide and water vapour. A kind of slow burning also takes place in our body when we turn food into energy. That is why we breathe out carbon dioxide. It is also produced during fermentation, for example when yeast makes bread dough rise.

Plants take in carbon dioxide through small openings in their leaves. With the help of sunlight and water they make sugar from it and give off **oxygen**. This process is called **photosynthesis**. In this way a cycle is formed: animals and humans breathe out carbon dioxide, and plants take it in again. Forests and oceans store huge amounts of carbon in the process.

Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**: it lets sunlight through but holds back part of the Earth's heat. Without this natural effect it would be icy cold on Earth. But since the beginning of industrialisation people have burnt a lot of coal, oil and natural gas. As a result, the share of carbon dioxide in the air has risen sharply, from about 280 to more than 420 parts per million (as of 2024). This is a main reason for the warming of the climate, which can also be seen in Switzerland in the shrinking of the glaciers.

Carbon dioxide has many uses in everyday life. It provides the bubbles in sparkling mineral water and lemonade. It is found in some **fire extinguishers**, because it takes the oxygen away from flames. At minus 78 degrees it becomes solid and is then called **dry ice**. Dry ice does not melt into a liquid but turns straight back into gas, which is used for fog effects in the theatre.

begriffe.erklaerung: Gas in the air that holds back heat like the glass of a greenhouse.
Process in which plants use light to make sugar from CO2 and water.
Frozen carbon dioxide at a temperature of about minus 78 degrees.
Tiny particle that all substances are made of.

gewusst: When baking, carbon dioxide from yeast or baking powder puffs up the dough, which is why bread has holes.
The Scot Joseph Black discovered the gas in the 18th century and called it “fixed air”.

teile.einleitung: A bell is a device that draws attention to something with a loud sound, for example at the front door, on a bike or, in the past, at school. The electric bell is a classic example of electromagnetism at work. In it, electrical energy is turned into movement and sound.
wichtigste: A bell makes a sound to draw people's attention to something.
In an electric bell an electromagnet attracts the armature with the clapper.
The Wagner hammer interrupts the current again and again, so that the clapper strikes back and forth quickly.
A spring pulls the armature back after each strike.
Electrical energy is turned into movement and sound.
At the front door you press a push button to switch on the bell.
A bell transformer lowers the mains voltage to a harmless extra-low voltage.

abschnitte.text: A bell is a **signalling device** that produces a bright, often shrill sound. There are mechanical bells, for example the bike bell, where you move a lever with your thumb. There are also electric bells on front doors, in schools or at level crossings. In the past telephones and alarm clocks also had a built-in **bell** with a clapper.

The heart of the electric bell is an **electromagnet**, a coil of wire around an iron core. When current flows through the coil, the iron core becomes magnetic. It then attracts a movable strip of iron, the **armature**. A small hammer, the clapper, is attached to the armature and strikes a metal gong.

So that the bell does not strike just once, there is the **Wagner hammer**, a self-interrupter. When the armature is attracted, a contact opens and the current is cut off. The magnet loses its force and a **spring** pulls the armature back. This closes the contact again and everything starts over, many times a second. When the contact opens, a small **spark** often forms.

At the front door you operate the bell with a **push button**, a switch that only lets current through as long as you press it. The bell wiring does not work with the 230 volts of the socket. A **bell transformer** in the fuse box lowers the voltage to a harmless extra-low voltage of about 8 to 12 volts. That is why the bell wire at the door is not dangerous.

An electric **chime** does not make a continuous sound but a “ding-dong”. An iron rod moved by a coil strikes once each against two plates tuned to different notes. Today there are also electronic doorbells that play tunes. Modern video doorbells even show on your mobile phone who is at the door.

begriffe.erklaerung: Coil with an iron core that is only magnetic while current flows.
Movable piece of iron that is attracted by the magnet.
Arrangement that keeps interrupting the current in the bell by itself.
Switch that only stays on as long as you press it.
Device that raises or lowers electrical voltage.

gewusst: The Wagner hammer is named after the German inventor Johann Philipp Wagner, who developed it in the 19th century.
The same self-interrupter used to be found in buzzers and in induction coils.
A bike bell needs no electricity at all; there your thumb drives the clapper through a small gear.

teile.einleitung: Internal energy is the total energy contained in the tiny particles of an object. It includes the energy of their jiggling movement and the energy of their attraction to each other. When an object gets warmer, its internal energy rises.
wichtigste: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles in a system.
For an ideal gas with a fixed amount of substance it depends only on temperature.
Each degree of freedom of a particle contributes on average one half k times T.
A diatomic molecule such as nitrogen has 5 degrees of freedom at room temperature.
One mole of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 kelvin has about 3.7 kilojoules of internal energy.
After a complete cycle the change in internal energy is zero.
Enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms and molecules that constantly move, vibrate or rotate. **Internal energy** is the sum of all the kinetic and potential energies of these particles. When a substance gets warmer, the particles move faster and the internal energy rises. Its symbol is usually U, and it is measured in joules.

In an ideal gas the particles do not attract each other, so only their movement counts. That is why, for a fixed amount of substance, internal energy depends only on **temperature**. For a monatomic gas such as helium it is three halves times amount of substance times gas constant times temperature. For one mole at 300 kelvin that is about 3.7 kilojoules, and if you heat 2 moles by 10 kelvin, the internal energy rises by about 249 joules.

A **degree of freedom** is an independent way in which a particle can move. A single atom can move in three directions and has 3 degrees of freedom. A diatomic molecule such as nitrogen can also rotate about two axes and has 5 degrees of freedom at room temperature. According to the **equipartition theorem**, each degree of freedom gets on average one half k times T, where k is the Boltzmann constant.

The **first law of thermodynamics** says that internal energy changes only when heat is added or work is done. When you rub your hands, work is turned into internal energy and your hands get warm. When you pump up a bike tyre, the pump gets warm because you are doing work on the gas. If a gas in an engine goes through a complete **cycle**, it is back in its starting state at the end, and the change in internal energy is zero.

In the 19th century researchers such as Julius Robert Mayer, James Prescott Joule and Rudolf Clausius realised that heat is a form of energy. Joule showed with a paddle wheel in water that mechanical work warms the water. For processes at constant pressure, for example in chemistry, **enthalpy** is often used. It is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit of energy, named after James Prescott Joule.
Independent way in which a particle can move.
Process in which a system returns to its starting state.
Internal energy plus pressure times volume.

gewusst: Because of its enormous mass, an iceberg has more internal energy in total than a hot cup of tea.
According to quantum physics, even at absolute zero the particles would still have a small leftover energy.
The unit joule is named after a brewer who did physics in his spare time.

teile.einleitung: Infrared radiation is invisible light whose wavelength is longer than that of red light. We cannot see it, but we can feel it as warmth on our skin. Every warm body, including humans, constantly gives off infrared radiation.
wichtigste: Infrared radiation has longer wavelengths than red light.
It reaches up to a wavelength of about 1 millimetre.
On the skin you feel infrared radiation as warmth.
William Herschel discovered it in 1800 with a thermometer.
Remote controls and thermal imaging cameras use infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases hold back the infrared radiation from the Earth's surface in the atmosphere.
Rattlesnakes can sense infrared radiation with special pit organs.

abschnitte.text: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and colours differ in their **wavelength**. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see, about 780 nanometres. Beyond that begins **infrared radiation**, which reaches up to a wavelength of about 1 millimetre. The name means below red, because its frequency is lower than that of red light.

In 1800 the astronomer **William Herschel** split sunlight into its colours with a glass prism. He put thermometers in the different colours and found that it got warmer towards red. It was actually warmest next to the red light, where nothing could be seen at all. That is how he discovered invisible heat radiation.

Every body that is warmer than absolute zero gives off **thermal radiation**. At room temperature and body temperature it lies almost entirely in the infrared. Humans also constantly radiate infrared because of their body heat. About half of the energy from the Sun that reaches us is infrared radiation, which is why sunshine feels warm.

An ordinary **remote control** sends invisible infrared flashes to the television. A **thermal imaging camera** shows how much infrared radiation objects give off and so makes warm spots visible. It can be used to find heat leaks in houses, missing people at night or overheated parts of machines. The James Webb Space Telescope also observes space in the infrared and so sees through clouds of dust.

The Earth's surface is warmed by the Sun and gives the heat off again as infrared radiation. **Greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour hold back part of this radiation in the atmosphere. Without this natural greenhouse effect, the average temperature on Earth would be about minus 18 °C. More greenhouse gases from humans strengthen the effect and lead to global warming.

**Rattlesnakes** and other pit vipers have small pit organs between the eye and the nostril. With them they sense the infrared radiation of warm prey, even in complete darkness. Some boas and pythons can also sense heat. A few beetles even find forest fires with infrared sensors, because they lay their eggs in freshly burnt wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance from one wave crest to the next.
Radiation that every warm body gives off.
A camera that makes infrared radiation visible and so shows temperatures.
A gas in the air that holds back thermal radiation.
The division of light or radiation by wavelength.

gewusst: With a mobile phone camera you can often see the flashing of a remote control, which is invisible to our eyes.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be an icy planet.
Herschel had already discovered the planet Uranus in 1781, before he found infrared radiation.

teile.einleitung: The Hubble Space Telescope is a large telescope that has been orbiting the Earth since 1990. Because it observes from above the atmosphere, it delivers razor-sharp images of planets, stars and very distant galaxies. It is one of the most famous scientific instruments of all time.
wichtigste: Hubble was carried into space by the Space Shuttle in 1990.
It is named after the American astronomer Edwin Hubble.
Its main mirror is 2.4 metres across.
It circles in a low Earth orbit at a height of about 500 kilometres.
The first images were blurred because of a mirror fault, spherical aberration.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier took part in servicing missions to Hubble.
The Hubble Deep Field of 1995 showed thousands of galaxies in a seemingly empty patch of sky.
Hubble helped to measure the Hubble constant, and with it the expansion of the universe, more precisely.

abschnitte.text: Hubble is a **reflecting telescope**: a curved main mirror 2.4 metres across gathers the light. The telescope is about as long as a bus and weighs about 11 tonnes. On Earth the restless air blurs the images, which is why stars twinkle. In space there is no such disturbance, and Hubble can also see ultraviolet light, which the atmosphere swallows.

On 24 April 1990 the Space Shuttle Discovery put the telescope into an orbit at a height of about 500 kilometres. It soon turned out that the images were blurred, because the edge of the main mirror had been ground very slightly wrong. This fault is called **spherical aberration**. The grinding was off by only about a fiftieth of the width of a hair, but that was enough for fuzzy images.

In 1993 astronauts flew to Hubble with the Space Shuttle and fitted a kind of pair of glasses that corrected the mirror fault. Altogether there were five **servicing missions**, the last in 2009. During them, cameras, batteries and gyroscopes were replaced. The Swiss astronaut **Claude Nicollier** took part in 1993 and 1999, and in 1999 he even made a spacewalk at the telescope.

In 1995 Hubble pointed at a tiny, seemingly empty spot in the sky for many days. On the image, the **Hubble Deep Field**, thousands of galaxies could be seen, each with billions of stars. Hubble also helped to work out the **Hubble constant** more precisely using pulsating stars called Cepheids. It describes how fast the universe is expanding.

abschnitte.titel: The man it is named after
abschnitte.text: Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer who showed in the 1920s that there are many other galaxies besides our Milky Way. He also discovered that the galaxies are moving away from each other. From this, researchers concluded that the universe is expanding. Today Hubble works alongside the James Webb Space Telescope, which has been in space since the end of 2021 and mainly observes infrared light.

begriffe.erklaerung: A telescope that gathers light with a curved mirror instead of lenses.
The path on which a satellite circles the Earth.
A huge collection of billions of stars, like our Milky Way.
An imaging fault in which light from the edge and from the middle of a mirror does not meet at the same point.

gewusst: Hubble circles the Earth about every 95 minutes, that is around 15 times a day.
A Swiss man, Claude Nicollier, personally worked on Hubble with tools.
Hubble is the only large telescope that has been repaired by astronauts in space.

teile.einleitung: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle is a fundamental law of quantum physics. It says that you can never know both the position and the momentum of a particle with any precision you like at the same time. This is not because of poor measuring instruments but is a basic property of nature.
wichtigste: Werner Heisenberg published the uncertainty principle in 1927.
The product of the uncertainty in position and the uncertainty in momentum is at least ħ/2.
The more precisely you know the position, the less precise the momentum, and the other way round.
The uncertainty is a basic property of nature and not a measuring error.
Spectral lines have a natural width because excited states live only briefly.
At normal pressure helium does not become solid even at absolute zero, because of its zero-point energy.
Heisenberg received the Nobel Prize in Physics for founding quantum mechanics.

abschnitte.text: In everyday life you can know at the same time where a ball is and how fast it is flying. In the world of tiny particles such as **electrons**, this is not possible. The uncertainty principle says: the product of the uncertainty in position Δx and the **uncertainty in momentum** Δp is at least ħ/2. The symbol ħ is the reduced Planck constant, a tiny constant of nature of about 1.055·10⁻³⁴ J·s. So if you know the position very precisely, the momentum becomes very uncertain.
