Heisenberg explained the idea with a **thought experiment**. To locate an electron precisely, you need light with a very short wavelength, for example gamma rays. But such light is very rich in energy and gives the electron a hard push when it hits it. This changes its speed strongly and unpredictably. Today we know that the uncertainty goes even deeper: a particle simply does not have an exact position and an exact momentum at the same time.

An electron in an atom is confined to a region of about 1·10⁻¹⁰ metres. The uncertainty principle then gives an uncertainty in speed of at least about 5.8·10⁵ m/s. That is over 2 million km/h. That is why an electron in an atom can never sit still at one point. With a football, on the other hand, the uncertainty is so tiny that you would never notice it.

A similar uncertainty applies between energy and time. Because excited states in atoms have only a short **lifetime**, their energy is somewhat uncertain. That is why spectral lines have a natural width. Even at **absolute zero**, particles never stand completely still; they have a zero-point energy. In helium this is so great that at normal pressure it stays liquid even at the lowest temperature.

**Werner Heisenberg** was born in Würzburg in 1901 and died in Munich in 1976. In 1925, on the island of Heligoland, he developed the foundations of **quantum mechanics**. Two years later, in 1927, he published the uncertainty principle. He worked closely with Niels Bohr in Copenhagen and with Wolfgang Pauli, who later taught at ETH Zurich. For founding quantum mechanics Heisenberg received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1932.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, that is the force behind a movement.
The physics of tiny particles such as atoms and electrons.
A very small constant of nature that appears everywhere in quantum physics.
An experiment that you only play through in your head to test an idea.
The smallest energy that a particle always keeps, even at the lowest temperature.

gewusst: Heisenberg was only 25 years old when he found the uncertainty principle.
Without the uncertainty principle, electrons would fall into the atomic nucleus and atoms would not be stable.
Helium can only be made solid if it is also put under high pressure.

teile.einleitung: The fundamental equation of mechanics is F = m·a, and it is one of the most important formulas in physics. It says that a force accelerates a body more strongly the greater the force and the smaller the body's mass. Isaac Newton described this connection as the second of his three laws of motion.
wichtigste: The fundamental equation of mechanics is F = m·a, that is force equals mass times acceleration.
It is Newton's second law and was published in 1687.
It always means the resultant force, that is the sum of all the forces on the body.
A force of 1 newton accelerates a mass of 1 kg at 1 m/s².
If you double the force and the mass at the same time, the acceleration stays the same.
In its most general form, force is the rate of change of momentum.
The equation is used to calculate the movements of cars, rockets and planets.

abschnitte.text: The formula **F = m·a** links three quantities: the force F in newtons, the mass m in kilograms and the acceleration a in m/s². The harder you pull or push on a body, the faster it becomes. The heavier the body, the more force you need for the same acceleration. That is why an empty shopping trolley is easier to push than a full one. If you rearrange the formula, a = F/m or m = F/a.

Often several forces act on a body at the same time. The formula then needs the **resultant force**, that is what is left after adding them all up. A ball of 0.5 kg has a weight of about 4.9 N. If the air is braking it with 1 N at that moment, 3.9 N remain, and the ball accelerates at 7.81 m/s². If all the forces cancel each other out, the acceleration is zero and the body stays at rest or keeps moving steadily.

A force of 12 N accelerates a body at 3 m/s², so it has a mass of 4 kg. A car of 1000 kg accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 8 seconds, which is 2.5 m/s². This needs a force of 2500 N. If a force of 30 N pulls two connected blocks of 2 kg and 4 kg, both accelerate at 5 m/s². The **rope** between them has to pull the rear block and therefore carries a force of 20 N.

On a frictionless **inclined plane** only part of the weight pulls the body down the slope. At a slope of 30° it is exactly half. That is why a body slides down there at about 4.9 m/s², half as much as in free fall. On steep ski slopes in the Alps, skiers therefore become faster than on gentle slopes. In reality, however, friction and air resistance slow them down.

**Isaac Newton** published his three laws of motion in 1687 in his book “Principia”. He formulated the second law more generally: force is the rate of change of **momentum**, that is of mass times velocity. This form also applies when the mass changes, for example with a rocket burning fuel. In Newton's honour the unit of force is now called the newton. 1 N equals 1 kg·m/s².

begriffe.erklaerung: The cause of a body becoming faster, slower or deflected, measured in newtons.
How much matter there is in a body and how much inertia it has, measured in kilograms.
How quickly the speed changes, measured in m/s².
Mass times velocity, that is the force behind a movement.

gewusst: A 100 g bar of chocolate is pulled downwards on Earth with about 1 newton.
Engineers even use F = m·a to calculate how much thrust a rocket needs to fly into space.
Only at speeds close to the speed of light is the theory of relativity needed instead of Newton's formula.

teile.einleitung: The Higgs boson is an elementary particle that was discovered at the CERN research centre near Geneva. It belongs to the Higgs field, which gives many other elementary particles their mass. Its discovery in 2012 was one of the greatest sensations of modern physics.
wichtigste: In 2012 CERN announced the discovery of a Higgs boson.
The two experiments ATLAS and CMS at the LHC particle accelerator detected it together.
The Higgs boson has a mass of about 125 GeV.
The Higgs field gives elementary particles such as W bosons and quarks their mass.
Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013 for predicting it.
Most often a Higgs boson decays into a bottom quark and a bottom antiquark.
The decay into two photons was one of the most important discovery channels in 2012.

abschnitte.text: The **Higgs boson** is an elementary particle, that is a building block of matter that cannot be broken down any further. It belongs to the **Standard Model**, the great theory of particle physics. You can think of it as a small wave or excitation of the invisible Higgs field that fills the whole universe. Its mass is about 125 GeV, which is roughly 130 times that of a proton. It lives for only a tiny fraction of a second and then decays into other particles.

Without the **Higgs field**, many elementary particles would have no mass and would fly around at the speed of light. Particles such as quarks, electrons and W bosons get their mass through their interaction with this field. The more strongly a particle interacts with the field, the heavier it is. Most of the mass of a proton, however, does not come directly from the Higgs field. It comes from the binding energy of the strong interaction, which holds the quarks together.

In 1964 several physicists predicted this mechanism independently of each other. Among them were the Briton **Peter Higgs** and the Belgians François Englert and Robert Brout. For almost 50 years people searched in vain for the matching particle. In 2013 Higgs and Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics; Brout had already died in 2011. Peter Higgs died in 2024.

At **CERN**, on the border between Switzerland and France, stands the **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short. In this ring, about 27 kilometres long and deep underground, protons crash into each other at almost the speed of light. The collisions occasionally produce Higgs bosons, which decay at once. The huge detectors **ATLAS** and CMS search for their traces in billions of collisions. On 4 July 2012 the researchers in Geneva announced the discovery.

You cannot see a Higgs boson directly, only its **decay products**. Most often it decays into a bottom quark and a bottom antiquark. But this decay is hard to tell apart from other events. Easier to recognise is the rare decay into two photons, that is two particles of light. In 2012 this channel was one of the most important pieces of evidence for the discovery.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest building block of matter, which cannot be broken down any further.
A huge machine that brings particles almost to the speed of light and makes them collide.
Gigaelectronvolt, a unit in which particle physicists give energy and mass.
The theory that describes all known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces.
A measuring device that records the traces of particles.

gewusst: The Higgs boson is sometimes called the “God particle”, but most physicists do not like this name.
The ATLAS detector is about as tall as an eight-storey building.
The LHC ring runs beneath fields and villages in the canton of Geneva and in neighbouring France.

teile.einleitung: Interference is the overlapping of two or more waves. When wave crests meet, they reinforce each other; when a crest meets a trough, they cancel each other out. This creates patterns in water, sound and light.
wichtigste: In interference the displacements of waves add up.
Two coherent waves reinforce each other most when the path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength.
With an odd multiple of half the wavelength, waves of equal strength cancel each other out.
For a stable pattern the waves must be coherent.
Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference with anti-noise.
Two notes of 440 and 444 hertz produce a beat of 4 hertz.
With two sources in phase in a ripple tank, the lines of cancellation lie on hyperbolas.
The energy does not disappear when waves cancel; it is redistributed to places of reinforcement.

abschnitte.text: If you throw two stones into a pond at the same time, two circular waves travel towards each other. Where two crests meet, a particularly high crest forms; this is called **constructive interference**. When a crest meets a trough, they cancel out; this is **destructive interference**. In a ripple tank with two sources in phase, the lines of cancellation lie on hyperbolas.

Whether waves reinforce or cancel depends on the **path difference**, in other words how much further one wave has to travel to a point than the other. If it is a whole number multiple of the wavelength, crest meets crest. If it is an odd multiple of half the wavelength, crest meets trough. If two loudspeakers in phase send out a note with a wavelength of 1 metre, you hear almost nothing at a spot with a path difference of 0.5 metres.

For a stable pattern to form, the waves must be **coherent**, meaning they vibrate in step. Two ordinary light bulbs are not coherent, which is why you see no interference fringes with them. Laser light, on the other hand, is very coherent. At the beginning of the 19th century the Englishman Thomas Young showed with the **double slit experiment** that light forms interference fringes and is therefore a wave.

Headphones with active **noise cancelling** pick up surrounding noise with microphones. Then they produce anti-noise in which crests and troughs are exactly swapped, and the noise largely cancels out. If two tuning forks of 440 and 444 hertz sound at the same time, the note swells and fades four times a second. Musicians use this **beat** when tuning their instruments.

With **interferometers** you can measure lengths extremely accurately, because even tiny shifts change the fringe pattern. In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley used one to try to measure the movement of the Earth through a supposed ether, and found none. In 2015 huge laser interferometers in the USA detected gravitational waves for the first time. By the way, no energy is lost in interference; it is only redistributed from the dark places to the bright ones.

begriffe.erklaerung: Difference in the distance two waves travel to the same point.
Waves vibrate in a fixed rhythm with each other.
Regular swelling and fading of a note when two almost equal frequencies sound together.
Measuring device that uses interference for precise measurements.

gewusst: In holograms on banknotes and identity cards, the image is stored as an interference pattern.
Gravitational wave detectors change the length of their arms, which are several kilometres long, by only a tiny fraction of an atomic nucleus.
Water waves in a harbour basin can also become especially high in some places because of interference.

teile.einleitung: A chain reaction is a process in which each step sets off the next, like a row of falling dominoes. In physics it usually means the nuclear chain reaction, in which neutrons keep splitting new atomic nuclei. It is the basis of every nuclear power station.
wichtigste: In a nuclear chain reaction, neutrons from fissions trigger further fissions.
The multiplication factor k shows how many new fissions one fission triggers on average.
At k = 1 the chain reaction runs at constant power; this is called critical.
If k is greater than 1, the state is supercritical and the number of fissions grows.
The critical mass is the minimum mass for a self-sustaining chain reaction.
Control rods made of boron or cadmium capture neutrons and slow down the reaction.
Under the direction of Enrico Fermi, the first controlled, self-sustaining chain reaction was achieved in Chicago in 1942.

abschnitte.text: In a **chain reaction** each step sets one or more new steps in motion. A good picture of this is **dominoes** falling one after another. Reactions like this also happen in chemistry, for example in some kinds of burning. In physics it is mainly about the splitting of atomic nuclei.

When a slow **neutron** hits a nucleus of uranium-235, the nucleus can break into two smaller nuclei. This releases a lot of energy and usually two or three new neutrons. These neutrons can split more uranium nuclei, which release neutrons again. This creates a **nuclear chain reaction** that keeps itself going.

The **multiplication factor** k tells you how many new fissions one fission triggers on average. If k is less than 1, the reaction dies out; at k equal to 1 the power stays constant, which is called **critical**. With k greater than 1, the number of fissions grows very quickly. If each fission triggers exactly 2 new ones, there are already 1024 fissions in the 10th generation.

In a nuclear power station k should stay exactly at 1. For this, **control rods** made of substances such as boron or cadmium are pushed more or less deeply into the reactor, because they absorb neutrons. The reason the reaction can be controlled mechanically fast enough at all is the **delayed neutrons**. A small share of the neutrons, less than one per cent, is only released seconds after the fission and so slows things down.

In 1933 the physicist **Leo Szilard** was the first to have the idea of a chain reaction with neutrons. In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin discovered nuclear fission, which Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained. On 2 December 1942 a team led by **Enrico Fermi** achieved the first controlled chain reaction beneath a sports stand at the University of Chicago. The experimental reactor was called Chicago Pile 1 and consisted of graphite blocks and uranium.

Controlled chain reactions produce electricity in nuclear power stations around the world, in Switzerland for example at Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt. Research reactors also use them, for example to make substances for medicine. If a chain reaction runs out of control, an enormous amount of energy is released in a very short time. That is why strict **safety regulations** apply in nuclear facilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Particle with no charge in the atomic nucleus.
Breaking of a heavy atomic nucleus into two lighter nuclei.
Smallest amount of a fissile substance in which a chain reaction keeps itself going.
Rod that captures neutrons and so slows down the chain reaction.

gewusst: About two billion years ago there were natural nuclear reactors at Oklo in what is now Gabon, in which chain reactions ran by themselves.
Fermi's first reactor had no cooling and no shielding, because it only ran at very low power.
The element fermium is named after Enrico Fermi.

teile.einleitung: Derailleur gears are the most common kind of gears on bikes, especially on racing bikes and mountain bikes. They move the chain between sprockets of different sizes and so make pedalling easier uphill or faster on the flat. Behind them is simple maths with teeth and turns.
wichtigste: Derailleur gears consist of chainrings at the front and sprockets at the back.
The front derailleur moves the chain between the chainrings.
The rear derailleur guides the chain onto the sprockets at the back and keeps it tight.
You get the gear ratio by dividing the teeth on the chainring by the teeth on the sprocket.
A large chainring and a small sprocket give the hardest, fastest gear.
A small chainring and a large sprocket give the easiest gear for steep climbs.
With derailleur gears you only change gear while pedalling.

abschnitte.text: At the front on the crank there are one to three **chainrings**, and at the back on the hub of the rear wheel there is a whole stack of small toothed wheels, the **sprockets**. The chain connects a chainring with a sprocket. The **front derailleur** pushes the chain at the front from one chainring to another. At the back the **rear derailleur** guides the chain onto the chosen sprocket and keeps it tight with a spring. Everything is operated with gear levers on the handlebars, which work through cables or electronically.

The **gear ratio** tells you how often the rear wheel turns for each turn of the cranks. You divide the number of teeth on the chainring by the teeth on the sprocket. With 48 teeth at the front and 16 at the back, the rear wheel turns 3 times; with 34 and 34, only once. If the rear wheel has a circumference of 2.1 m, at a ratio of 3 you travel 6.3 m for each turn of the cranks. If you pedal 80 times a minute and go 5 m each time, you cover 400 m a minute, or 24 km/h.

With a large chainring and the smallest sprocket you ride in the hardest gear: every turn of the pedals takes you a long way but needs a lot of force. This is good for fast riding on the flat or downhill. With a small chainring and the largest sprocket you ride in the easiest gear. With it you can get up steep climbs such as an Alpine pass, though more slowly. The aim is a comfortable **cadence**, at which you can pedal evenly and not too hard.

With derailleur gears you can only change gear while pedalling, because the chain has to be moving to jump onto another sprocket. You should change gear before a climb and press a little less on the pedals while changing. The combination of the largest chainring with the largest sprocket is a bad idea. Then the chain runs at a steep angle, makes noise and wears out faster. A clean, oiled **chain** changes gear better and lasts longer.

Besides derailleur gears there are **hub gears**, in which the gears are well protected inside the rear wheel hub. Their advantage is that you can also change gear when standing still, for example at a red light. They need little maintenance and are therefore found on many town bikes. Derailleur gears, on the other hand, are lighter and often offer more gears. Modern mountain bikes often have just one chainring at the front and 12 sprockets at the back.

begriffe.erklaerung: The large toothed wheel at the front on the crank.
One of the small toothed wheels at the back on the rear wheel.
The part that pushes the chain onto another chainring at the front.
The part at the back that guides the chain onto the sprockets and keeps it tight.
How many turns of the cranks you pedal per minute.

gewusst: A bike with 2 chainrings and 11 sprockets has 22 gears in theory, but some of them are almost the same.
In the Tour de France the professionals now ride with electronic gears that change at the press of a button.
Track bikes on the velodrome have no gears and no brakes at all.

teile.einleitung: A high-pressure area, or high for short, is a large region of the atmosphere in which the air pressure is higher than in the surroundings. Highs usually bring calm, dry and sunny weather. On German-language weather maps you can recognise them by the large letter H.
wichtigste: On German-language weather maps a high-pressure area is marked with an H.
In a high the air sinks, warms up as it does so, and clouds break up.
At the centre of a high the wind is usually weak.
A long-lasting high can bring heatwaves and drought in summer.
Nights in a high are often especially cold, because without clouds a lot of heat escapes into space.
In winter, fog and fine dust often collect in the Central Plateau during high-pressure spells.
The names of the highs and lows in Central Europe are given by the Free University of Berlin.

abschnitte.text: The air presses on the Earth's surface with its weight; this is **air pressure**. It is measured in hectopascals and at sea level averages about 1013 hPa. In a high-pressure area the pressure is higher than in the surroundings. Experts also call a high an **anticyclone**. On German-language weather maps a large H stands at its centre, and a low gets a T.

In a high, air slowly sinks from above. As it sinks it is squeezed together and warms up. Warm air can take in more water vapour, which is why clouds break up. At the ground the air flows away outwards. In the northern hemisphere the air turns **clockwise** around the high as it does so, and at the centre the wind is usually weak.

In summer a high brings a lot of sunshine, and a long-lasting high can lead to **heatwaves** and drought. For Swiss summer weather the **Azores High** over the Atlantic is often important. On clear nights without clouds a lot of heat radiates into space, which is why it gets cool at night. In winter, bitter cold often comes from a high over Russia. Then an icy bise blows from the north-east across the Central Plateau.

During high-pressure spells in winter, cold air collects in the valleys and in the Central Plateau. Above it lies warmer air like a lid; this is called an **inversion**. Under the lid, stubborn **high fog** often forms, sometimes for days. Because the air hardly mixes, exhaust fumes and fine dust collect. Anyone who then climbs a mountain such as the Rigi or the Napf often sees a beautiful sea of fog in the sunshine.

Since 1954 the **Free University of Berlin** has been giving names to highs and lows over Central Europe. You also hear these names in Swiss weather forecasts. Since 2002 you can buy a **weather sponsorship** and so give a high or a low a name. Every year female and male names switch between highs and lows. The money is used to support weather observation at the university.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing on a surface, measured in hectopascals.
The technical term for a high-pressure area.
A weather situation in which warmer air lies above cold air.
A measuring device for air pressure.
A cold north-east wind in Switzerland.

gewusst: When the air pressure on the barometer rises, the weather often gets better.
During an inversion it can be sunny and warm on the mountain while it is cold in the valley under the fog.
If you buy a weather sponsorship, you can give a high your own first name, for example.

teile.einleitung: The International System of Units, SI for short, sets out the units in which lengths, masses, times and other quantities are measured. Today it is used in almost every country in the world and in science. Thanks to it, a metre in Switzerland means exactly the same as in Japan or Brazil.
wichtigste: The abbreviation SI comes from French: Système international d'unités.
The system was officially given the name SI in 1960.
It is based on the Metre Convention of 1875, which Switzerland also signed.
There are seven base units, for example the metre, the kilogram and the second.
All other units are derived from the base units.
The SI is coherent: derived units are formed without extra number factors.
The litre is not an SI unit, but it is accepted for use with the SI.

abschnitte.text: The **International System of Units** is a system of units of measurement that is valid worldwide. The abbreviation SI comes from French and stands for Système international d'unités. In the past almost every region had its own measures, such as the ell, the foot or the pound, which were a little different everywhere. This led to quarrels and mistakes in trade, so people wanted the same measures for everyone.

At the end of the 18th century France introduced the metric system with the metre and the kilogram. In 1875, 17 states signed the **Metre Convention** in Paris, Switzerland among them. They founded the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris. In 1960 the system was officially named SI, and it has been developed further ever since.

The SI has seven **base units**: the metre for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time, the ampere for electric current, the kelvin for temperature, the mole for amount of substance and the candela for luminous intensity. Since 2019 all seven have been defined by fixed constants of nature, for example the speed of light. Before that, the kilogram was still defined by a metal cylinder in Sèvres, the **International Prototype Kilogram**.

All other units are put together from the base units. The newton for force is kg·m/s², the coulomb for charge is A·s, and the pascal for pressure is kg/(m·s²). Because no extra number factors are needed, the SI is called **coherent**. Units such as the litre, minute, hour or degree Celsius are not SI units, but they may be used together with the SI.

For very large and very small values there are **prefixes** that are placed in front of the unit. Kilo means a thousand, as in kilometre, and milli means a thousandth, as in millimetre. Mega stands for a million, micro for a millionth. This makes it easy to give everything from tiny bacteria to huge distances.

In Switzerland the SI is required by law, for example in trade and on packaging. The **Federal Institute of Metrology** METAS in Wabern near Bern makes sure that measurements throughout the country are correct. It checks scales, petrol pumps and speed cameras, for example. Only a few countries, such as the USA, still mainly use other units like miles and pounds in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the seven basic units of the SI.
International treaty of 1875 on uniform measures.
Syllable such as kilo or milli that makes a unit bigger or smaller.
The science of accurate measurement.

gewusst: For decades the old prototype kilogram was kept in a safe under three glass bell jars.
In 1999 a NASA space probe to Mars was lost because one team calculated with American units and another with metric units.
The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium atoms, which are counted in atomic clocks.

teile.einleitung: An isochoric process is one in which a gas heats up or cools down while its volume stays the same. The gas is sealed in a rigid container. If you heat it, the pressure rises; if you cool it, the pressure falls.
wichtigste: In an isochoric process the volume stays constant.
The expansion work is zero.
The pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature in kelvin.
This law is often named after the French physicist Guillaume Amontons.
On a p-V diagram the process appears as a vertical line.
You must not throw aerosol cans into a fire, because the pressure rises sharply with temperature.
The gas thermometer uses the change in pressure of a sealed gas at constant volume.

abschnitte.text: The word **isochoric** comes from Greek and means equal space. In this process a gas is sealed in a container that cannot expand. Heat is added or removed, and pressure and temperature change as a result. But the volume always stays the same.

A gas consists of tiny particles that constantly fly around and hit the walls. These collisions create the **pressure**. When the gas is heated, the particles move faster. They therefore hit the wall more often and harder, and the pressure rises.

At constant volume the pressure is proportional to the **absolute temperature** in kelvin. This law is often named after Guillaume Amontons, who lived around 1700, and sometimes after Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. A gas at 100 kPa and 300 K has three times the pressure at 900 K, or 627 °C. A bike tyre at 200 kPa and 20 °C would have about 220 kPa at 50 °C if its volume stayed the same.

Because the volume does not change, the gas does no **expansion work**; it is zero. All the heat supplied therefore increases the internal energy and with it the temperature. On a **p-V diagram**, where pressure is plotted against volume, an isochoric process is a vertical line. Together with isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes, it forms one of the basic building blocks of thermodynamics.

An **aerosol can** is a rigid container holding gas under pressure. If you throw it into a fire, the pressure rises sharply until the can may burst. That is also why gas cylinders must not stand in full sunshine or next to heaters. In a car engine the petrol and air mixture burns so quickly that in theory this step is treated as isochoric.

A **gas thermometer** measures temperature through the pressure of a sealed gas at constant volume. Because gases behave very evenly, such thermometers are very accurate. With their help people realised that the pressure of a gas would have to become zero at about minus 273 °C. This led to the idea of **absolute zero**, where the kelvin scale begins.

begriffe.erklaerung: At constant volume.
Temperature in kelvin, measured from absolute zero.
Work that a gas does when it expands or is compressed.
A diagram that shows the pressure of a gas against its volume.
The energy contained in the movement of the particles of a substance.

gewusst: A car tyre has a higher pressure after a long drive, because the air inside has warmed up.
A pressure cooker is almost an isochoric container, which is why the pressure rises when it is heated and water only boils above 100 °C.
At absolute zero, minus 273.15 °C, the particles of a gas would almost completely stop moving.

teile.einleitung: High-voltage direct current transmission, HVDC for short, is a method of transporting large amounts of electricity as direct current over very long distances. Normally alternating current flows in power grids, but on long lines and in undersea cables direct current often has the advantage. HVDC lines connect countries, islands and wind farms at sea.
wichtigste: With HVDC, electricity is transmitted at a very high direct voltage.
Converter stations turn alternating current into direct current and back again at the end.
Modern stations use semiconductor components such as thyristors or IGBTs.
The world's first commercial HVDC link led to the Swedish island of Gotland.
HVDC can link grids with different frequencies or grids that do not run in sync.
A bipolar HVDC link needs only two conductors.
The main disadvantage is the expensive converter stations.

abschnitte.text: In the home and in most power grids, **alternating current** flows, which in Europe changes direction 50 times a second. With HVDC, on the other hand, the electricity is transmitted as **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction. The voltage is very high, often several hundred thousand volts. In this way huge amounts of electricity can flow over hundreds or thousands of kilometres. The German abbreviation HGÜ stands for the same thing as HVDC.

At the start of the line there is a **converter station**, which turns alternating current into direct current. At the receiving end a second station turns the direct current back into alternating current. In the past, mercury vapour valves were used for this; today **thyristors** or IGBTs made of semiconductor material are used. A bipolar link manages with two conductors, one with positive and one with negative voltage. If both stations are in the same place, with no long-distance line at all, it is called a **back-to-back link**.

Over very long distances, less energy is lost with direct current than with alternating current. The **skin effect**, which pushes alternating current to the surface of the conductor, plays no part with direct current. In long undersea cables, alternating current would simply push a large part of the energy back and forth without delivering it. In addition, HVDC can link power grids that run at different frequencies or not in step. The flow of electricity can also be controlled very precisely.

The **converter stations** are large, complicated and very expensive. That is why HVDC only pays off above a certain length of line. With undersea cables this is the case after a few dozen kilometres, with overhead lines only after several hundred kilometres. Branches for towns along the way are also more difficult than with alternating current. For most short and medium distances, alternating current is therefore still used.

In 1954 the first commercial HVDC link went into operation between the Swedish mainland and the island of **Gotland**. It was built by the Swedish firm ASEA, which merged in 1988 with the Swiss firm BBC from Baden to form **ABB**. Today HVDC undersea cables connect Norway with Germany and Great Britain, for example. Wind farms in the North Sea also send their electricity to land by HVDC. In China there are HVDC lines more than 3000 kilometres long.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that always flows in the same direction, as with a battery.
Current that keeps changing its direction, as in the socket.
A system that turns alternating current into direct current or the other way round.
An electronic switch made of semiconductor material for very large currents.
A power cable laid on the seabed.

gewusst: In the 19th century Thomas Edison and George Westinghouse argued about whether direct or alternating current was better.
A single HVDC undersea cable can carry as much electricity as hundreds of thousands of households need.
The valves in a converter station stand in huge halls as tall as churches.

teile.einleitung: Infrasound is sound with such low notes that humans can no longer hear it. It lies below about 20 hertz. Elephants and whales communicate with it, and volcanoes or earthquakes produce it in large amounts.
wichtigste: Infrasound has a frequency below about 20 hertz.
Low notes are hardly absorbed by the air and therefore travel particularly far.
Elephants also communicate with infrasound over several kilometres.
The blue whale makes very low sounds, some of which are in the infrasound range.
Volcanic eruptions produce strong infrasound.
Humans perceive very strong infrasound as pressure or vibration.
Infrasound monitoring stations around the world check whether nuclear weapons are being tested in the air.
An infrasound note of 10 hertz has a wavelength of 34 metres in air.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of pressure waves, and the number of vibrations per second is called the **frequency**. Humans hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz. Everything below about 20 hertz is called **infrasound**, everything above 20,000 hertz ultrasound. Infra comes from Latin and means below.

Because the vibrations are so slow, the waves are very long. A note of 10 hertz has a **wavelength** of 34 metres at a speed of sound of 340 metres per second, as long as a swimming pool with a diving tower. The air hardly absorbs such low notes, which is why infrasound travels hundreds or even thousands of kilometres. Walls and hills do not stop it well either.

**Elephants** make deep rumbling sounds, some of which lie in the infrasound range. Other elephants pick up these sounds over several kilometres, partly even through their feet as vibrations in the ground. The **blue whale**, the largest animal on Earth, also makes very low sounds that spread far through the sea. Researchers suspect that some birds also use infrasound to find their way.

Volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, avalanches, thunderstorms and strong storms produce powerful infrasound. When Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, the pressure wave travelled round the whole Earth several times. Sea waves and wind over mountain ridges also produce a constant, quiet infrasound noise. Measuring instruments can even use it to detect avalanches in the Alps.

The organisation that monitors the **Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty**, based in Vienna, runs infrasound monitoring stations around the world. They are meant to detect nuclear weapons tests in the air, because an explosion produces a strong infrasound wave. The same stations also record meteors that explode in the atmosphere. Humans perceive very strong infrasound as pressure on the ears or as vibration in the stomach, even though they cannot hear it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
Distance from one wave crest to the next.
Sound that is too high for the human ear.
International agreement that bans all nuclear weapons tests.

gewusst: The pressure wave of the Krakatoa volcano was recorded on barometers around the world in 1883.
Large organs have pipes whose lowest notes are almost in the infrasound range and are felt rather than heard.
The Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013 was recorded by infrasound stations all over the world.

teile.einleitung: The hearing range is the range of pitches that a person or an animal can hear. Young people hear sounds from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. Anything lower or higher stays silent for our ears, but some animals hear much more.
wichtigste: Young people hear sounds from roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
As people get older, the upper limit of hearing falls.
The ear is most sensitive at about 2000 to 5000 Hz.
Dogs hear much higher sounds than people.
The human hearing range covers about 10 octaves.
The threshold of hearing shows how quiet a sound can be at each frequency and still just be heard.
A hearing test, the audiogram, checks how well someone hears.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of vibrations of the air. How often the air vibrates back and forth per second is called the **frequency**, measured in hertz (Hz). The higher the frequency, the higher a note sounds. The **hearing range** tells you which frequencies a living thing can perceive.

Young people hear from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. That is roughly 10 **octaves**, because the frequency doubles with each octave. The lowest note on a normal piano has about 27.5 Hz. The ear is most sensitive at about 2000 to 5000 Hz, where, for example, important parts of speech lie.

With age the upper limit of hearing falls; older adults often hear high sounds only up to 10,000 Hz or less. That is why there are signal tones around 17 kHz that mainly young people can hear. Too much **noise** also damages the ears for good, for example loud music through headphones or at concerts. Ear protection helps to protect your hearing for a lifetime.

Sounds below 20 Hz are called **infrasound**, and sounds above 20,000 Hz are called **ultrasound**. Dogs hear much higher sounds than we do, which is why dog whistles work even though people can hardly hear them. Bats call in ultrasound and find their prey in the dark using the echo. Elephants, on the other hand, communicate over long distances with low infrasound.

In a hearing test the ear doctor plays sounds of different pitch and loudness through headphones. You press a button as soon as you hear something. The result is an **audiogram**, which shows how well you hear each frequency. The level at which a sound just becomes audible is called the threshold of hearing.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often something vibrates per second, measured in hertz.
The unit of frequency: 1 hertz means one vibration per second.
Sounds so high that people can no longer hear them.
Sounds so low that people can no longer hear them.
A curve from the hearing test that shows how well someone hears the different pitches.

gewusst: You cannot hear very low sounds below 20 Hz, but you can sometimes feel them as a vibration in your stomach.
Bats can produce and hear calls of well over 100,000 Hz.
Ultrasound is used in medicine to look inside the body without radiation.

teile.einleitung: The gravitational constant G is a constant of nature that shows how strongly two masses attract each other. It appears in Newton's law of gravitation and has the same value everywhere in the universe. Its value is so tiny that we do not notice the attraction between everyday objects.
wichtigste: The gravitational constant G has a value of about 6.67·10^-11 m³/(kg·s²).
It appears in Isaac Newton's law of gravitation.
Two masses of 1 kg each, 1 m apart, attract each other with only about 6.7·10^-11 N.
G is the same everywhere in the universe, whereas the acceleration due to gravity g depends on the body in space.
In 1798 Henry Cavendish was the first to determine the attraction between masses in the laboratory.
With G you can calculate the mass of the Earth and of other bodies in space.
Compared with other constants of nature, G is known only relatively imprecisely.

abschnitte.text: Newton's **law of gravitation** says that the force between two masses is F = G·m1·m2/r². Here m1 and m2 are the masses and r is the distance between their centres. The number G turns this formula into a real force in newtons. Its value is about 6.674·10^-11, and its SI unit is m³/(kg·s²). That is a zero, a decimal point and then ten more zeros before the first digit 6.

Two masses of 1 kg each that are 1 m apart attract each other with about 6.7·10^-11 newtons. That is much less than the weight of a speck of dust. Two lead balls of 100 kg each, whose centres are 0.5 m apart, attract each other with about 2.7·10^-6 N. Only with huge masses such as planets and stars does **gravitation** become the deciding force. It keeps the Earth, for example, in its orbit around the Sun.

The big **gravitational constant G** and the small **acceleration due to gravity g** are often confused. G is a constant of nature and is the same everywhere, whether in Zurich, on Mars or in a distant galaxy. The acceleration due to gravity g is about 9.81 m/s² on Earth and only about 1.6 m/s² on the Moon. It depends on the mass and radius of the body in space. If you know g, the Earth's radius R and G, you can calculate the Earth's mass with M = g·R²/G; it is about 6·10^24 kg.

Newton knew the law, but not the value of G. In 1798 the English researcher **Henry Cavendish** built a sensitive **torsion balance**. Two small lead balls hung from a thin wire, and large lead balls next to them pulled them very slightly. From the tiny twist of the wire, the force of attraction could be determined. Because this made it possible to calculate the mass of the Earth, the experiment was also called “weighing the Earth”.

abschnitte.titel: Why G is hard to measure
abschnitte.text: Gravitation is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature. Between two protons it is about 10^36 times weaker than their electrical repulsion. That is why even the smallest influences such as air currents or vibrations disturb measurements. Other **constants of nature** such as the speed of light are known much more precisely than G. Researchers all over the world, including at Swiss universities, have measured G again and again with new methods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number in physics that never changes and is the same everywhere.
Newton's rule for how strongly two masses attract each other.
A measuring device in which a thin wire is twisted by the tiniest forces.
One of the four basic forces of nature, such as gravitation or electromagnetism.

gewusst: You and your desk really do attract each other, but this force is far too weak to feel.
Cavendish actually wanted to determine the density of the Earth and found that it is about 5.5 times as dense as water.
Although gravitation is the weakest fundamental force, it shapes planets, stars and whole galaxies.

teile.einleitung: Communicating vessels are containers that are connected at the bottom and open at the top. If you pour a liquid into them, it stands at the same height in all of them, however wide or oddly shaped they are. This simple principle is found in locks, water pipes and even in the trap under the washbasin.
wichtigste: In communicating vessels a liquid at rest stands at the same height everywhere.
The shape and width of the vessels make no difference.
The water level used by builders works on this principle.
The trap under the washbasin uses water to block bad smells.
Locks for ships are also based on communicating vessels.
Water reservoirs are usually higher than the houses they supply.
Different liquids stand at different heights depending on their density.

abschnitte.text: If you connect two glasses at the bottom with a tube and pour water into one of them, it flows across until it stands at the **same height** in both. Such containers are called **communicating vessels**. This is also true if one glass is wide and the other narrow. The reason is that the **pressure** at the bottom must be the same everywhere, and the pressure depends only on the height of the liquid, not on its amount.

Builders fill a long, transparent hose with water to mark two points far apart at exactly the same height. This tool is called a **hose level**. The water stands at the same height at both ends, even if there is a wall or a corner in between. Even the ancient Egyptians are said to have used water in channels to make their buildings level.

A **water reservoir** is usually on a hill, higher than the houses. The water in the pipes wants to rise to the height of the water level in the reservoir, which is why it comes out of the tap under pressure. Under the washbasin is the curved **trap**, a U-bend in which some water always remains. This water blocks off the air from the sewers and keeps bad smells away.

A **lock** raises or lowers ships between two water levels. When a valve is opened, water flows into the lock chamber until the water level is the same as outside. Then the gate can open and the ship can sail on. On the Rhine near Basel, large cargo ships pass through locks like these.

The opening of the spout of a watering can is at least as high as the rim of the can, otherwise the water would run out of the spout before that. In an **artesian well** the groundwater lies under a watertight layer and rises to the surface by itself without a pump, because it is pushed up from a higher area. The water level indicator on some coffee machines and water heaters also works like this.

If you fill a U-tube with two liquids of different **density**, they no longer stand at the same height. If on one side there is a 10 cm column of oil with a density of 800 kg/m³ above the water, the water on the other side stands only 8 cm above the boundary. Mercury is 13.6 times denser than water, so a 13.6 cm column of water is needed to move the mercury level by 1 cm. So lighter liquids stand higher.

begriffe.erklaerung: The surface of a liquid at rest.
A U-shaped bent pipe under washbasins that blocks off smells.
How heavy a substance is compared with its volume.
The pressure in a liquid at rest, which increases with depth.

gewusst: With a hose level you can measure to within a few millimetres even over a distance of many metres.
A narrow and a huge container press equally hard on the bottom if the water is at the same height; this is called the hydrostatic paradox.
